headline: WHITEAWAY'S
text:

Oct. 2nd

from Wales to the effect that in the early hours of the morning a arrangement was made between the miners' leaders and the Ocean Collieries, Rhondda Valley, that the owners consent not to reopen pits until Saturday when the leaders will not interfere with willing workers.

These collieries normally employ 11,000, and it is expected that 60 per cent. will return.—Reuter. Conference Adjourned.

London Sept. 30

The Miners' Delegate Conference has decided to refer the Government's proposals back to the districts, with the request that the vote of the districts be taken and a report made to the adjourned Conference, to be held on October 7.—Reuter.

headline: A YOUTHFUL ROGUE.
text:
A three years' old police record sheet was produced before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning to prove that a Chinese youth had been given nine strokes with a cane for a larceny offence.

Defendant, who had now passed the age I�mit, was sentenced to four week's hard labour this time for stealing a watch and chain valued $4.

Divisional Inspector Blackmanningionized that in pawning the articles defendant gave his proper name, and this led to his arrest. A sum of $2 was found on defendant when he was arrested. His Worship ordered this money to be returned to the complainant to help him to redeem his property.

headline: ON THE FRONTIER
text:
. The "China Mail" learns from an authentic source that the pickets did not leave Samchun yesterday.

The No. 1 in charge of the pickets informed a detective under the Assistant Superintendent of Police, New Territory, yesterday that he is waiting for fresh instructions from Canton and that the pickets will be withdrawn by October 10 at the latest. Two strike pickets were on duty at Lowu (on the Chinese side of the border, near the railway bridge) yesterday afternoon and again this morning.

They have been searching goods and passengers as before.

No pickets have been seen elsewhere on the frontier.

headline: Cook Holds Out for National
text:
Seven nations were represented at the Miners' International Committee convoked to consider international measures to support the British miners. It adjourned till to-morrow without officially issuing any statement.

Messrs. A. J. Cook and Herbert Smith represented Great Britain. It is reported that two currents of opinion developed, firstly, by the General-Secretary, Mr. Frank Hodges, favouring conciliation, and, secondly, by Mr. Cool, who is credited with a desire to continue the strike to obtain a national agreement.

It was early revealed that there is no chance of an international oo! strike. The Germans particularly opposed the idea on the ground that they are obliged under Treaty to export coal to Italy, France, and Belgium on account of reparations.

The British delegate announced that the total subscriptions toward relief of the British miners—$1,250,000—were practically all

It was staked out the export coal to Great Britain as million tons weekly. Some of which emanates from the United States and Poland. Reuter.

headline: NOT USING WHARF YET.
text:
"Not until the boycott is officially finished," was the reply of Mr. John Arnold to-day when asked as to when the Steamboat Co.'s vessels were going alongside the wharves at Canton again.

The “China Mail” asked, in view of Chinese expectations that the Hong Kong, Canton and Macao Steamboat Co., Ltd., will take the lead in “restoring” communications,” would the steamboats go to the wharf instead of anchoring in the stream at Canton.

Mr. Arnold, as secretary, said that the company did not intend to do so until the boycott is actually and officially over.

Nor is there any truth in rumours that the Company has been overhauling the wharves at Canton. "None of the company's officials have been near the wharves for over a year," stated Mr. Arnold.

headline: Thoue who dred with awared of the
text:
Reliable sources in Canton now state that more time has been needed to withdraw the pickets. October 5 is the first date promised, possibly October 10 and even a little later if necessary.

Beyond yesterday's reports there is nothing further to indicate the calling off of more pickets.

To the present state of affairs, Hong Kong can only point out that Mr. Eugene Chen categorically mentioned “on or before October 10 (most probably at the end of September),” while his second communique gave no date, the words reading “that arrangements have been made with the Strike Committee for the termination of the boycott.”

Of course, Mr. Chen qualifies the second statement with:— “To what extent this step will lead to a restoration of Chinese-British trade relations must depend on British policy……”

Actually the boycott has not ended yet as "Strike" activities are still in evidence at Canton itself, not mentioning any outport.

Chinese passengers for Hong Kong can now go unmolested into Shameen, whence they tranship by sampan or motorboat to the Hong Kong steamer. They are not interfered with. On the other hand, passengers going up from Hong Kong leave the boat in the stream and land wherever they can.

headline: TARIFF CONFERENCE PROPOSAL NOW MADE PUBLIC.
text:
In the absence of further information from Canton, speculation has arisen as to the construction to be placed on the two communities from Canton with regard to the termination of the boycott.

An article in Thursday's "Common Gazette" throws light on an intriguing situation but readers who wish to read between the lines must come to their own conclusions.

As it is worded, the introduction to this article in our contemporary indicates that publication is with the approval of the authorities, if not actually at their request.

This point is brought up for a purpose. Not long after the strike began, the Nationalist Government was asked if official recognition was accorded the Strike Executive, the query being based more or less on statements in the "Gazette." A categorical denial followed.

"Quite recently came the two historic despatches. On September 18, Mr. Eugene Chen wrote to the acting British Consul-General that arrangements have been made to end the boycott.....(in the same sentence, without any punctuation) and that the proper Chinese authorities will levy.....&c."

The question that presented itself was: Is the settlement contingent upon these fiscal conditions being put into effect? The Second Communique.

On September 22 the Foreign Office issued the second document which said “arrangements have been made with the Strike Committee for the termination of the boycott.”

In the very next paragraph, the communique says:—“To what extent this step will lead to a restoration of Chinese-British trade relations must depend on British policy and action and on British comprehension of Chinese Nationalism, its ideas and force as a principle of energy in the work of unifying and modernising China.”

This qualification is, perhaps, too broad to define in the space of even a volume. The question that one asks is:—If the boycott ends, on what exactly does restoration of trade depend? On British policy generally, or on any specific point?

The “Canton Gazette” is explicit. It says:—“In view of the Government’s intention to levy a special tax for the primary object of facilitating the settlement of the anti-British strike...” Unless there is a misunderstanding, the only construction to place on this statement—which as pointed out, appears to bear the inspiration of Nationalist Government—is that the new taxes are a measure towards settlement. As the tax has yet formally to be put in force through the agency of the Chinese Maritime Customs (as stated), the primary object to facilitate the settlement of the strike has not yet been achieved. The hoped-for withdrawal of the pickets, the resumption of communications and the return to normal conditions may or may not be separate issues.

The “Canton Gazette” refers to the boycott and liking together, thus:—

In view of the Government's intention to levy a special Consumption tax on imports and luxuries, as well as a Production tax on exports, for the primary object of facilitating the settlement of the Anti-British Strike, and which may serve as a preliminary to the abolition of likin, the Government has decided to make public the following Memorandum "outlining the proposals of the British Delegation to the Tariff Revision Conference in Peking in the matter of compensation in lieu of likin".

Sir James Jamieson's letter to Dr. Wu, which is now published, reads:—

Dear Mr. Wu, I enclose here with a memorandum, outlining the proposals of the British Delegation to the Tariff Revision Conference in Peking in the matter of compensation in lieu of liking, and would be glad if, prior to my departure, you would be so good as to afford me the benefit of your own views and those of your colleagues in the Government with regard thereto.

Is it to be expected that all forms of taxation of foreign goods will be abolished on compensation being paid, and would the Government be prepared to send a representative to sit on the proposed Commission in Shanghai?

I would welcome any suggestions you may have to offer on this or other points connected with the Customs' question generally.

The Memorandum

The memorandum, which is too lengthy and full of technical detail to reproduce in full here, has the following paragraphs which are particularly informative:—

In view of existing political conditions in China, however, the foreign Powers would doubtless require to be satisfied, before agreeing to the levy of the Liking Compensation Tax, that the arrangements made by the Chinese Government for the allocation of the proceeds of the Tax to the Provinces in lieu of liking, and their measures for the abolition of liking, will be carried out with the co-operation of the Provincial Authorities concerned. It should be added that it is assumed in this memorandum that the Chinese Government will levy an Excise (words missing?) will be collected with the concurrence of the Powers concerned on goods manufactured by foreigners in China, on the understanding that the same taxation will be imposed on the same kinds of goods manufactured by Chinese and that satisfactory arrangements will be made (on the lines indicated below) to free such manufactured goods from all further taxation inland.

[The “China Mail” draws attention to the words “will be collected with the concurrence of the Powers concerned.”]

The Likin Compensation Tax will be collected by the Maritime Customs (subject to any other arrangements that may be made in regard to articles of local manufacture, such as wines and tobacco products) simultaneously with the Import Duty or Excise, and the proceeds will be lodged in Banks to be designated by the Chinese Government at Shanghai.

The proceeds of the Likkin Compensation Tax paid on account of goods under inward transit pass will be allocated by the collecting administration, acting on behalf of the Likkin Compensation Committee, direct

southern troops have never been within miles of the town.

What appears to have happened was that local troops mutinied and Marshal Sun Chuan-fang sent up his own men to clean them up, which was done with comparative ease.

Very slowly foreigners in Hankow are coming round to the belief that the fighting qualities of the southern forces have been over-rated, and the same is being said among certain classes of Chinese.

They point out that the Cantonese have never yet had to meet any strong troops, and that most of the towns that have fallen to them have done so by the means of treachery and greed.

Whilst they are admittedly well equipped and well trained, there is likely to be a different tale to tell when they come up against the forces of Marshal Sun, who, as any foreign observer who has seen them willingly admits, are smart and efficient troops, well trained and well disciplined.

Wuchang is still holding out and shows no signs of surrendering. On the contrary all reports go to show that the spirit of the defenders is extremely high and the shortage of food is not so bad as Southern propaganda would have us believe.

The general in charge of the defence appears to be a vigorous and able soldier, and under his guidance a number of sorties have been made from the city as a result of which bodies of Cantonese troops have suffered humiliating reverses and food supplies and animals have been captured.

The negotiations which were previously being conducted are now believed to have been deliberately prolonged by the defending commander in order to stall for time.

The Wuchang garrison is confident that relief will come within the next week or so, either from the north or from Sun Chuan-fang.

Few southern soldiers are to be seen on the river banks below Hankow, and after a very few miles, none at all are to be seen. —“N. C. Daily News.”

headline: A Secondary Object.
parent_headline: TARIFF CONFERENCE PROPOSAL NOW MADE PUBLIC.
text:
It is also interesting to note that a secondary object of the special levy is that it "may serve as a preliminary to the abolition of likin."

Several months ago, the Tariff Conference made certain proposals.

The then British Consul-General in Canton, Sir James W. Jamieson, wrote to Dr. C. C. Wu (who was Mr. Eugene Chen's predecessor at the Foreign Ministry) on March 29. At that time, of course, Canton had not mentioned the settlement of the boycott nor the new taxes. Sir James's communication, enclosing the draft of the proposals, related only to suggested reforms in China's tariff, with a view to abolishing Ilkin

headline: Not Anxious For Peace.
text:
Arrangements are being made between the besiegers and the besieged to allow women and children to evacuate. Wuchang. It is stated that the evacuation will begin to morrow, the refugees being looked after by the Hankow Benevolent Association. In spite of the fact that negotiations for the surrender of the city are continually going on, General Liu Yu-chun does not seem anxious to come to terms with the south. In the meantime there have been no further attacks, while aeroplanes have not been in evidence for the last two days.

Hankow, Sept. 24. Wuchang is still holding out. The proposed evacuation of women and children has not ye eventuated, further disagreement having arisen between the five parties.

headline: Government Attitude.
text:
A meeting of the Executive of the Kuomintang party is announced for October 10, presumably to discuss the boycott settlement.

It is expected that one section of the party will raise strenuous objections but the Government is reported to be firm in its attitude. There is little or no change to report from Canton or other stations.

When the “Lungshan” arrived in Hong Kong yesterday, there were nearly 2,000 Chinese on the Praya waiting to hear the latest news.

Mr. Eugene Chen is reported elsewhere to have declared that the boycott cannot end until Oct. 10 and that this will be effective only if there are no reprisals.

A vernacular paper states that two "outside" river steam boats will be running between Hong Kong and Canton in about five weeks.

headline: STRIKERS TO CONTINUE
text:
Canton Government Considering Proclamation

About the only development of importance during the week-end; in connection with the settlement of the boycott, is a very reliable report that the Canton Government is considering a mandate to call off the strike and to resume communications with Hong Kong.

The “China Mail” also learns that the officials engaged in the task are meeting with difficulties in finding suitable wording for this proclamation.

The strikers, on the other hand, give the impression that they intend to continue, their attitude being one of a “change from the old form of blockade to a new boycott movement.”

Vigilance can be said to have relaxed a little more but strike pickets are still pursuing their activities.

headline: Pensioner Molested.
text:
The Strike Executive (comprising so-called delegates from unions) held a full meeting on September 30 when they passed eight resolutions, the gist of which is given below.

Foreign ships are not allowed to pass the martial law area at Whampoa between the hours of 7 p.m. and 6 a.m.

Last week a pensioner of the Hong Kong, Canton and Macao Steamboat Co., Ltd., entered Shaomeen to draw his pension. As he was leaving, he was brutally dealt with by pickets who put him in a basket and arrested him.

On the other hand, sampan folk are displaying more initiative in intercourse with the Hong Kong steamboats and merchants are still optimistic.

headline: Position Summed Up.
text:
The position can be summed up as:—A minority faction in the Canton Government is still firmly opposed to a settlement. The Government intends to call off the pickets and therefore permit resumption of communications. The real end of the boycott, as pointed out in Saturday's "China Mail" is contingent on the fiscal conditions.

Unofficial views are that Canton will probably have called off all pickets by October 10 or thereabouts and that the strikers will have all been demobilised in four months, during which period, they will still be assisted.

"Although the cordon has been relaxed somewhat, traffic has shown little improvement."

The resolutions passed by the strikers are:—

headline: Strikers' New Policy.
text:
1. In order to consolidate and increase the revolutionary force, the old form of blockade is to be changed to a new boycott movement to be extended to all over the country. Before a satisfactory settlement of the massacre cases of May 30 and June 23, and cancellation of unequal treaties, this new movement will not stop even for a single day. 2. The Strikers agree with the Government to impose the proposed new tax and will urge the Government to enforce the operation of this tax at an early date. But at the same time the Government will be requested to fulfill its word that the proceeds from this tax will be entirely appropriated as subsidies for the strikers and will not be used for any other purpose. 3. headline: MOTOR DANGERS
text:
SEVERAL ACCIDENTS IN

DIVE INTO RIVER.

Several motor accidents occurred during the week-end, none fatal, but a European resident was rather seriously injured while cycling yesterday and now lies in hospital.

Mr. G. H. de Veer of the Netherlands Trading Society had to receive first aid treatment on the road.

At Taipo, a lorry full of passengers and goods dived into the river.

Details follow:

A Dangerous Bend?

Mr. de Veer was on the round-the-island road, going from Stanley towards Shaukiwan. He was on an Indian solo. Taking a bend at an incline, he seemed either to lose control or to have rounded at a faulty angle, with the result that he charged into the embankment. He was thrown off by a violent compact and his left leg was seriously injured above the ankle. Dr. J. K. Milward, a local practitioner, happened to be passing. First aid was rendered by the doctor, who also took Mr. de Veer to hospital.

Mr. de Veer is a sub-accountant in the local office of the Netherlands Trading Society.

A friend of his, who was cycling with him, on another machine, notified the police.

Lorry Through Railways. The incident at Taipo was on Saturday.

About 2.10 p.m., a transport motor lorry (No. 1372) left the market with passengers and merchandise for Fanling. Almost immediately after the start, the lorry crashed through the iron railings on the roadside and dived into the shallow river below, not far from the railway.

Several of the passengers received cuts, none serious.

They were all picked out but the driver of the lorry absconded for fear of the consequences.

Yesterday morning, Mr. John Arnold's car (driven by his Indian chauffeur) accidentally knocked over a Chinese shop coolie (39) in Connaught Road Central, near Douglas wharf, when the man ran right across the road, to foul the front of the car.

The coolie was found to have suffered a compound fracture in the ankle and he was taken to hospital.

Just below the Saiyingpun School was the scene of another accident yesterday.

"If there is any revival of the boycott, Hong Kong will know exactly why.....there could be no longer any pretence of shifting the responsibility. And what it has suited the Canton Government to take off, they must not be allowed to reimpose."

Goodwill & the Future. On Canton—foreign relations the "N. C. Daily News" says:—

headline: REPORTED THREAT OF USING. FORCE IF NECESSARY.
text:
Optimism has not increased with regard to the proposed settlement of the Canton boycott and latest developments point to more difficulties for the Nationalist Government in their attempt to arrive at a solution.

Conditions at Lowu railway station, on the New Territory border are now the same as before, practically the full complement of strike pickets being on duty on the frontier.

Passengers on the Kowloon-Canton Railway are now subjected to the same interference as in previous months.

Fresh difficulties—in addition to opposition by a minority of politicians—are confronting the Canton Government.

One point that may further complicate the issue is the reported demand of the strikers for their share of the projected new taxes.

headline: Eugene Chen's Threat.
parent_headline: REPORTED THREAT OF USING. FORCE IF NECESSARY.
text:
Canton, Oct. 4. Mr. Eugene Chen has informed the strikers that recommendation will be made to the Government to use force against opposition.

Li Cheung-tat, Police "Commissioner, has sent out additional armed patrols to prevent unlawful acts by labourers.

The Seamen's Union has asked that to settle the boycott all men previously employed on ships between Hong Kong and Canton to be reinstated.—Wah Tsz Yat Po. To Last 8 Months.

Besides their claim to an interest in the import, luxury and export levies, the strikers are asking for a Government allocation of $10,000 a month as assistance.

Another request is that the Government, the Strike Executive "and all classes" co-operate to form

employment agencies to facilitate the return to work of strikers, the quota to be 3,000 per month, each man on returning to work to be presented with a $100 bonus by the Government as recognition for the "share in the victory."

This scheme is to last for eight months, it is stated, when the movement will be entirely ended. "Meanwhile, the strikers ask that dormitories and free meals continue as hitherto "until a big scheme can be devised to effect a settlement."

Strikers' Attitude.

Another query that is given by rumour is that strikers are now asking? what about the several millions of dollars allocated by the Government to pay us off? So Shiu-ching, chairman of the Strike Executive, is reported to have expressed their attitude as fully supporting the Government in terminating the strike, present strike institutions will be continued and an interest in the new taxes.

"On the face of things, little has developed" to show which way the wind is blowing.

Each day brings added strength to the opinion that the Canton Government will call off armed pickets to restore communications, but that the real boycott will continue and that the pickets will function under some other name as plain-clothes men.

Shanghai Comment Commenting in an editorial on October 1 (when it was assumed in Shanghai that the Canton boy-cott had terminated), the "N.-C. Daily News" observes:—

“The point to emphasise is that the Canton Government, by calling off the boycott when it suited their purpose to do so, have openly confessed that the boycott was always theirs to maintain or terminate as they pleased. Mr. Eugene Chen's phrase about ‘arrangements with the Strike Committee’ (if possible to-day, why not months ago?) is mere camouflage.

“This is one of the most unblushing admissions of past duplicity that could be found.”

"Hitherto the Canton Government have always pretended that the boycott was the spontaneous expression of a virtuously enraged people, which they were powerless to prevent."

"And more than once negotiators from Hong Kong have been referred to the Strike Committee on the excuse that the affair was none of the Canton Government's."

"All this is now conveniently forgotten on the Cantoness side Not so, however, on the foreign especially in view of the hard!"

headline: Break From the Past.
parent_headline: REPORTED THREAT OF USING. FORCE IF NECESSARY.
text:
"In Canton are numbers of earnest men and women, whose ambitions for their country are worthy of respect, even though their efforts are liable at the outset to go astray and to give an impression of themselves as displeasing as it is really inaccurate."

"And this same nationalist spirit is at work in varying degrees in all parts of China. It is the one source of energy and life to which she can look for the future and foreigners must learn to look to it also....".

"There is something monstrous in the perversity of it all from which one would pain break away to make a new start, forgetting the past and determined only to do the best for the future. It will not be Great Britain's fault if the lifting of the boycott in Canton does not prove the'starting point of a new era.'"

As the “China Mail” explained at the time, there can be no two views on Canton's proposed new taxes, says the “N. C. Daily News”:—

“Acceptance or rejection of this proposal does not depend on Great Britain alone, but is a question for all the Powers. This should clearly be understood.

"No Power could act alone in such a change, without detriment to her nationals; and the full scheme to include abolition of likin necessarily requires the acquiescence of all Powers."

"Speaking generally, we see no reason why they should not agree. The extra taxation is not heavy; not the merchant, but the consumer would pay; and he should not feel it greatly."

Canton's Expensive Failure.

"The question is whether the Powers would be willing to do in one district what they are not yet doing, though they are quite ready to do it, in all China....."

"In all probability the Canton Government realised that, whatever harm it (the boycott) might be doing to Hong Kong, it was a highly expensive failure from Canton's point of view and contributed to a state of lawlessness most undesirable while General Chang Kaf-shek was conducting a life-and-death campaign in the north."

headline: LATEST PIRACY. / H. K. SEAPLANE IN PURSUIT.
text:
The China Merchants S. N. Co.'s s.s. "Hsinfung" has been pirated at Bias Bay.

Only mengre details are to hand at the moment but there seems no room for doubt.

As in the case of the "Kwang Lee" (of the same company), the steamer was on the Shanghai-Canton direct run.

In pre-strike times these boats called at Hong Kong en route, but this port is now omitted.

This morning, the China Navigation Co.'s s.s. "Szechuan" left Hong Kong for Amoy and Shanghai.

She wirelessed back a report that the "Hsinfung" had been seen to be pirated in Bias Bay, that hotbed of pirates in the province of Kwangtung.

On receipt of the message, the local Naval authorities despatched a seaplane to scout over the vicinity and report.

The “Szechuan” also indicated that the pirated steamer was on her way to Hong Kong but the local office of the China Merchants. Co. state that she may go round Hong Kong, direct to Canton, unless there are casualties on board which may need urgent medical attention.

headline: A. Surmise.
parent_headline: LATEST PIRACY. / H. K. SEAPLANE IN PURSUIT.
text:
The "Hstinfung," of course, is of the usual type of China. Merchants steamer. Before the strike, she occasionally called here, but was mostly on the northern runs. Usually she carries six European officers, who are most likely to be British, but there are quite a number of Scandinavians in the company's employ.

The only opinion expressed so far is that the pirates shipped as passengers and followed the old-time modus operandi, subsequently bringing the vessel to Bias Bay to be looted.

Few European passengers travel by this route to Canton.

headline: OFFICIAL DESPATCH.
text:
The following is published by courtesy of the Hong Kong Naval authorities:—

An anti-British demonstration has been planned for tomorrow, Tuesday, but will probably not amount to much.

Southern flags are disappearing in the Chinese city and in the ex-Russian Concession and there is a general feeling that the northerners will be back here shortly.

Heavy fighting is reported between Wang Shih-ko and Hwang-chow; the former is held by the northerners and the latter by the southerners.

It is reported that a big drive towards Nanchang will be made by the southerners to relieve the pressure on Hankow.

General Yang Sen is sending large forces to Ichang and Shash against the southerners.

headline: OUR MARINES LAND?
text:
SEQUEL TO WANHSIEN

Events not unlike those of last year have been repented at Hankow where masses of Chinese threatened to demonstrate in the British Concession.

Fortunately, on this occasion the H.M.'s warslips at that port, and the untoward incident.

The trouble is due to anti-British agitation. Last year mischievous agents "made capital of the Shanghai shooting. This year the agitators point to the events at Wanhsien.

H.M.S. "Hawkins" (flagship of of Admiral Sir E. S. Alexander-Sinclair, commander-chief of the China Fleet) is at Hankow and so is H.M.S. "Despatch," another of the cruisers of the Squadron.

Hankow is a regular port of call of the gunboats of the Yangtse Flotilla and it is believed that at least one or two are there now.

The following is released by courtesy of the Naval authorities n Hong Kong:

Hankow, Oct. 5. A big anti-British meeting took place in Hankow to-day (Tuesday), in connection with the Wanhisen incident.

The procession announced officially their determination to enter the British Concession, but

capture Te-an with from 4,000: 5,000 troops.

This is in the centre of the Kiangsi-Hunan front.

In the northern sector (ie., along the banks of the Yangtse), the northerners had their own way. But as they have been held up at Hwangchow and other points, their claim to have entered Wuchang-hsien (in return for Te-an) is open to doubt.

All this week the “China Mail” has hinted at the Cantonese not being in 'flight, but rather, retiring till a more favourable opportunity.

This startling success by the 7th army has cheered up the tired troops on other sectors and General Chang Kai-shek is reported to have made Nanchang his objective.

Elsewhere the southerners are holding their ground and Sun Chuan-fang is no nearer Wu-chang, if that is his goal.

headline: RONTIER PICKETS / ALLEGED EXCESSES AND ARRESTS.
text:
UNUSUAL PROSECUTION

Alleged to be strike pickets, two Chinese are facing a rather unusual prosecution in the Police Court as a sequel to a shooting incident over the New Territory border.

On the night of September 27, some men were loading a junk with vegetables to be smuggled into Hong Kong.

Armed pickets opened fire and the men dived into the river.

The boat was taken further down the river to strike headquarters.

Alleged to have been instigated by the powers that be, defendants are accused of having taken the vegetables into "Hong Kong for disposal, because "higher prices were obtainable here.

The two complainants in the case also came into Hong Kong—by another route—and traced their cargo.

Are Pickets Wealthy.

Some of it had been sold to market stallholders but no money had been paid over and the goods were perishable.

When the case came before Major C. Willson this morning, Mr. G. R. Haywood appeared for the prosecution and Mr. D. McCallum for the defence. Chief Det.-Inspector T. Murphy was present for the Police.

In a discussion as to ball, Mr. Haywood ventured that if defendants had been pickets for any time, they would have no difficulty in raising the sum ($800 each). Mr. McCallum remarked that there was an "if" there and questioned about a third man—it having been alleged that three pickets were concerned with the incident.

Mr. Murphy declined to say whether the third man was in custody or would be charged. Hearing was to start this afternoon.

headline: BOYCOTT END.
text:
MR. EUGENE CHEN'S PART.

Public Atmosphere "Ready for

attacking and have struck a vital blow at Sun Chuan-fang by capturing Te-an and piercing his lines.

On the other hand, the northerners claim to have occupied Wuchang-hsien, the capital of Hupeh province.

[By Our Special Correspondence.] This game of give and take is hard to explain. For want of a better example, the present situation may be best understood by supposing that a war was on between England and Scotland. Sun Chuan-fang has advanced along the east coast and captured Edinburgh while Chang Kai-shek has come down the west coast and taken Manchester!

Te-an is in Kiangsi province to the north of Nanchang, the capital of one of Sun Chuan-fang's provinces.

General Li Chung-jen (7th southern army), who had difficulty a few days ago in indicating himself from an advanced position, is reported to have broken through the allied line to

right through Hunan and into Hupeh. More recently he has commanded the most northerly wing of the southern army in the Hupeh-Kiangsi front, and Chang Kai-shek has left Hankow, &c. in his hands.

Yesterday - Mr Eugene Chen sent Mr. Wai Yuk (of the Foreign Office) to Shameen to inform the Consuls that the Nationalist Government had come to a definite decision to resume communications between Canton, Hong Kong and other places and that the previous promise will be kept.

Mr. Eugene Chen has informed the Strike Committee that "out of the proceeds of the special new taxes, a sum of $2,000,000 will be applied to relief of strikers and that the Ministry of Finance will take the matter in hand." Wah 'Tsz Yat Po."

headline: Course of Procedure
text:
Authentic news was received last night that the Canton Government is to call off the boycott, officially, at midday on October 10.

The course proposed is attributed to a desire to get the necessary public atmosphere. Pro-Kuomintang organisations will, it is stated, promote a procession on that day, to express support for the Government's decision.

At the east parade ground, the speakers are to include Mr. Eugene Chen and Mr. Chan Shuyan (Head of the Labour Department).

headline: Still a “But”—
text:
officials are said to be working strenuously to remove opposition and lay down the details for the inaugural of the new era.

It is significant that influential bodies are still referring to the termination of the boycott as "the alteration in principal policy" and not as the end of the movement.

The only course now is to wait until the Republican holiday on October 10 and see what developments follow.

Best informed opinion is that the pickets will be demobilised and communications restored but that trade will still be hindered by an under-current of agitation.

headline: CANTON'S VICTORY. / NEARING ALLIED HEADQUARTERS. / BLOW STRUCK AT HEART OF NORTHERNERS' TERRITORY.
text:
Following up their surprise advantage, the southerners are now striking at the very heart of Sun Chuan-fang's territory. Hostilities on three of the four sectors in the Kiangsi front are of little consequence at the moment.

Both sides are concentrating on one part of the front in a desperate struggle and the Cantonese are winning again.

[By Our Special Correspondent.] General Li Chung-yen (of Kwangsi), who commands the 7th Nationalist Army, is the Cantonese hero of the hour.

Before embarking on the northern expedition, this 7th Army had little experience of warfare. Whether it is due to the inspiration of victory, or to Russian strategy, these hitherto untrained troops have brought off the coup of the present war.

Along the Yangtse, the allies had one column marching on. Wuchang until held up at Hwangchow. An armistice has been declared on this sector, it is reported.

Squeezed in Between. The centre column was making overland for Changsha and Yo-chow to cut the Cantonese line of communication. This is now in hilly country near Shaoshui. The southern column, after retaking Nanchang from the Nationalists had marched out to Kao-an and fought two battles. In between the northern and centre sectors, General Li Chungen stole up to an advanced position, met difficulty in extricating himself, and then surprised Te-an.

Northerners Withdrawn. He has only about 5,000 troops with him. Unless there is an allied debacle, there is no immediate prospect of other southern de-tachments joining hands with him.

Nevertheless, General Li has deflected northwards, leaving Nanchang to colleagues further south, and is making for Kiukiang where he hopes to catch Sun Chuan-fang's headquarters unawares.

Several engagements have been fought by this mobile division of the 7th army and the northern allies are falling back.

To stem the advance of General Li, Sun Chuan-fang is bringing back his men posted along the Yangtse.

On Way to Success. Shoud Kiukiang fall, the Canonese will then have accomplished the first big step towards sub- uing the “allied 5 provinces.”

Sun Chuan-fang still has the territorial advantage. His centre and southern columns can both wheel round and attack Gen. Li from the rear. But as they are also facing. an enemy on their front they show no immediate desire to take this step.

"The allies seem to be relying on the troops being withdrawn from advanced positions along the Yangtse who—it is expected—will return down river, land, and make a stand at or near Kiukiang."

headline: At Wuchang.
parent_headline: CANTON'S VICTORY. / NEARING ALLIED HEADQUARTERS. / BLOW STRUCK AT HEART OF NORTHERNERS' TERRITORY.
text:
The siege of Wuchang continues unabated.

Yesterday and today more non-combatants were allowed to leave the city, including several foreigners, while it is understood that similar facilities are being extended for the next several days.—Reuter.

March to Nanchang. " Han Plow Oct

It is reported that the southerners have commenced a fresh and more powerful drive to Nanchang, under the personal direction of General Chang Kai-shek.

Despite assurances to the contrary, steamers are again being subjected to rifle fire, this time in the vicinity of Hwangchow.

Two Japanese steamers arrived yesterday, and Messrs'. Butterfield and Swire's "Shengking" to-day, badly riddled, though, fortunately, there were no casualties.—Reuter.

headline: PICKETS STILL AT SAMCHUN
text:
Dictator Said to be Keen on "Settlement."

ل

General Chang Kai-shek, the virtual dictator of the Canton Government, is reported to have cabled back that he may return before October 10 if his presence is imperative.

Rumour says that the present leaders in Canton have cabled the commander-in-chief who is preoccupied with a momentous struggle in Kiangsi. But if the settlement can only be achieved by his being on the spot he may return.

There is no change to report except that an improved tone continues, following the Canton Government's statement that communications will be restored after October 10.

Strike pickets are still on duty at Samchun (across the New Territory border), examining the usual quota of from 100 to 200 passengers who travel daily on the railway between Canton and Kowloon.

No indication has been noticed of a general withdrawal of pickets to Canton from outports for the promised demobilisation.

A message from Canton states that Mr. Eugene Chen, the Foreign Minister of the Canton Nationalist Government has informed the (British?) Consul at Shameen that his Government has now definitely decided to resume communication between Canton and Hongkong in pursuance of the intention to terminate the boycott.—British Wireless Service. A combined meeting has been held between representatives of all classes and the Strike Committee.

It was resolved that after communications between "Canton and Hong Kong" had been restored, an organisation be formed to promote the development of Chinese products.

Another decision arrived at was that the Strike movement would be withdrawn but that other bodies would be formed to assist trade and protect labour—"Wah Tsz Yat Po."

The "New Boycott"? A series of resolutions were adopted at the 166th meeting of the Strikers' Representatives Committee at which it was claimed that 700 representatives and over 1,000 visitors were present.

Mr. Kam Nai-kwong of the Kuomintang and Mr. Tang Chung-ha of the All-China Labour Union spoke about new strike tactics.

It will be noticed that stress is laid not on the boycott being settled but on a transformation of policy!

headline: DOMESTIC LEVY: BUT CUSTOMS CO-OPERATION WANTED.
text:
〣〣〣〣〣

Further concrete evidence is available as to Canton's intention to terminate the boycott, it being now revealed that the new taxes will be collected unless the Powers intervene.

The Nationalist Government chooses the obvious date of Oct. 11 for the levy to commence.

Reading between the lines it appears that Canton is particularly desirous of working through the Maritime Customs. But should facilities not be forthcoming, the Government will use their own organisation.

The Canton Information Bureau has issued an important communique through Reuter:—

The acting Minister for Foreign Affairs has addressed an identic note to each of the local representatives of the Foreign Powers whose nationals are in trading relation with Liang Kwang provinces.

“I have the honour to communicate to you the following translation of a mandate issued by my Government on October 4:—(1)—The Ministry of Finance is hereby instructed to levy a temporary internal tax on the consumption or the production of such articles as are the subject of trade between the Liang Kwang provinces and the other provinces in China and foreign countries.

(2)—The rate of taxation shall be equivalent to half the usual Maritime or Native Customs tariff (as the case may be) on general articles and to a full tariff on articles of luxury such as silk, silk-stuff, toilet articles, fur and leather articles of decoration, 'gems' and precious stones and similar goods. Cigars, cigarettes, imported wines, kerosine and gasoline, which are the subject of other special taxes, are exempt from this tax. (3)—The Ministry of Finance, for purposes of convenience, may collect such taxes at or near the various Maritime and Native Customs barriers and is instructed to make detailed regulations governing the collection of the said tax.

(4) —Any person selling or buying or otherwise dealing with articles on which the said tax has not been paid shall be liable to a term of imprisonment not exceeding three years and/or a fine equivalent to the times the value of the article or articles which shall also be confiscated.

(5)—This mandate shall come into effect on October 11, 1926.

"It seems desirable to emphasise the fact that the new tax is in principle an internal tax to be distinguished from the imposts levied as Customs duties under the Chinese Maritime Customs system. There is, of course, no intention to interfere with the latter as at present administered, though possible misunderstanding and friction would be avoided if Maritime Customs co-operation should be available in the collection of the new tax by fiscal authorities to be appointed by my Government."

headline: Picket Activities to Cease on
parent_headline: DOMESTIC LEVY: BUT CUSTOMS CO-OPERATION WANTED.
text:
With only a few more days to go, there now seems little doubt that the Canton Government will succeed in calling off the pickets whose activities are expected to cease on Monday at the latest.

Merchants in Canton predict that the restoration of communications will be slow as the majority of the populace will hesitate for a few days at least before openly resuming trade.

Strike pickets at Namtau and Samchun are gradually returning to Canton by railway to-day.

The Strike Executive has appointed Mr. So Shiu-ching (chairman) to receive $50,000 from the Finance Ministry as the first funds to mobilise (or re-organise) the pickets. The Strike Committee is expected to have completely dispersed by three months.

General Chang Kai-shek, in a telegram to General Li Chai-sum (at Canton), inter alia, instructs General Li to complete the strike settlement rapidly.

The Foreign Office intends to publish a history of the Strike movement for circulation abroad and internally.—Wah Tsz Yat Po.

headline: Kongmoon Favourable.
parent_headline: DOMESTIC LEVY: BUT CUSTOMS CO-OPERATION WANTED.
text:
[From Our Own Correspondent.] Reikki Konomm. Oct. 5.

An order has been given by the mayor of Kongmoon city to the police at Pakkai (the port of Kongmoon) that British mercantile vessels are to be protected from molestation when such steamers arrive in port, or at any time after October 1.

All strike pickets here are expected to go to Canton on Friday, October 8 (to-day).

Information concerning the probable arrival of Hong Kong steamers has been favourably received. —By courtesy of the Naval authorities.

The "Kung Sheung Yat Po" also reports relaxation of picket activities at Namtau (Deep Bay), which is near the New Territory border, and to which three Hong Kong ferries run every day.

This vernacular paper predicts the formation of a Nationalist S.S. Co. (in which a prominent official is reported to be interested) with steamers plying between Canton, Swatow, Shanghai, Pakhol and Holhow and that the concern will receive a subsidy from the Canton Government.

text:
GARAGE EMPLOYEE'S STOLEN GOOD

Det.-Sergeant Carey said that these were the articles he had helped himself to when he obtained leave from his employers to return to the country. The total value of the stolen goods found in defendant's bag as he was boarding a boat for Macso was given at $150. Defendant was sentenced to six

headline: MORE DISORDER / NAVAL LANDING AT HANKOW.
text:
FOREIGNERS SURROUNDED.

Latest developments on the upper Yangtse, from the point of view of anti-British agitation following the Naval engagement at Wanhsien, are reported in the following despatches published by courtesy of the local authorities:

It is reported that Mackenzie's compound has been surrounded by agitators and the disorderly element and that all the native staffs and most house employees (or British subjects?) have left; but it was expected that the (Chinese?) officials would take steps to reduce the agitation.

H.M.S. "Mantis" and H.M.'s armederd mérchantman "Kiawo" arrived to-day.

H.M.S. "Widgeon" left Wanhien his morning for Chungking. Hankow, Oct. 7.

A big anti-foreign demonstration is scheduled for October 10 (the National Day of the Republic). No disturbance is anticipated but as a precautionary measure Naval forces are being landed in the Concession to-morrow (Friday) and will remain ashore over the weekend.

headline: MUST BE REBUILT.
text:
Reasons for Choosing Adjacent

Relative to the Government's decision to rebuild the Government Civil Hospital on the lawns adjoining the present site, a "China Mail" representative had an interesting interview yesterday with Dr. J. B. Addison, Principal Civil Medical Officer.

Our representative asked Dr. Addison whether, in view of the expense which would be incurred in erecting a new building, the present building could not be adapted to the changing needs or, in the event of a new building being necessary, was not a site in a more reserved and less noisy neighbourhood preferable?

It appears that the present building is considered by the Public Works Department to have "come to the end of its life" and that, to continue to pay out on alterations, renovations and other maintenance items would in the long run be an uneconomic policy. Similarly, from the medical point of view, it is felt that the only permanent solution to the problem of providing adequate accommodation and facilities is in the erection of a new building.

As regards the vicinity of the Hospital and the question of whether it was a desirable one, Dr. Addison said that undoubtedly it was extremely handy for the poorer classes of Chinese with whom they were very largely concerned. Again, the Hospital was in a far more convenient place as regarded the University for students of which the Hospital provided a valuable training ground.

By utilising a site in the vicinity for the new Hospital there would be a considerable saving in other ways, it was further pointed out. The enlarged sisters' quarters would still be available as would the present "A" block, which would be re-adapted as servants' quarters, and the present operating and X-ray room which would be the new stewards' quarters. The site of the present Government Civil Hospital will be used partly as an open space or gardens and partly for providing sites for residences.

The work of building the new Hospital is calculated to take three years. It will have greater accommodation all round, including more European wards; and will be designed to meet the more pressing

needs of the Colony since the present Hospital was erected, some 60 years ago.

headline: MINERS AT SEA.
text:
EXECUTIVE IN A QUANDARY.

The Miners' Delegate Conference, this morning, decided to take no immediate action on the South Wales resolution, but to refer it to the districts for ratification.

The resolution of the Miners' Delegate Conference yesterday, in favour of intensifying the coal dispute, imposes a difficult task upon the Miners' Executive. It is generally agreed that if instructional are given immediately to withdraw the safety men the response will be doubtful. "Anyhow the Miners' Federation controls only a proportion of safety men. In other organisations the safety men, including those of the South Wales Colliery dad Craftsmen's Association comprising sixty per cent of the safety men of South Wales, have already announced that they will remain at work. It is pointed out that the Federation has already vainly tried to secure an embargo on the import of foreign coal and the Trades Union Congress has decided that to make a levy on other Unions is impracticable.—Reuter.

At the resumed 'conference of the miners' delegates to-day the programme decided upon on the previous evening was considerably modified.

Extreme measures, including the withdrawal of safety men, had been

passed by a majority after much discussion and a division of opinion, and at to-dry's meeting ways and means of carrying out these measures were to have been discussed.

Instead of giving instructions that they should at once be put into operation, however, the conference referred the matter to the districts with a recommendation that the results of local decisions should be in the hands of Federation officials next Thursday.

The newspapers point out that the withdrawal of safety men has consistently been opposed by the Secretary of the Federation, Mr. A. J. Cook, and its President, Mr. Herbert Smith, and on Tuesday last the Vice-President, Mr. Richards, spoke strongly against the proposal, whilst moderate men of the Federation have frankly recognised that it was a mistake of the 1981 strike.

Although in certain areas the Federation claims to control 85 per cent. of the safety men, in others 65 per cent. of the men engaged in this work belong to other Unions, which have definitely declined, to accept the withdrawal policy: The “Manchester Guardian” points out that the Federation has no power to carry out the other proposals of yesterday's resolutions—an embargo on foreign coal, a levy on other Trade Unions, and the cessation of outcrop working.

headline: PICKETS STILL AT SAMCHUN.
text:
Perhaps the "good news" that the majority have been waiting for—in connection with the termination of the boycott—has come.

The manager of the Tung On S.S. Co. signified to the "China Mail" this morning that it was proposed to send up the U.S. "Sai On" on Tuesday to Canton, after an absence of over a year.

The "Sai On" will anchor in the stream and the management intend to wait a few days before using the company's wharf at Canton.

A few days ago, Mr. John Aurlold, secretary, Hong Kong, Canton and Macao Steamboat Co., Ltd., informed the "China Mail" that the wharves would possibly be in use a week after the official end of the boycott.

headline: Pickets Report.
text:
It is also gathered that another "outside" company is sending up a boat on Tuesday. This is the "Kwong Sai," due to leave Hong Kong on Tuesday night and thereby resuming the night-boat service.

The “Charles Hardouin” and “Paul Beau” are not ready yet. Vengels on the Hong Kong-Wu-

Pickets are still on duty at Samchun. These have informed employees of the British section, Kowloon-Canton airway, that they are waiting for midday tomorrow when they hope to receive an order to return to Canton.

headline: The New Taxes
text:
Sáys. the “Canton Gazette”:—

"On Sunday, October 10, the General Strike which was started against British Imperialism and its Colony in consequence of the May 30 and June 23 Massacres will be definitely called off. "Shipping communication with Hong Kong will no longer be interfered with by the Strike pickets.

"The Government will issue a declaration for the information of the people."

"The Ministry of Finance has been engaged in making the necessary arrangements for the collection of the special tax on imports and luxuries as well as the production tax. It is hoped that the special collectorate will be ready to function immediately after the termination of the strike."

One Chinese case of enteric fever (typhoid) was reported to the Medical Officer of Health on Friday.

It is ordered that a valuation of the tenements in the Colony for the year commencing July 1, 1927, shall be made before April 30, 1927, or as soon thereafter as may be.

headline: BOYCOTT END. / PICKETS NOW ALL WITHDRAWN.
text:
INDICATIONS OF OFFICIAL SETTLEMENT AS PROMISED.

Strike pickets at Canton and out-stations were all withdrawn yesterday as previously indicated by the Kwangtung Government. Latest reports from all sources point to the first step of settlement having been effected smoothly.

The lack of information as to any definite official declaration of the calling off of the boycott led to a little pessimism this morning as to the eventual outcome of the movement for settlement in Canton. The “China Mail” gathered this morning from a reliable source that a special National Day issue of the “Canton Gazette” yesterday, contains an announcement calling off the boycott, signed by members of the Central Council of the Kuomintang.

The declaration refers to strengthening the "anti-imperialistic" movement without defining "such" however. Yesterday's procession to the East Parade "ground passed off peaceably, the nature of the speeches being unknown at present.

From the same source it is gathered that the pickets' examination shed is in process of demolition. This is on the Bund, near the Customs building and the Hong Kong steamboat wharves. A gradual resumption of trade is regarded as a certainty, its volume being dependent on the measure of sincerity placed in the latest developments by the ship owners and merchants.

More people are now travelling from Hong Kong to Canton than, say, a fortnight ago. The last reports from Canton were that the city was quiet.

As regards the imposition by the Canton Government of a Customs surtax, the Diplomatic Body has agreed on the whole either to decline to comply with or to lodge a protest against the proposal of the Canton Government, in view of the fact, however, that for some reasons, the attitude of the British Government is somewhat ambiguous, the Diplomatic

Body has not yet definitely manifested its attitude.—“Toho.”

A plea for better relations between the Chinese Kuomintang and the British Government was made by Comdr. Kenworthy, M.P., speaking at the dinner of the Kuomintang Society in London. He said the talk about the Kuomintang being under the thumb of Russia was all nonsense. It represented organised Liberal and Progressive opinion, working for the restoration of the Chinese constitution and parliament, and was bound to triumph finally, because democracy always triumphs over dictatorship.—Reuter. [By Our Special Correspondent.]

headline: When Pickets Left.
parent_headline: BOYCOTT END. / PICKETS NOW ALL WITHDRAWN.
text:
Private advice down from Euroropean quarters in Canton indicate that there is no sign of the Canton Government's order being ignored.

Pickets were not to be seen yesterday" afternoon but as no boat for Hong Kong has left since noon yesterday it is not possible to say whether the strikers have definitely withdrawn.

From inquiry made at the frontier, the “China Mail” learns that the strike pickets posted at Sam’s churn, on the Chinese side of the New Territory border, left for Canton by the last train yesterday evening. They ceased activities at midday and the last withdrew about 2 p.m.

At the time of going to press, the fast train from Canton had not come through. "This morning, however, there was no interference at Lowu bridge whatsoever.

headline: Strikers Praised.
parent_headline: BOYCOTT END. / PICKETS NOW ALL WITHDRAWN.
text:
On account of yesterday's holiday, the local Chinese papers did not come out this morning. "Extras" were issued, all indicating that the termination of the boycott had been effected as promised.

There is no likelihood of celebrations among the Chinese in Hong Kong at least until news is brought back that river steamers are going alongside the wharves at Canton, unmolested. But the general tone is that "the past should be forgotten" so that firecrackers and other forms of thanksgiving are not expected.

The Kuomintang has addressed an open letter to the Strike Committee, expressing admiration for the service performed and explaining the Canton Government's change in policy. The Kuomintang earnestly requests the strikers to conform. Large matsheds are being erected in and near Canton for the returning nickets.

headline: Favourable Reports.
parent_headline: BOYCOTT END. / PICKETS NOW ALL WITHDRAWN.
text:
From other stations there are also favourable reports.

Between Mira Bay and Bias Bay (including the border village of Shataukok)—territory under Commander Lo Kwan, there are no pickets.

At Deep Bay—ports of Nam Tau, Hau Hoi, etc.—there are also no pickets but there is no trade owing to the absence of direct communication.

Two trains still run between Hong Kong and Canton daily.

An official of the Chinese Kuowloon administration, Canton-Kowloon Railway, is coming down to see Mr. H. P. Winslow, manager of the British section, to arrange about the resumption of the through train service.

headline: COSTLY "SMOKES" / THEFT FROM EUROPEAN STORE.
text:
EURASIAN JAILED.

A Eurasian by the name of George Clayson was charged before Major C. Wilson at the Central Magistracy this morning with the theft of a quantity of cigarettes valued at $17.

Defendant pleaded guilty to the charge.

Det.-Sergeant Carey in giving the facts of the case said that the defendant went into the store of Messrs. Donnelly and Whyte on Thursday and stating that he was a seafarer asked the salesman for 1,000 Kensitas cigarettes. While the salesman held the package in his hand and turned round to fetch some bottles of whisky which was then asked for, defendant snatched the package and ran down the street. He was chased and caught by a Chinese/constable.

A record being produced to show a previous conviction for the first one year ago, defendant via sentenced to one month's hard labour.

headline: ANTI-BRITISH BOYCOTT.
text:
In connection with the Wanhsien incident, the Chinese Government is reported to have decided to submit three demands, namely:

Reservation of right to claim damages.

Punishment of responsible persons on the part of the British Navy.

And guarantee for non-recurrence of such incidents, on the part of the British Government. It is reported also that should the demands be not accepted by the British Government the Chinese Government will declare the cancellation of all unequal treaties concluded between China and Great Britain, and issue orders to all the Provincial authorities to enforce control over the navigation of British men-of-war in Chinese rivers.

A big anti-foreign demonstration is planned for October 10. The Concession is well guarded and all precautions have been taken. The boycott at Chungking is serious and difficulties are arising as to food and supplies for the gunboats and the British community.

Some women and children are evacuating Chengtu, where a serious boycott is expected, and, it is feared that a general evacuation will be necessary.—Naval Despatch.

The local N.K.K. offices received a telegram from Hankow to the effect that the Company's vessel "Suiyang Maru" was riddled by bullets fired by the southern troops about noon last Sunday (Oct. 2) when sailing downstream off Huangchow. B. and S.'s, "Ta Tung" is reported to have also become a target of fire by the southern troops at the same spot.—"Shanghai Mercury."

headline: ARMISTICE MOVES.
text:
Since the occupation of Nanchang and Tayeh, by the Allied forces, leading merchants in the Wu-Han district, fearing the district may possibly be involved, have been making strenuous efforts to bring about an armistice, acting in cooperation with the peace missions from Klangsu and Chekiang Provinces.

It is rumoured that owing to conflict of views between General Chang Kai-shek and General Tang Sang-chee, the latter intends coming to terms with the Allies independently.—Toho.

To restore peace in Hupeh, negotiations between Marshal Sun Chuan-fang and General Tang Seng-chee are now being conducted at Hankow through the good offices of leading Chinese merchants.

It is reported that Gen. Tang Sang-chee (commanding 7th Nationalist Army) is dissatisfied with his position in the southern army and has made overtures to Marshal Sun Chuan-fang.

It is also reported that Marshal Chang Kai-shek has gone to Canton owing to the situation there.

Wuchang has capitulated, and it is probable that this is not unconnected with Gen Tang's alleged defection.—Naval Despatch

headline: IMPROVEMENT AT CHUNGKING.
text:
There were large processions in Hankow yesterday (Sunday) but these were diverted by Chinese troops and were prevented from entering the Concession without difficulty. There was no disturbance of any kind. H.M.S. "Cockechafers!" the s.s. "Wantung" and s.s.s. "Wanhsien" have arrived in Hankow. They have come from up the five following the negotiations which followed the taking possession of the two B. and S. boats by General Yang Sen.

Chungking is, quieter. Supplies have been obtainable during the last two days and local officials have promised to afford protection. The outlook in Szechuan province is, however, uncertain at present.

Chungking is the last British trenty port up the Yangtse., in Szechuan province, and has suffered much as the result of intense feeling among the Chinese following the Wanhien incident, demonstrations having been held outside foreign residences, which were threatened, and hillside bungalows had to be hurriedly evacuated by foreign residents.

There have been a few cases of desultory firing at passing ships at Shasi and Hwangchow.—Naval Descatch.

[Shasi is further up than Hawkow and Hwangchow below. "Both ports are believed to be held by the southerners.]

The "Wanhsen, " arrived back in port a few days ago, Her Chief Officer Mr. Johnstone, and Chief Engineer Mr. Kerr went up to Kueifu for her and brought her down.

General Yang's Sen made use of her as he did of the "Th Ling" an American ship, and of three flying the French flag, to bring down what looks more like a horde of roughs than what they claim to be—soldiers. They were from Kuéifu and Wushan only.

The main army, following Yang Sen are said to be coming down from "Wanhsien," but just to-day news has come through that the troops favouring the south have started to attack Yang Sen, so they may be kept nearer home.

"The 'Wanhsien' shows much evidence of the attack made on her, and like, the 'Wantung' much sign of wanton destruction."

The British gunbouts "Mantis," "Teal" and "Widgeon" accompanied by the "Kiawo" have left for up river. A rise in the river made it possible for the larger of the gunbouts to go up. The "Bee," with Rear Admiral Cameron on board, the "Cricket," and the "Cockchafer" are still here. Mr. A. P. Slunt; the British Consul for Teang, has gone up river on the "Mantis" to continue the negotiations over the "Wanhsien" attack. There is much fear amongst the Chinese that, if Yang Sen arrives here with his army, he will go no farther.

The Chamber of Commerce has already raised $100,000; and now a similar sum is demanded.—N. C. Daily News.

headline: Slow Improvement.
text:
Conditions at ports on the upper Yangtse, recently swept by serious anti-British demonstrations which led to the evacuation of Chungking by the British community are reported to be slowly improving, according to reports received in Shanghai yesterday.

Anti-British agitation is reported to be still proceeding but no serious incident is reported.—“Shanghai Times.”

headline: And Then Worse?
text: The position of the foreigners in Szechuan has become worse. A rigid anti-British boycott in Chungking and Wanhsen is being maintained by agitators who are striving to extend a similar boycott to Chengtu and elsewhere. Chinese are also threatening the missionaries at the mission stations in various cities in Szechuan, particularly in Chengtu—Reuter.

headline: CANTON'S MANIFESTO / BOYCOTT SETTLED: BUT STRIKE NOT OVER! / PRESENT KUOMINTANG POLICY DEFINED.
text:
Blockade of Hong Kong Given Up—Intensified Struggle Continues. NATIONALIST GOVERNMENT SILENT: PICKET & COMMITTEE TO REMAIN.

A long official announcement by the Canton Government makes two statements of fact which are of the utmost importance from the point of view of “settlement of the boycott.” These are:—

A bureau of the government (the Canton Information Bureau) says categorically:—the Strike Committee called off the boycott.

In a declaration, the Strike Committee emphasises:—Therefore, we cannot say that the Canton and Hong Kong strike is settled.

The Nationalist Government has issued no proclamation.

The Kuomintang declaration lays stress on:—the giving up of the policy of direct boycott and the blockade of Hong Kong. But this same declaration, in a mass of political and other utterances, gives prominence to "intensification of the struggle against Imperialism." It is noteworthy that the Strikers specifically refer to Hong Kong and the Kuomintang does not.

Latest reports on the situation to-day appear below, revealing the effect of Sunday's decision.

headline: OFFICIAL MANIFESTO.
text:
The following despatch has been sent by the Canton Information Bureau (a Government institution), via Reuter:—

"At a great gathering at the East Párade ground yesterday at noon the Strike Committee called off the boycott."

In this connection two Declarations have been issued:—one by the Strike Committee and the other by the Kuomintang addressed to the general body of Hong Kong and Canton strikers.

The Nationalist Government has issued no statement, the boycott being a patriotic popular movement under the leadership of the Strike Committee as the elected executive of the general body of the strikers.

The general sense of the Declarations is that though the specific struggle which has found expression in the boycott was directly caused by the Shanghai massacre of May 30 and the Shameen-Shakee massacre of June 23, the same is but a part of the general nationalist struggle against imperialism. Owing to fundamental change in the national situation brought about by an extension of Nationalist power and influence to the Yangtse, there is necessity to change the technique of the specific struggle and to resort to a new policy as well as to propaganda in order to make the people of the whole country realise the semi-colonial status of China and lead them to join the active anti-imperialist movement whose nim and purpose is the liberation of Nationalist China from unequal Treaties and the redress of wrongs.

After a review of the national revolutionary movement in China the Kuomintang Declaration to the strikers emphasises that "the giving up of the policy of direct boycott and the blockade of Hong Kong" (which is a specific struggle) does not mean the cessation of the general struggle of Chinese Nationalism against Imperialism but its intensification "on a national scale until the independence of China is completely secured." Argument is developed by comparing Kwangtung to "one" wing of a wide front and this one wing has advanced, very far while the rest of the front is not yet in a position for a similar advance.....Kwangtung.

Therefore, although successful in the anti-imperialist struggle is arresting its advance in order to concentrate its efforts in different directions in accordance with a new policy.

[Note: The above sentence is obviously mutilated in" transmission.]

Victory, Not Defeat. This policy which is now being arried out with the same spirit of self-discipline and self-sacrifice as as the advance is not a defeat, but great victory.

What is the new policy? Briefly, it means to consolidate the revolutionary base in Kwangtung, in other words, to consolidate the people's movement and make it a base for political and economic development, to improve local and provincial administration, to build ports and roads, to improve the living conditions of the workers, peasants, teachers, merchants, etc., to destroy banditry and make the political liberties of the people secure—all this means to make the national revolutionary base in Kwangtung so

strong that no aggression by imperialists could affect us. About the Future.

But this is not all. The new policy means a widening and strengthening of the National revolutionary base in other Provinces so that they can join in the active anti-imperialist front. The new policy means that much effort must be used in the re-establishment and strengthening of the people's organisations throughout the country and in securing revolutionary provincial and district government in the places which have already been occupied, or will be occupied in the future. When all this is done, then the anti-imperialist front will become unshakable and its final victory asquared. Then the independence and liberty of China and the welfare of the suffering masses will be secured.

In the "declarations of the Strike Committee after referring to the decision to "withdraw voluntarily all our pickets from various parts at 12 o'clock noon on October 10," they "solemnly declare to the public that we recognise the new policy as most suitable to our modern revolutionary environment and as the most

headline: CONDITIONS. FULFILLED.
text:
On arrival of the China Navigation steamboat "Fatshan" here to-day, she "anchored in the stream.

Passengers went ashore and cargo was landed without interference.

All examiners (of the Strike organisation) have been withdrawn from boats plying between Canton and inland ports and cargo is now released. directly after examination by the Maritime Customs—" Wah Tsz. Yat Po."

headline: Strike Not Settled.
MUCH IMPROVEMENT.
text:
The boycott has been publicly announced at an and the Strike Committee have issued a proclamation to this effect.

Chinese are returning to duty with their former employers and the situation is much improved.

Arrangements are now being made for a general resumption of trade and business, but movements and berthing of steamboats are handicapped due to the sifting up of wharves during the strike.

Processions and demonstrations on Sunday, October 10, passed off peacefully.—Naval Despatch.

Strike pickets have been withdrawn but, pending the return of two delegates sent to Canton to ascertain the position. the boycott is being continued, and no employees of British are yet allowed to return.—Naval Despatch.

headline: CONDITIONS TO-DAY.
text:
Hundreds of Chinese stood on the Praya this morning to see if it was true that communications had been resumed with Canton.

In addition to British shipping movements recorded below, the Tung On S.S. Co.'s "Sai On" left this morning.

There was no flourish of trumpets when the long-missed prodigal set off—after a year's exile on the Hong Kong-Macao run.

She carried between 200 and 300 passengers but no cargo. So soon as the "Tung On" comes out of dock, she will join her sister ship.

On inquiry from the management the “China Mail” was informed the “Sri On” would act on instructions from the British Consul General in Canton as to whether they should go alongside their own wharf or anchor in the stream.

They had also heard that the river near the wharves had silted in the interval. (Note: This is confirmed by a despatch published by courtesy of the Naval authorities). As yet no other "outside" boat has resumed the run. The "Kwong Tung's" owners wish to take up the night trip but are waiting for information as to the examination regulations—during the night—on account of martial law below Whampoa. (Continued on Page 7)

headline: TRADE RESUMING. / ADDITIONAL STEAMERS TO CANTON WITH MERCHANDISE.
text:
Further definite steps have been taken to resume traffic with Canton, following the settlement of the boycott.

Reports, on the whole, are not unfavourable:

In spite of the atmosphere of obscurity—as to their policy in future—created by the Strike Committee and the Kuomintang, belief is gaining ground that's a revival of trade will speedily follow the calling off of the boycott.

Actual figures show no immediate improvement. Merchants attribute this to Chinese characteristics and to the necessity of one transaction going through so many hands before completion.

Only from Swatow is there a report that pre-settlement conditions prevail. The pickets have left for (Canton but the local) strike executive is still intimidating.

headline: Spirit of Hope.
parent_headline: TRADE RESUMING. / ADDITIONAL STEAMERS TO CANTON WITH MERCHANDISE.
text:
Elsewhere there is nothing to contradict the spirit of hopefulness that has set in:

Discussion has been on three lines, viz., (1) whether both communications and trade will be fully restored; (2) whether if Canton does not collect the temporary surtaxes the boycott will be enforced again, and (3) if encouragement will be given to anti-British agitators to continue a trading boycott while communications are left unmolested.

Should the settlement be allowed to take its course, it is estimated that it will be a week at least before cargo, hitherto forbidden, is moving freely again.

Waiting for Dealers.

Take imported manufactures, for instance. It is not the foreign hong that ships cargo either on consignment or on own account to Canton for disposal. To send up for storage in foreign godowns would not be much use.

Dealers in Hong Kong—who hold stocks of some sort—have either to ship up old lots, or take delivery from importers and send the goods to connections in Canton who, in turn, place them on the market.

Until instructions come down from Canton dealers, the local native merchant cannot make things move. And the man in Canton prefers, to wait a few days before making a decision.

The Pioneers.

It is the same with exports. Inquiries come here from abroad. The European exporter turns to the Chinese dealer, who gets his supplies from another dealer in Canton. The Canton dealer collects his produce from up-country. When the produce finds its way into Canton again and dealers take the first step, the machinery of export will be in motion.

Briefly, the above is the situation to-day. Sampan folk in Canlon are beginning to carry foreigners, and Chinese to Shameen or the boats. This is done openly and not as a gamble in the dark as hitherto. Junkmen have also signified their willingness—in view of the sampans having set an example—to follow suit. Cargo coolies and shop fokis will, it is felt, also handle merchandise—as a few have been doing during the last few months.

Opposition Organisation. There is no evidence whatsoever of intimidation at shops nor is there any agitation on foot.

A minority movement is on foot, however, to engineer "no intercourse" with the British.

An organisation has been formed to "differentiate cargo." It is supposed to embrace students and labourers but its extent is a mystery so far. They have appointed a committee of investigation to examine merchandise. Neither names nor regulations have been announced.

Risk and possibility of trading loss have also deterred merchants from making any appreciable shipment either way. There must be a demand for goods before cargo moves, said a leading merchant to the "China Mail".

Then there is considerable speculation as to the outcome of Canton's surtaxes. No report has come through that collection has started nor that the Nationalist organisation has been set in operation. Matters will become clearer when the order goes forth for shippers to pay the levy but Hong Kong firms are consoling themselves with the fact that the Custom status is the concern of several Powers and not this Colony.

On the proposed new taxes, the "Toho News Agency" reports:

The Canton Government has detailed its officials to the Customs House to collect surtaxes, but foreign Consuls here have not yet held their meeting in this respect.

The rank and file are leaving in large numbers.

Those not seeking employment immediately are still provided with accommodation and food.

Some of the pickets are also going away but the majority remain in the camp.

Mr. Soong further stated that if Great Britain granted the Canton Government's proposition, it was more than likely that the United States would follow suit, although the attitude of Japan was somewhat doubtful.

Nevertheless, it appears that Consuls, of foreign Powers here are not so sympathetic towards the Canton Government. Such being the case, the situation is that complications of importance may be created, for the Canton Government authorities seem to be firmly determined to put their original scheme into practice at any cost.
