to pre-strike conditions with the exception that the steambout wharf is not used because it is too badly in need of repair.

The cargo coolie trouble has been settled. They will get a gratuity of $2.60 per day from the cargo-boatmen who land goods into the Customs' examination shed.

Passengers are travelling as usual without molestation and the hours of arrival and departure are the same as before.

As previously reported, cargo junks have refused to take merchandise on which the additional levy of 50 per cent. likin is payable.

headline: · Fight Against Likin.
text:
Some junks have not adhered to their mutual resolution. Taking advantage of the temporary monopoly they have earned high rates.

Accordingly the junk folk have passed another resolution to the effect that any member of their guild caught breaking the strike against the likin authorities will be subject to a "fine of $1,000. The same penalty applies to junkes carrying cargo on which the extra likin is payable.

The Canton-Kongmoon to-boat is expected to suspend operations to-morrow.

headline: Kongmoon
text:
Although the "new" boycott has subsided, agitators are still trying to stir up interest in the Association for the Severance of Economic Relations with the British, the sponsors of which in Canton have been singularly silent during the last three weeks. At Swatow, merchants have been notified to take stock of all goods of British origin, which must be liquidated by a fixed date. [From Our Own Correspondent.] Balksi, Koramoon, Nov. 23

For Nov. 30 (a week hence), an anti-British demonstration has been arranged to take place at Kongmoon, under the auspices of the Economic Suspension Association.

The proprietors of the Kam Ling Hotel (West Point) were summoned before Major C. Willson at the Central Magistracy this morning for obstruction. Mr. W. B. Hind, defending, urged that the offence was purely a technical one and asked for a nominal fine. The Magistrate said that he agreed with counsel and would impose a fine of $3 only.

headline: RESTRICTIONS RELAXED.
text:
South Wales and Northumberland Obdurate.

Colonel Lane Fox, Secretary for Mines, announced in the House of Commons to-day a relaxation of the coal restrictions. Although supplies were still far short of the normal demands, the output, he said, was steadily increasing, and the time had come when practically all restrictions except that which prohibited the export of coal ought to be withdrawn and freedom re-

The restrictions on gas and electricity for light and heating power would be withdrawn as from tomorrow. The restrictions on the domestic consumption of coal would be continued only to the end of the present week.

As from tomorrow, also, the colonies would be given freedom to dispose of coal as they pleased in this country.

Some 10,976 more miners are at work to-day, bringing the total up to 421,478.—British Wireless Service.

headline: EARLIER MESSAGES.
text: The miners returning to the pits yesterday numbered 20,121, the largest increase since the stoppage began, thus bringing the total engaged at the pits to 400,500. Good progress was made yesterday in the district negotiations between local leaders and colliery proprietors, and provisional agreements have been reached in several coalfields. Relaxation of coal restrictions, with particular reference to fuel industries, will be announced in the House of Commons to-day.—British Wireless Service.

headline: FINE INCREASED FIVE TIMES.
text:
“Fined $4—unless there is a previous conviction,” said Mr. R. E. Lindsell when a coolie was charged with hawking without a licence at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Divisional Inspector P. Grant is formed the Bench that the defendant had been convicted upon severe previous occasions.

“Oh!” said His Worship who promptly increased the fine to $20 with the alternative of 14 days' hard labour.

headline: RIVER SHIPPING TRIALS.
text:
"All" Vessels to Submit to Examination?

From Our Own Correspondent.J Samshui (West River), Nov. 24. The special tax bureau of the Nationalist Finance Ministry is now in full operation at Wuchow and there are many anomalies arising out of an impossible situation.

It is well known that the bureau levies 2½ per cent. on ordinary imports and 5 per cent. on luxuries. But for convenience, or some other reason, the staff of the bureau merely asks for half the amount collected by the Chinese Maritime Customs in Hai-kwan taels.

If a part of any shipment comes under the category of "luxuries," the bureau does not trouble to work out its own assessment, merely accepting the figures of the Customs.

Should the Maritime Customs make a seizure of goods not on the manifest, the bureau also puts in a claim for seizure, but the merchandise is only handled in these cases by the Customs. There is no harm in making a formal claim but the question of custody does not arise.

The staff of the bureau now wear a uniform much similar to that of the Chinese Maritime Customs. The outstanding exception is in the badge. Instead of the dragon in the middle of the emblem, the Nationalist bureau men have a blue medallion on which is superimposed the white-rayed sun.

Native exporters at Wuchow have been notified by the bureau that the penalty for a false declaration is three years' imprisonment. The staff board the pai's (pontoons serving for wharves), in harbour and scrutinise manifests.

Liquor Shipment Astray. I hear that the Custom's Club at Wuchow has not received a shipment of'stores which was sent some' time ago.

Inquiries among the Nationalist Inspection Corps at Do-singled to a belief that the stores had gone astray—to Canton.

Subsequently some stores were delivered through a British steamboat from Hong Kong.

A Portuguese merchant in the liquor business lost altogether 115 cases of wine on one trip, 7 of which were for up-country Roman Catholic missions. This gentleman has now open to him the course of interviewing the Finance Ministry in Canton.

Conditions at Do-sing are different. There the Inspection Corps is only authorised to effect seizures of alleged contraband, but there is no special tax bureau to make collections.

Between Two Fires

In this port (Samshui, further down river), merchants are literally between two fires.

The Chinese gunboat which previously left after an encounter with pirates has returned, and is anchored close to the tow, near the special tax bureau.

Native junks and cargo-boats are told that they must stop for examination at the Nationalist depot, which is outside Samshui harbour limits.

When that examination is over, they proceed to enter port, going a distance of 100 yards or so. But because they have to submit to the bureau they render themselves liable to a fine by the Maritime Customs for “anchoring in transit and breaking bulk.”

What Compliance Means. Not every Hong Kong merchant is aware that vessels going from Hong Kong to Vuchow must report to the Customs station at Samshui in case of any stoppage between Whangmoon and Samshui due to fog, breakdown or other unforeseen circumstance of navigation. Failure to do so can result in a smart fine.

But the special tax bureau intends to establish a depot three miles outside Samshul and traders have been informed that all vessels, of whatever nationality, will have to stop and submit to search, Compliance with the tax bureau can only mean running foul of the Customs.

headline: China / MURDER TRIAL. / CHASE BY UNARMED CONSTABLE.
text:
TO-DAY'S EVIDENCE.

The whole of this morning's proceedings in the Western Market, affray alleged murder case were taken up with the examination and cross-examination of the constable who first gave chase to the prisoner as he ran from the market with a dagger and heavy iron file in his hand.

Witness detailed the course of the chase along. Chonaught Road and Des Vceux Road Central and said that prisoner twice turned round and, threatening with his weapons, dared witness to come on. Witness was unarmed. When the prisoner was finally overtaken by other police who had come to the assistance of witness, he still held on to the dagger even when beaten to the earth with a bamboo pole. Witness had to strike his hand repeatedly with a chisel before he would let go of the dagger.

The Crown case against prisoner has not yet been concluded. There are six more witnesses to

be called. It was the original intention of the court to sit until late to-night to finish the case but it is doubtful whether this course will be possible owing to the length of cross-examination.

headline: UNUSUAL EXCUSE. / $ ^{1} $A $ ^{0} $ WOOD-CUTTER'S SORE
text:
An Indian watchman charged with cutting Government-owned trees, pleaded that he had been told to do so by a Chinese doctor, who directed that the leaves should be boiled and made into a medicine for application to his sore foot. Observing that people were not allowed to go about doing such things, the Magistrate, imposed a fine of $2.

The next case called in the same Court was that of a Chinese charged with a similar offence. Defendant, in denying the charge, hit upon the ingenious excuse that the wood had been cut by another Indian. "Oh I see," said the Magistrate," the last defendant came in very useful to you?" Divisional Inspector Grant proving a previous conviction: His Worship fined the defendant $50 or one month's hard labour.

headline: CANTON SEAMEN.
text:
Seamen who claim to have been employed by the Steamboat Co prior to the strike are again causing trouble.

After the resumption of traffic, they picketted the company's wharves in Canton and asked to be reinstated.

Negotiations between intermediaries brought about the withdrawal of the cordon. This week the ex-seamen are alleged to have demanded the dismissal of men of other departments on shipboard, who remained loyal during the boycott.

The truce has broken down as so-called “peaceful pickets” have re-appeared at the approaches to the West Bund, outside the Steamboat Co.'s wharves.

This had the instant effect of causing the number of passengers on one trip to drop below the 100 mark again.

From an unofficial source the "China Mail" learns that there is still a possibility of an understanding being reached by Dec.

It was reported in Chinese circles here yesterday that the negotiations between the Seamens' Union and the Hong Kong, Canton and Macao Steamboat Co., Ltd. (7), for the reinstatement of certain seamen who had left the Company's service during the strike had broken down.

text:
While officials hold the opinion that the United States cannot take action in Mexico, anyway, till Mexico enforces the oil land law which is due to operate in January, United States companies in Mexico are arming their employees with bombs and machine guns in order to protect their properties.

A message from Mexico City says that the situation is regarded as exceptionally serious. Some quarters hint that the severe tone of Mr. Kellogg's notes

headline: PARDONED. / JAMES EDWARD ATHERLEY RELEASED.
text:
NOW ON HIS WAY HOME.

The “China Mail” understands that a pardon has been granted James Edward Atherley, who, on January 17 last, was sentenced by the Chief Justice (Sir Henry C. Gollan) to two years' hard labour following a long and sensational trial at the Supreme Court for embezzlement of money the property of his employers, Messrs. Getz's Bros. (of the Orient), Ltd. Mr. Atherley is at present on his way to the United States.

The authorities concerned are reticent with regard to the matter, but as far as can be ascertained, Atherley, who had made several apparently unsuccessful attempts to have his sentence reduced, recently received intimidation that His Excellency the Governor had reviewed the case and that it had been decided that he be released from custody and given a passage to the United States. This was "accordingly done, Atherley being escorted one evening to a trans-Pacific liner by which he proceeded to his native country.

headline: STARTLING REVELATIONS.
dateline: Berlin, Nov. 25. War Guilt. Berlin, Nov. 25.
text:
Following the admission of Herr Gessler, Minister of Defence, in the Reichstag, that at the time of the Ruhr invasion, German Nationalist organisations contemplated forcible ejection of the invaders, it now appears that officers of the old German Army and extremists at one time planned to have "Sicilian vespers" in Germany in which all foreign troops would be murdered. They also proposed to form an army of 60,000 disciplined workmen in the Ruhr, while Russia's aid was also to be enlisted in "the fight for freedom."

The extremist leaders prepared to abandon Germany to the enemy as far as the river Elbe where a final stand would be made.—Reuter.

The Reichstag has rejected the non-confidence motion lodged by the Communists and extreme Nationalists. A resolution by the non-Socialist parties requesting the Government to examine whether the League Covenant offered a possibility of referring the investigation of war guilt to an international court of arbitration was adopted against the votes of the Socialists and Communists.

headline: COAL TERMS.
text:
SCOTLAND FALLING INTO LINE.

NOW 428,000 MEN BACK.

London; Nov. 26.

Satisfactory progress is being made in Scotland towards settlement of the coal dispute.

Matters have been left in the hands of a small joint. committee which will submit the terms to each side for ratification.

Officials of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Federation have discussed terms with the coal owners. These will be submitted to the miners' conference in London to-morrow.—Reuter.

428,000 miners were working today.—Reuter.

headline: Eight Hour Day.
text:
The Scottish coalowners' and miners' representatives have arrived at an agreement which will be submitted to both sides.

It is understood that the agreement provides for an eight hour day and a nominal minimum wage of $98.4d.

The Northumberland Miners' Council has decided to recommend acceptance of the owners' terms, including the 7½ hour shift for hewers and 8 hours for other workers.

After a lengthy conference at Cannock Chase the coalowners and miners at Birmingham failed to reach agreement, but the great majority of the men are working. —Reuter.

headline: SEX OF A CARP.
text:
DISPUTE LEADS TO KICK IN SPLEEN.

A quarrel over the sex of a carp at a stall in the Central Market had its sequel in Major Willson's Court at the Central Magistracy this morning, when a Chinese stall-holder was charged with assault and causing serious bodily harm to a customer. Inspector Marks informed the Magistrate that the complainant was in hospital suffering from a kick in the spleen and asked for an adjournment for a week. Defendant was accordingly remanded in custody.

"You are Government servants, it is your business to keep the peace, not to break it," said Mr. Lindsell to three Sanitary Board coolies charged with street fighting at the Central Magistracy this morning. His Worship fined each man $3.

headline: "TARANTULA" TO RESCUE.
text:
Canton Soldiers Removed on

West River.

In attempting to enforce the unrecognised right of examining all craft on the West River, a detachment of the Canton Government's inspection Corps met with H.M.S. "Tarrantula" a few days ago, with unexpected results.

This British gunboat was escorting two lighters (tbwed by a steam-launch) from Wuchow to Hong Kong.

At Do-sing the "Tarantula" put on speed and patted company. The inspection Corps has a depot at this port, working from a pair (pontoon) in the river. No effort was made at the time to intercept the lighters for foreible examination.

About 12 miles further down river, an armed launch from the depot caught up with the tow. The cowswain was told to bring his launch and both lighters back to the official pontoon. This, he pointed out, he could not do upstream, ignist the current.

The British Flag.

Accordingly, the Inspection Corps told him to anchor one lighter, being the other up, and then return for the second.

Having given these orders, the armed launch returned to Do-sing. But the "Tarrantula" came up river again and found three armed soldiers in charge of the launch and lighters.

These soldiers were removed, in a motor-launch, to the British gunboat which told the coxswain of the tow to proceed on his journey.

With the three soldiers and their gifts, the "Tarantula" steamed back to the Inspection Corps' pontoon at Do-singe where the officer in charge of the Government depot received back his men and their arms, but not the launch and the two lighters.

It was explained that neither the depot's armed launch nor the three Chinese soldiers had any right to hold up vessels under the British flag.

Foreigners Asked To Pay. Lighters and tow-boats controlled by the Standard Oil Co., have been convoyed from Canton upwards by armed launches of the Nationalist Government. This procedure has meant that craft under foreign flags have been "searched" by the Nationalist examiners at Samshui, but very few have submitted to the demand.

Requests by foreign merchants at Canton, to the Government, for Chinese Naval convoys, have brought about comical situations. Officials from the escorts, or from the Canton, Naval Department, have asked applicants if they will supply the necessary bunker coal for a round trip, or pay for the services in a sum practically equivalent to arrears of wages owing to the crew. Such suggestions have, of course, been turned down, but the inference is that if traders want protection they will have to find the funds with which the Canton armed launches can operate.

headline: "SQUEEZE" SEEN. "Pidgin" Rice Shipped at Wuchow.
text:
[From An Occasional Correspondent.

An incident of "squeeze" by so-called examiners—whether official or not, it has been impossible to determine—was witnessed here this week, prior to the departure of a British steamboat for Hong Kong.

Cargo coolies were putting some "pidgin" rice on board the boat when three men stopped the shipment.

The foki in charge of the cargo, which only consisted of about ten bags, handed over six or seven Kwangsi 20-cent pieces to the coolies who, in turn, squared the examiners, and the rice went on the boat without further trouble...

headline: IANKOW TROUBLE.
text:
KIUKIANG ANXIETY.

A message from Hankow suggests widespread strike possibilities, including servants, washermen, railwaymen, and shop assistants. Orders are being given to foreigners to lay in stocks of supplies.

From Kiukiang it is reported that the latest situation is causing considerable anxiety there. Southern troops are trying to enter the Concession.

A message from Nanking says that 5,000 Fengtien troops have arrived at Pukow, en route for Anking.—Reuter.

[Note: Pukow is the railway station opposite Nanking, capital of Kiangsu province. Anking is further south, on the Yangtze and is capital of Anhui province. Anking appears to the next objective of the Southerners now that they have captured Kukiong.]

headline: FOR THE LAST TIME?
text:
The conference of miners' delegates met in London to-day to review the district agreements. Reports were made of the stages which had been reached in the negotiations in the various coal-fields.

Although the negotiations have, it is understood, practically been completed throughout Scotland, Northumberland and Cumberland, no complete district settlement was put before the delegate conference. Therefore no action was taken. It was reported that in a number of districts the employers had refused to negotiate with the official representatives of the Miners' Federation and that in some cases they were making individual agreements.

The conference passed a resolution calling the attention of the Government to this action of the employers.

Emergency Regulations. "The House of Commons, was today engaged with further renewal of the Emergency Regulations.

" There was something like half a million miners back at work out of a million who were involved in the stoppage. "

If in a few days he could satisfy himself that the condition of affairs was such that he could safely waive any or all of the regulations he would get the necessary order and bring it before the House for immediate sanction.

He added that he was now going to retain the power of prohibiting meetings or processions in his own hands, taking it out of the hands of district Chief Constables. Any prohibition would be made entirely on his own responsibility.

To day's increase in the number of miners at work is 13,083, making a total of 441,571.—British Wireless Service.

Conference Indignation. London, Nov. 26.

The miners' delegate conference met to review the course of the negotiations in the district settlements, but adjourned without taking definite action, owing to the inconclusiveness of the negotiations up to the present.

The executive will decide further policy after receiving the district reports on the progress of negotiations. A resolution was submitted to the executive unanimously expressing the conference's indignation at the terms offered by the owners in several districts and inviting the Government's attention to the employers' refusal in Notts, Bristol; Leicester and Kent to meet the miners' representatives also in Somerset, until the men had resumed work.

The miners secretary, Mr. Cook, after the meeting, stated that terms had been provisionally reached in Scotland and Lancashire only but had not yet been submitted to "the men.—Reuter.

Three Year Truce

London, Nov. 26. Some 441,000 miners were working today.

In Lancashire and Cheshire the coalowners' and miners' representatives accepted the terms of the settlement, including the 8-hour day, continuance of the April rates of pay, and a temporary truce for three years.

A conference of colonators' representatives and miners in Dorbyshire reached an understanding with regard to the terms of agreement.—Reuter.

Rugby, Nov. 26. The miners' Delegates Conference meets to-day to consider reports on the district negotiations with the coalowners. In several coalfields, complete agreements have not yet been reached, although settlements are practically completed throughout Scotland, Northumberland and Cumberland. Despite the interference of log, the number of miners working increased yesterday by 7,000, reaching a total of nearly 480,000.—British Wireless Service.

headline: CHINESE DELEGATE'S SPECIAL STATEMENT.
text:
Important recommendations are contained in part four of the Extra-Territoriality Commission's report which was issued by the Chinese Foreign Office yesterday.

The Commission recommends a progressive scheme for the abolition of extrality. China meanwhile taking certain steps to improve the administration of justice.

The fifth recommendation deals with the question of taxation as follows:—“Pending the abolition of extraft, the nationals of the Powers concerned should be required to pay such taxes as may be prescribed in the laws and regulations duly promulgated by the competent authorities of the Chinese Government and recognised by the Powers concerned as applicable to their nationals.”

The Chinese delegate qualified his assent to the report, and issued a declaration expressing disappointment that the Commission found it inexpedient to recommend the immediate abolition of extrality owing to the conditions of the country but hoping that once China has completed her judicial reform programme, the Powers will open negotiations for the final abolition of extrality.

The Walchiaopu this evening issued part four of the Extrality Commission's report consisting of the Commissioner's recommendations.

The Commissioners express the opinion that when these recommendations have been reasonably complied with the several Powers would be warranted in relinquishing their respective rights of extrality. They declare that it is understood that upon the relinquishment of extrality, the nationals of the Powers concerned will enjoy freedom of residence, trade and civil rights in all parts of China, in accordance with the general practice in intercourse among nations, and upon a fair and equitable basis.

With regard to the existing special mixed courts, their organisation and procedure should as far as the special conditions in the settlements and concessions warrant, be brought more in accord with the organisation and procedure of the modern Chinese judicial system.

Lawyers who are nations of the extra-territorial Powers and who are qualified to appear before the extra-territorial or consular courts, should be permitted, subject to the laws and regulations governing Chinese lawyers, to represent clients, foreign or Chinese, in all mixed cases.

No examination should be required as to qualification for practice in such cases.

should correct certain abuses which have arisen through the extension of foreign protection to Chinese as well as to business and shipping interests, the actual ownership of which is wholly or mainly

Also the extra-territorial Powers which do not now require compulsory periodical registration of their nationals in China should make provision therefor at definite intervals.

Arbitration Machinery. (4) The necessary arrangements should be made with regard to judicial assistance [including commission regatoires] between the Chinese authorities and the authorities of the extra-territorial Powers, and between the authorities of the Powers themselves, for example:—

(a) All agreements between foreigners and persons under Chinese jurisdiction which provide for the settlement of civil matters by arbitration should be recognised and awards made in pursuance thereof should be enforced by extra-territorial or consular courts in the case of persons under their jurisdiction, except when in the opinion of the competent court the decision is contrary to public order or good morals.

(b) Satisfactory arrangements should be made between the Chinese Government and the Powers concerned for the prompt execution of judgments, summonses and warrants of arrest or search concerning persons under Chinese jurisdiction duly issued by the Chinese courts and certified by competent Chinese authorities and vice versa.

The fifth recommendation deals with the question of taxation as follows:—"Pending the abolition of extrality, the nationals of the Powers concerned should be required to pay such taxes as may be prescribed in the laws and regulations duly promulgated by the competent authorities of the Chinese Government and recognised by the Powers concerned as applicable to their nationals." Chinese Delegates' Statement. In attaching his signature to

the extrality report, Mr. Wang Chung-hui, on behalf of China, stated:—“By signing this report my approval of all the statements contained in parts I, II and III is not implied.”

Mr. Wang Chung-hui also issued a declaration expressing disappointment that the Commission found it inexpedient to recommend the immediate abolition of extrality owing to the present conditions of the country, and says that in view of the sincere intentions and unremitting efforts of China during the past decade to improve laws, judicial system and methods of judicial administration in China, and had hoped that the Powers would recognise the advisability of relinquishing without delay all the extra-territorial privileges enjoyed by their nationals. It is the firm intention of the Chinese Government on its own initiative to persist in the judicial reform programme, including the points mentioned in the recommendations. China is confident that when the judicial programme has been carried out the Powers will on the receipt of notice to such effect open negotiations for the final abolition of ex-quality

Evidence of Goodwill.

The declaration appreciates as evidence of the Powers' goodwill the recommendations respecting immediate discontinuance of the practices which are not warranted by the treaties, and other improvements in the existing relations which will promote better understanding between the Chinese and foreigners.

The declaration emphasises that the earnest hope of the Chinese people is to see the extraterritorial regime abolished and replaced by a condition consonant with the sovereignty of their country, and this aspiration can be aided in its fulfillment by a sympathetic attitude on the part of the Powers.

The Chinese people confidently anticipate a further manifestation of that attitude and early realisation of their legitimate aspirations.

headline: COUNSEL RAISES QUESTION OF HANDCUFFS
text:
Twenty of the men who, it is alleged, were connected with the piracy of the s.s. "Sunning" were again brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Mr. T. H. King, Director of Criminal Intelligence, appeared on behalf of the Crown. Mr. G. A. Gordon Leask, of Messrs. G. K. Hall-Brutton and Co. defended the 19th. accused—a Ningpo man, Mr. Leo d'Almada defended the second accused whilst Mr. M. K. Lo appeared on behalf of So Tik-sai (the 6th. accused) and ten others.

At the commencement of this morning's hearing His Worship informed counsel that he understood that the Police intended asking for a formal remand until Thursday.

Mr. King: That is so. If Your Worship will remand this case until noon on Thursday we shall then be in a position to fix a date. Application for Ball.

Mr. Lo.: I quite appreciate the fact that in a case such as this, your Worship will find it somewhat difficult to allow bail. In one case, however, I must submit a very strong application. This is the case against the sixth accused, So Tik-sai. In this case I sent proof of the man to the Crown Solicitor. I understand that the papers are at present in the hands of Mr. King. In making this application, I must necessarily disclose my defence. My client is the proprietor of a mason's shop in Aberdeen with a branch at Amoy. He received a contract for the grave of the late Mr. Ho Fook and proceeded to Amoy in this connection. When in Amoy he bought stone and engaged a number of masons. Part of that stone has already arrived in the Colony and more is expected by a ship which is due here in

I am not only prepared to produce cash security for almost any amount that your Worship may determine, but I am in a position to produce sureties from men well-known to the Secretary for Chinese Affairs—men whose integrity is beyond question.

I understand that the case against this man is that he was identified by someone. Your Worship will not dispute the fact there may be every likelihood of a case of mistaken identity. When I first went to Europe I recall that almost every Englishman appeared to look the same. I submit that such a case is more than probable when Englishmen are called upon to identify Chinese.

His Worship: Has this man been identified by any of his fellow-countrymen?

Need For a Prima Facie Case. Mr. Lo: I think the prosecution must satisfy your Worship that they have a prima facie case before bail can be definitely refused.

L can produce satisfactory security that this man will turn up. His sureties will

Mr. King: At this stage I must strongly oppose bail. I don't know whether I am called upon to open my case to-day. I agree that this man has been in business here for some years and that he did go to Amoy, but he has been identified and I cannot acquiesce to any grant of bail at this stage.

His Worship: I am afraid that in view of the seriousness of the charge I shall not be able to entertain your request, Mr. Lo. Mr. King: I can read evidence of identification from one witness. His Worship: Would you like to hear it, Mr. Lo?

Mr. Lo: I certainly should. Mr. King: A Chinese woman passenger has stated as follows: —I sure remember this man. He had a gun and he came to the passengers' cabins. He came to my cabin and demanded my jewellery.

Continuing, Mr. King said that the man had also been identified by the Captain of the ship, who pointed him out as a pirate. His Worship: The Captain being a man with experience on the China coast for many years? Mr. King: That is so.

The Magistrate: It sounds as though the prosecution has made out a prima facie case.

Mr. Lo: I thought Mr. King's position was that while he could not approve my application, he could not oppose it.

His Worship: Bail is refused. All are remanded in custody until Thursday noon. (To Mr. King): It has been suggested that each man should have a "card hanging round his neck bearing his number in English and Chinese. Mr. King: Arrangements are being made for that connection.

Question of Handcuffs. Mr. Lo: I do not knew what will happen when the trial opens. I notice that the defendants are handcuffed. I think I am right in saying that this is contrary to practice.

His Worship: I was asked about it. In view of the serious nature of the charge, I thought that every consideration should be shown to the Police.

Mr. King: It is merely a matter of saving policemen: the men will not be handcuffed when the case is opened.

Mr. d'Almada: We might release the handcuffs if we closed the doors.

Mr. Lo; I should strongly oppose anything of the kind. His Worship left the Court with counsel discussing the matter. A very smart Patent Leather Shoe that has been expressly designed for Dancing.

headline: Who Mr. Chan Is.
text:
When Hankow was in Wu Pei-fu's hands, a Northerner held the position but Mr. Chan succeeded him on the Cantonese entering the city.

Prior to going North, Mr. Chan was head of the Government Labour Department (not Ministry). He was nominated as one of the official delegates to the Boycott Conference but did not serve, as he left for the front.

At Hankow now, some of the extremists are agitating for the native employees of the Customs to form their own union.

headline: Trouble Anticipated.
text:
Such a union was started in Canton. Loyal employees were intimidated but Colonel F. Hayley-Bell (then Commissioner) was' adamant. A stage was reached when some of the loyalists had to be quartered" in the Customs House. Then the trouble blew over and Chinese in the Canton Customs remain without a union.

It is alleged that the formation of a Customs employees' union is contrary to good working.

Mr. Chan Kung-pok is reported to have made a speech in which he called upon the employees of the Hankow Customs to join the (proposed) union, if only from patriotism, as the Customs "should be run by Chinese and not by foreigners." Accordingly, a certain amount of trouble is anticipated.

A general anti-foreign strike and boycott is threatened for December 4, embracing servants, office workers and all Chinese in foreign employ. British residents have cabled the Foreign Office for additional protection. Arrangements are being made for the formation of a corps of special constables, since the agitators are intimidating the Chinese municipal police and threatening their families.

The French are taking up a very strong attitude with the result that after a complaint to the military a soldier and a civilian were executed this morning for creating a disturbance in the French concession last night. The various concessions are making plans for storing up food.—Reuter.

Peking, Nov. 28. One of the Legations has received a telegram from its Conful General at Hankow stating that the Hvass and property of its nationals was in danger. a few days. He is a Fukien man and is well known.

headline: HANKOW TROUBLE.
text:
The Flotilla Leader Keppel went to Hankow this morning. The American destroyers "Peary" and "John D. Ford left yesterday. —Reuter.

A union of the lower grade employees of the Chinese Maritime Customs was formed on November 21 with the support of the superintendent who was a Chinese official. This union had announced that its aim was to oust the foreign element from the management of the service and bring it under purely Chinese control. The "Commissioner of Customs hoped it might be "possible" to keep the Customs House open and maintain the light service for foreign nations, but this might be difficult. The Customs House, which was in the Chinese City was picketed.

headline: "Situation Essier."
text:
The latest report was that the situation in some respects appeared to be easier. The union had presented its demands, and these were not expected to be of an impossible nature, though it might be that they were only a preliminary move.

At the same time the general strike had made great progress. Chinese servants of Japanese were already on strike, and Japanese had had to import their food supplies from other centres.

The Communist section was showing great activity, and there was a fear of a general strike being forced. This, if carried out, would throw out of employment thousands of the lower grade workers, and it would be easy to incite these to riot. The situation was being watched by British Government.

Sir Austen Chamberlain, replying to a further question, said the Foreign Office had received a cable from the British community at Hankow stating that the situation was very grave indeed, that they were in daily expectation of an incident which would involve blood-shed, and that the naval forces were not adequate for protection of the community, and asking the Government to give an assurance that these forces would be strengthened. Sir Austen Chamberlain said that this appeal was under the consideration of the Government, including the Admiralty. Situation

In official circles in London it is pointed out that Hankow is easily defensible. Though it is 800 miles from the mouth of the Yangtse, the River at that point is a mile and a half wide, and comparatively large battleships can lie off the waterfront—British Wireless Service.

headline: Customs Position.
text: In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, Leader of the Opposition, whose first appearance it was since his return from abroad, Sir Austen Chamberlain. Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, referred to the grave anti-foreign movement at Hankow, including the aims of the newly-formed union of the lower grade customs employees.

Sir Austen Chamberlain said that the Commissioner of Customs hoped to keep the "Customs House open and maintain the lights service with foreign labour, but this might be difficult if the Customs House were picketed.

The latest report showed that the situation in this respect was somewhat easier. The union had presented demands, but these were understood not to be of an impossible nature, though possibly this was only a preliminary move.

headline: Navali Forces.
text:
Sir Austen Chamberlain mentioned the latest facts about the progress of the general strike, movement and Communist activities. He hoped to afford Mr. Ramsay MacDonald information on December 1 if he would repeat his question.

Replying to Mr. H. W. Looken Sir Ausur Chamberlain said that a British request from Hankow for the strengthening for the naval forces there was being considered by the Government and Admiralty. —Reuter.

[Mr. Herbert William Looker has been Unionist M.P. for Essex since 1924. He came to Hong Kong in 1895 to join the local firm of solicitors now known as Deacon's. "He was admitted a partner in 1900 and retired in 1919.]

headline: Naval Forces Being Landed.
text:
Following threats of a general strike at Hankow against foreigners, the Shanghai Chinese General Chamber of Commerce has received anonymous threatening letters demanding that a strike be called here.

A message from Hankow of November 28 says shipping employees and the municipal policemen have threatened to strike unless certain demands be granted.

headline: ST. ANDREW'S DAY.
text:
CITY HALL TRANSFORMED..

Compliments to Chief and K.O.S.E

To-day is St. Andrew's Day. Needless to say the interests of Scottish residents—and their friends — will be centred in the Ball and dinner at the City Hall to-night where the spirit of revelry will hold sway till the small hours of the morning.

A Scottish battalion of infantry is in Hong Kong. The occasion will be properly honoured to night as indicated below. The decorations are on a lavish scale, no effort having been spared by Mr. George Duncan and his Committee to transform the building into a veritable winter-garden. Needless to say, the Lion Rampant ensign and Cross of St. Andrew were very much in evidence, whilst the Ferguson and Leslie Clans have been introduced where possible by way of

General Li Chai-sum, at presenting commander-in-chief at Canton, whose troops have arrested the chairman of the Strike Executive.

Much significance is attached to the arrest, by the highest military authority in Canton, of the chairman of the Executive of the Strike Committee and four other delegates who have all along had an active voice in the management of the boycott of Hong Kong.

On Sunday night, a detachment from the headquarters (in Canton) of the commander-in-chief (General Chang Kni-shek), was sent out to make the arrests.

Mr. Sp Shiu-ching is the Strike chairman, sitting on the Executive of delegates as the representative of the Seamen's Union.

In the 1922 shipping strike at Hong Kong, he was one of the leaders. Subsequently one of his colleagues fell into disgrace following a scandal, and the first general secretary of the Hong Kong Union seceded after a dispute which culminated in a stormy meeting in the Des Voeux Road headquarters, at which the Police were present.

headline: " Who the Chairman Is:
text:
Mr. So presided at that momentous meeting and since then" has been head of the Seamen, with offices at Canton.

When the Strike began last June, he became chairman of the Strike Executive, the highest position in the movement.

Earlier this year, some of the delegates who sat on the Strike tribunal were detained by the Nationalist Government but what happened to them is not definitely known.

Mr. So was also the spokesman of the strikers when a delegation of Hong Kong Chinese merchants went up last year to explore the possibilities of a settlement.

headline: Speculation Rife
text:
Three weeks ago, the Strike headquarters at East Garden, Canton, were destroyed by a fire. A committee of investigation reported that “enemies of the movement” had committed arson.

The present opinion is that, accusations were laid against the Strike Executive by two bodies. Formerly, it had been alleged that several millions of dollars had to be accounted for, and a semi-official announcement followed to the effect that an authoritative statement of accounts would be presented when ready.

Speculation is rife as to the motive behind the arrest of Mr. So. In the circumstances the Canton Government can hardly be expected to make a statement, at least until investigations are complete.

headline: Merchants' View.
text:
The report, it is interesting to note, says that Mr. So and his four colleagues are under close detention at general headquarters.

Merchants, of course, regard this incident in the light of the Canton authorities making a definite move to curb boycott agitation, it having been announced that the Nationalist policy is to preserve communications.

This is only surmise and, in the light of developments in other directions, can only be treated as such.

headline: SEAMEN'S TROUBLE.
text:
Intimidation — it is called “peaceful picketting”—continues against intercourse with the Steamboat Co.'s vessels and wharves at Canton.

Other than providing armed police to preserve order generally at the wharves, steps have still to be taken to curb the activities of ex-seamen strikers, who are alleged to be sponsored by their Union.

The seamen want the dismissal of certain members of the crews in addition to their own reinstatement and a deadlock has been reached in the negotiations.

headline: OTHER DIFFICULTIES.
text:
Several other difficulties are engaging the attention of the Nationalist and the Canton (municipal) Governments.

The four Chambers of Commerce have petitioned the Municipality to take precautions to protect the public food supply, in view of the portents of the present general strike at rice shops.

The waterworks dispute is still outstanding.

In connection with the removal of the seat of Nationalist Government from Canton to Wuchang, a number of obstacles “behind the scenes” remain to be cleared.

One section of the officials are stated "to be not in favour—although not openly opposing—the drastic change. Their argument is that Kwangtung is the home of the Party and is still the most important province.

Military Powers. Gossip is also busy with the delay in the assumption by General Li Chai-sum of the post of head of the Military Department.

General Li is acting commander-in-chief of the Canton garrison, in the absence of General Chang Kai-shek. He is also the commander of the 4th Nationalist Army, two divisions of which (the 10th and 12th) have won the highest honours in the war.

The disposition of the Canton Navy is blamed for the delay. The present Commander of the Navy is reported to be reluctant to go under the control of General Li and he is said to have communicated with General Chang Kai-shek in the matter.

The creation of the new department of military affairs was approved by the last Kuomintang Conference in Canton.

headline: CHRISTIANITY.
text:
CHINESE ARE FAILING TO ACCEPT.

Shanghai, China, Sept. 28.—The success of the Christian cause in China is not what most optimists have expected in the past few years. With the recent anti-foreign agitation and anti-Christian movement the Chinese have ceased to accept Christianity.

This is the uncompromising verdict of Rev. Arthur H. Smith, octogenarian, who spent 54 years in China and who is the author of numerous volumes on missionary work in the Orient. His views are supported by not a few of the leading secretaries now in the field. Those Americans, who have dug deep in their purses to convert Chinese are doubtless surprised but the bald statement of fact is probably true. Especially in those centres where foreign commercial men have been boycotted, has Christianity been barely able to hold its own.

The solution of the problem has been searched for by those at home in China—the enigma to date is unsolved.

As counter-irritant to student and atheist propaganda, leaders of the Christian movement have hit upon the plan of making the Oriental convert carry on. With this programme in full operation, leaders believe that the Church will come into its own again.—"United Press."

text:

The teachers in these schools, who have salaries due them since April 1925, met to-day and will appeal to the presidents to reconsider their resignations. They will also send delegations to the new acting Premier, to the Minister of Finance, and to the Minister of Education, but the school problem seems insoluble without millions of dollars on hand—and there are no millions even remotely in sight.

Peking is filled with out-of-town students, and they are now in a distressful condition. The authorities have given them permission to live in the dormitories free for one month, on the slim hope that the schools may be able to open, within 30 days. Most of them, however, have no lights and no water—both services having been cut off because the government could not pay the bills.

The coal situation is admittedly very serious, and if something is not done at once Peking will have not only no heating, but also no power of any kind, no trams and no lights. The Peking Electric Co. has appealed to the Government, and also to General Chang Hsuehliang: (Chang Tso-lin's "son) for cond-cars, and says it will have to close down if fuel is not forthcoming.

headline: Sneaking to Canton.
text:
An official order has been put out forbidding students here from leaving for universities at Canton. Especially since the Cantonese captured Hankow, Canton propagandists have been busy among the students, and many have sneaked away for Canton. They go disguised as coolies, or as soldiers.

Heads of all schools have been instructed to search dormitories and libraries for Red literature, and the police are destroying all such reading matter that is found.

Chang Tso-lin, from Mukden, has issued an order forbidding the Fengtien troops now controlling Peking from interfering in any way with the civil administration, and from oppressing the merchants or collecting arbitrary taxes.

The military has also shown its goodwill by issuing an order to the effect that hereafter all soldiers must pay fares on the trams. Last week the street railway represented to the government that because the soldiers rode free it was about to go into bankruptcy.

To-day "Young" Chang announced that he was moving his troops out as fast as possible. There are now about 24,000 troops in and immediately around Peking. He promises that within a week only one regiment will be in Peking, and one at the Temple of Heaven. The rest will be south-bound to aid Wu Pei-fu.

headline: HONG KONG'S POSITION. / IMPROVEMENT SINCE THE BOYCOTT.
text:
OVERSEAS MONEY FOR PROPERTY: "NOT DEVOID OF HOPE."

Hong Kong's trade position has improved since the "settlement of the boycott." After extensive inquiries the situation vis-à-vis Canton is "summed up as "not devoid of hope."

In spite of agitation and intimidation, I can state on the best authority that at least $3,000,000 worth of "piece" goods has been sent from Hong Kong to Canton since Oct. 10, when the blockade of this Colony was voluntarily called off by the Strike Committee.

Much has been said about the restrictions to trade through the boycott not having completely ended, but from investigations I have made, I have come to the conclusion that a good deal of the recent impprovement in the Colony has been directly or indirectly attributable to the settlement.

In Nam: Pak Hong the sugar market has had a small boom now that former outlets have been reopened. Not only are the products of the two local refineries exported from Hong Kong but large quantities of raw sugar are transhipped here to the two Kwang provinces and other parts of China.

headline: Effect of the Dollar.
parent_headline: HONG KONG'S POSITION. / IMPROVEMENT SINCE THE BOYCOTT.
text:
The property market has shown signs of a new lease of life but the hapse of the Rents Restriction Ordinance and other causes have also contributed.

Metals and other foreign manufactures have found their way up to Canton, Wuchow, &c., as I saw on making a trip this week at the invitation of the “China Mail.” “While some trades have been adversely affected by the slump in the dollar, others have received benefit.

Gold currencies having gone up, Chinese emigrants are remitting more money home, mostly through exchange banks in Hong Kong. Shops known as “California” dealers have done more business now that intercourse has been resumed with the interior.

headline: Good Sign of the Times.
parent_headline: HONG KONG'S POSITION. / IMPROVEMENT SINCE THE BOYCOTT.
text:
Good trade in Malaya and other places down South has resulted in more money, earned by overseas Chinese, being sent back to Hong Kong.

This week there were several inquiries by brokers, on behalf of principals returned from Singapore, for Chinese house property situated on the central Praya.

Obviously such premises are required for business purposes—a very desirable sign of the times.

Because landlords are not now encumbered by law and are at liberty to retrieve possession, there is now inducement for merchants to buy property for their own accommodation, in preference to paying higher rentals elsewhere.

headline: Abundance of Money?
parent_headline: HONG KONG'S POSITION. / IMPROVEMENT SINCE THE BOYCOTT.
text:
House owners have been able to increase rents, thereby enhancing the relative value. Some of those who secured mortgages during the boom have now found buyers who paid enough to let them wipe off the loans.

It is not strictly correct to say that money is plentiful. The absence of other forms of investment has deflected funds (in the hands of native bankers) to the property market.

Interest on mortgage has lowered slightly but there is no hard and fast rate. Quotations vary somewhat: Short terms and long margins command low rates. Advances are worked out in ratio to the desirability of the security so that fairly high-interest will have to be offered on suburban lots.

headline: Feeling of Restraint.
parent_headline: HONG KONG'S POSITION. / IMPROVEMENT SINCE THE BOYCOTT.
text: Exchange fluctuations and uncertainty as to the future have jointly mitigated against new business in the piece goods market. But when the blockade was lifted, dealers in both Canton and Hong Kong did their best to replenish the very low stocks in Canton. Mostly in fiscal shipments, lots have been shipped up to meet the autumn and winter requirements in Canton, but a feeling of restraint available. This uneasiness is not due entirely to the threat that British goods will not be handled after Nov. 8. Having satisfied the first rush so to speak, dealers are waiting for the next development before further committing themselves. Such prudence can hardly be deplored.

Hardware and metals have also had outlets so that the market is not so stagnant as a month ago.

Merchants Own Interests. The threat of the Transport Union in Canton to "strike" against British trade as from Monday has caused considerable alarm in both ports. Merchants are looking forward, not without confidence, to the Nationalist (or Provincial). Government to take the initiative should a deadlock ensue. The situation is not devoid of hope.

To the traders themselves, those engaged in commerce are looking for means to tide over the agitation to sever economic relations at a future date. The circular forbidding searchers and/or pickets from entering shops is an indication that the Canton merchants are alive to preserving their own interests.

headline: NOT SCOTSMEN
text:
EGYPTIAN RATHER THAN BE

K.O.S.B. "BOMBSHELL."

Scotsmen prefer to be Egyptians than Englishmen or Americans!

Such was the startling discovery made by a Highlander while riding on a lower level tram in Hong Kong.

There were two young men who hotly denied that they were Sassenachs or Yankees and, ex-asperated, pronounced themselves to be "natives of Egypt. They were two privates of the 2nd. King's Own Scottish Borderers, the new infantry regiment on the station.

The Tramway Co. extends to men in the Services the right of paying half-fare while travelling in uniform. Men of foreign Armies and Navies are debarred. Under Suspicion.

If the two Privates concerned see this, they must excuse the conductor who, although plainly tactless and ignorant of military pageant, was merely doing his duty. Men in uniform, who were neither in the British Army or Navy, had proferred ten cents in the past and unknowingly pocketed five cents change till a European inspector happened to examine the ticket.

This conductor was trying to ascertain if the two Scottish soldiers were in the British forces, evidently viewing with suspicion the tarant trews they wore. He particularly disliked their Glengarry caps which, in his humble opinion, too "closely resembled the "hat of disgrace" mated out to the vixen-foccd, white-bearded villain of the Chinese stage type of mandarin.

The Good Sembritan. His vocabulary did not include the word British so he asked, when offered ten cents for two first-class fares: — "You Engish?"

"No," returned the Privates with sorrow plainly written on their young faces. In a moment of inspiration, the conductor rejoined: "You, the American?"

“No, we are Egyptian,” roared one of the couple but further trouble was saved when a gentle man who was on the train and had overheard the conversation went to the rescue.

headline: A YEAR'S SHIPS.
text:
FEATURES OF LLOYD'S REGISTER.

The report of Lloyd's Register of Shipping on the Society's operations for the year 1925-26, contains a further gloomy forecast, but also a comment which to some extent, is gratifying. The report predicts that the effects of the coal dispute on shipbuilding will be much more seriously felt next year the amount of new work coming forward showing already a considerable falling off. On the other hand, although the total of the projected tonnage is less than that of last year, the proportion of the amount to be built in Great Britain and Ireland has increased by 13.3 per cent. Plans for 361 new vessels of 1,089,360 tons gross have been passed by Lloyd's Committee, of which total 63.3 per cent. is to be built at home. This may be compared with five 63.7 per cent. of 1913-14 when plans for vessels aggregating 1,688,060 tons were approved.

With regard to classification, 410 rew vessels of 1,330,507 tons gross have been assigned classes. This tonnage is more than that of last year though the number of vessels is markedly less, which indicates a year of larger individual vessels than the preceding one. It may be noted that of this increase Germany has contributed a larger share, the tonnage of vessels built by her and classified under the Society being 140,000 more than her figure of last year. The increasing adoption of the Society's classification is well illustrated by the fact that the figure "for merchant vessels" at the end of June, 1926, is the largest that has ever been recorded, viz., 29,172,698 tons. Of this tonnage Great Britain and Ireland of course take nemier place with 47.4 percent, to which is to be added 4.5 per cent. for the British Domingons to make the Empire's total. These figures show that as other countries hold nearly half the total, Lloyd's Register can claim with no little justification, to be an international institution. In this connection it is interesting to note that in January of this year the Committee subscribed to a convention with the Scandinavian countries, as a result of which these countries are now added to the list of nationalitigs by which the Surveys and Certificates of Lloyd's Register are recognised as exempting vessels from Government inspections of various kinds. The countries comprised in this list are the British Dominions, France, Holland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Spain, Greece, Belgium, Portugal, and Latvia.

At the end of June there were 297 vessels under construction to the Society's classification, and, on completion of these, Lloyd's Register will cover in the aggregate, 9,854 vessels with a gross tonnage of over 30.5 millions. Of vessels individually over 10,000 tons gross, 8 steamships have been constructed under the Society's special survey, the list being headed by the Conte Biancamano, of 24,416 tons, for the Lloyd Sabudo Societa Anonima per Azioni, with next in order the Carinthia, 20,277 tons, and the Otranto, 20,032 tons, for the Cunard Steam Ship Company, Limited, and the Orient Steam Navigation Company, Limited, respectively. The steam turbine has maintained its position; 14 vessels, of 146,354 tons gross, were fitted during the year with turbines; as against 12 vessels, and 114,009 tons gross in the previous year. One of these vessels, the "Itiyo Maru" of 4,274 gross tons, is fitted with turbo-electric drive, 10 of them have single-reduction gear, the remainder double reduction.

The use of the heavy-oil engine is spreading with remarkable rapidity. The year completed in June establishes a record in the number of vessels of all types fitted with this means of propulsion, and under the Society's classification. This record is 118 vessels aggregating 601,427 gross tons. The previous year's figures were little more than half these, namely, 69 vessels and 302,189 gross tons. The previous year's figures too are excelled in point of size of individual vessels, except in the case of the Aorangi, whose 17,491 gross tons made her the largest vessel of 1924-25. The Gripsholm, of 17,300 gross tons, however, was not far behind, while others were the Amerikaland, 15,355 gross tons, and the Canadolite and Montolite, each of 11,309 tons. The largest and highest-powered oil-engined vessel afloat will be the Augustus, which is now being constructed under the Society's superintendence at Sestri Ponente.

At the end of June, 1926, 45 vessels, each of more than 8,000 tons gross, aggregating 439,907 tons and fitted with Diesel engines, were classed with the Society. headline: SHIPPING STRIKE.
text:
POSITION IN SHANGHAI LAST WEEK

The following from the "Shanghai Mercury" of November 15, supplements Reuter's cables of that date:

Nine coasting vessels and one liver steamer of the China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company are at present tied up at the company's wharf and in the stream as a result of the strike among seagull employees of the company over the question of compensation of the victims of the U.S. "Klang Yung" explosion in which 88 members of the crew lost their lives.

Owing to the week-end intervening, negotiations for a settlement were temporarily halted and it is not quite clear at the moment what are the prospects for a settlement. On Saturday, the anticipated departure of the Ningpo steamer "Hsin Kiangteen" took place and there is also a likelihood of vessels destined for Foochow and ports other than Swatow and Canton getting away in the near future, these being ports unaffected by agitation to the same extent as the two named.

There has been no trouble experienced with the strikers except their refusal to work. There has been no sabotage or violence and the crews are patiently waiting on board their vessels while their delegates settle the matter with the parties responsible and able to bring about a settlement. Cargo is still being loaded and discharged and in most cases vessels due or overdue for departure are filled with cargo ready to sail at short notice.

Monday, according to officials of the company, is not a good day to judge the position of the strike any way. It is what is termed by the company a “neutral” day, when under ordinary circumstances, hardly a vessel of this company leaves port. To-morrow there will be better prospects of telling just how strong the strike really is for several vessels are due to sail. It is difficult to discover how the negotiations are proceeding for they are being carried on between Chinese officials of the company and the strikers' representatives who are not given to publishing the results of their efforts. During the week-end one or two more coasting steamers arrived in Shanghai but their captains received no notification from their crews that the latter intended to quit. How sympathetic they are towards the strike will be discovered when the vessels are due to sail again.

The river steamer "Luen Yi" at present running under the British flag, but jointly owned by the three leading shipping companies operating along the China coast, is the only river boat remaining to the China Merchant's Company, the other eight having been commanded by the Northern Commander, Sun Chuan-fang and the ninth, the "Kiang Yung"; having been sunk following the explosion which is the cause of the present strike.

The “Luen Yi” is loaded with a big cargo of sugar which was taken aboard at Anking for Kiukiang but, due to the fighting in the latter port, was over-carried to Shanghai. This cargo is still in the holds of the “Luen Yi” waiting to be carried back to Kiukiang.

Actually, matters are at a standstill, though negotiations are reported to be in progress. The foreign officials of the company are in the dark as to what is going on and it is believed that there is more behind the strike than the mere claim for compensation which the China Merchants' Company is hardly likely to refuse, being but a fraction of the sum being lost daily while the strike lasts.

The Shanghai Seamen's Union entertained six Chinese journalists to dinner in the Yoh Yah Leu Restaurant, in Frenchtown, between 7 p.m. and 8 p.m. yesterday. Cheng Chung-ling, a representative of the Union, who presided, gave a full account of the labour dispute in the China Merchants Steam Navigation Co., and appealed to the press to give their wholehearted support to the strikers, who now number 200.

headline: $250 FINE. / OPIUM ON A DOUGLAS STEAMER
text:
FIRST TIME IN COURT

The Master and Agents (Messrs. Douglas, Lapraik & Co.) of the s.s. "Haiching" were the defendants in a case heard by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy yesterday afternoon in connection with the seizure, by Chief Preventive Officer Clarke on November 7 of a quantity of raw and prepared opium found concealed in a disused pipe in the ship's stoke-room.

Mr. L. D. Turner appeared on behalf of the defendants.

C. P. O. Clarke, in the witness box, said that, acting upon information received, he boarded the s.s. "Haiching" on November 7. He entered the stoke-room and, after searching and removing a quantity of coal, he found a quantity of opium concealed in a disused pipe. Altogether he seized 360 lbs. of raw opium and 245 lbs. of non-Government opium. Officers of the ship gave him every assistance in his search. Cross-examined. witness said that there were five or six feet of coal on top of the disused pipe. Mr. Turner: Why did you issue the warrant?—My instructions from the Superintendent are to issue a warrant in every case where there is reason to believe that someone on board the ship is implicated.

Captain Alan H. Stewart said that he was master of the s.s. "Hutching." He had a been employed by the owners for 23 years, of which for 17 years he had been in charge of one or other of their vessels. This was the first occasion upon which his company had been summoned under the Opium Ordinance. Witness had four Indian guards and three officers on board. The officers and crew were informed that they must be on the look out for smugglers and the ship was searched before leaving every port and that was done on the voyage in question.

His Worship: Once or twice?—After leaving Amoy and again after leaving Swatow.

Continuing, witness said that it was four or five years since his vessel had used oil fuel. He had no reason to suspect any member of his crew as being implicated in any way with opium smuggling. His present crew had been with him only since the strike. His ship was always coaled when in Hong Kong. In witness' opinion, the opium must have been put on board some considerable time ago. Reviewing the heroic defence of the "Sunning" by its officers against the pirates who had obtained control, the "Peking and Tientsin Times" states:—

The recovery of a pirated steamer seized by forty despernados, by two unarmed officers is a fent of gallantry and endurance seldom if ever equalled in the annals of the British merchant marine. The "Sunning," unlike ships on the Northern run, "was equipped with grilles, in addition to wireless. The former proved no protection. The latter, as we have always anticipated, proved useless at the time of the ship's capture. It was simply the courage of a handful of men that saved the vessel from the usual fate of ships captured in China waters, and ensured the death of capture of nearly all the pirates. It is difficult to find words in which to express one's admiration of the bravery of the officers responsible for recapturing the vessel. It is equally difficult to find strong enough words to condemn those responsible for tolerating a state of affairs under which this kind of crime flourishes.

In addition, to countless piracies of native craft, and a prute raid in view of Hong Kong harbour, itself, the Southern pirates have captured no fewer than six coasting steamers—two of them vessels on the Northern run—during the past twelve months. They seized the C.N.S. "Tungchow," on December 18, last year, the French steamer "Jade" on February 8, the C.M.S.N.Co.'s str. "Kwanglee" on July 13, the same Company's vessel "Hsinfung" on October 1, the French steamer "Hanow" about November 11, and the "Sunning" last Monday. In every case but one—the "Kwanglee," which was run ashore near Macao—the pirates have steered for Bias Bay. In every case but one—the "Sunning"—they have escaped with their booty, and in some instances, with kidnapped passengers. Bias Bay is less than one hundred miles from Canton, the seat of "the most efficient of all the authorities in China" (video Colonel Malone), and less than 25 miles from the important city of Waichow, yet not a finger has been raised against this pirate rest by the local Chinese authorities, although, as the "Tungchow" Court of Inquiry put it, "the only satisfactory way of dealing with the pirate menace is to destroy the pirate bases ashore, without which attacks such as that on the s.s. "Tungchow" would be impossible. And the British Navy, conforming to the policy of patience and conciliation—which apparently recognises even the "sovereign right" to piracy—has taken no action against the Bias Bay pests.

Significance of Struggle. Is this policy of inaction on the part of the “National Canton Government” and the British Navy to continue? The “Sunning” epic reveals what can be done by a handful of brave men, who, in this case appear to have escaped with few casualties, and comparatively unimportant damage to their steamer. But it is well to emphasise the probable consequences of this midnight struggle. Hitherto the Bias Bay pirates have generally refrained from molesting the foreign passengers and officers after they have once gained control of the vessel. In future such moderation is not to be expected. The heroism of the “Sunning” officers will jeopardise the lives of every foreign officers and passenger who may fall into Chinese pirates' hands. These pirates, as events on the “Sunning” have shown, are desperate ruffians. Their threats to set fire to captured vessels are not mere bluff. And unless strong measures are taken immediately for the destruction of this pirate stronghold, we may at any moment expect news of a much more tragic piracy than that of which the cables have brought us the news during the past two days. Wireless installations, grilles, armed guards, searches of passengers, etc., are only palliative measures, while pirates can continue to land, unmolested, with their loot, within fifty miles of Hong Kong.

The “Shanghai Mercury” concludes a review of the action of the officers in the following terms:—Another epic has enriched the tales told of the turbulent sea... Britishers may well be proud of the fact that the officers on board the steamer, “Sunning,” were faithful to the finest traditions of the mercantile marine and the British Navy. Heroism was shown in a marked degree, as the story unfolded testifies.
