headline: A SATURDAY CLUSERIE.
text:
There remain eight days to the day upon which we are assured by Mr. Eugene Chen that the complete removal of the boycott pickets and of all restrictions on the movement of cargo between Hong Kong and Canton will have been effected. Although it would be unfair to adopt as a criterion for the standard of sincerity of the assurance any happenings prior to that date, the reference in the note from Canton to the "probability" of pickets (and with them of all restrictions) being removed by the end of September assumes greater importance in view of the statement made by the Chinese officer in charge of the pickets at Samchun to the Customs officer there that the pickets had received instructions to leave by September 30. The pickets have not, in fact, withdrawn from Samchun and in Canton those that had previously been withdrawn from Shakespeare have now returned. It is difficult to gauge the exact significance of this renewal of activities unless it is attributable to the functioning of the very human instinct to make it while the sun shines. If Canton is sincere in its over

tures, the sun will cease to shine on the pickets from October 10 onwards. In the meantime, shipping companies have no alternative but to "wait until the boycott is officially finished" (in the words of the Secretary of the Steamboat Company) before they venture to send vessels alongside the Canton wharves again.

The last few years have been well up to normal as regards rainfall (and consequently water supplies) and this year the storms which have caused such considerable damage and loss of life have at any rate filled all our reservoirs to overflowing. But it is a matter of considerable doubt whether our water supply resources on the island would be sufficient in the event of acute rain shortage such as has been experienced in the past years when the population on the island was far less than it is to-day and the problem correspondingly less acute. The total rainfall for the year has, in years past, been down to little over 40 inches. At present, we may feel temporary secure with one of already well over 90 inches but it would be a foolish policy which did not look to the future. It was with an eye to future water requirements on the island that the scheme was formulated for the supply of Hong Kong and Kowloon from the Shing Mun Valley and, with pipes laid across the harbour for the conduct of filtered water to a service bed near the Botanical Gardens, Hong Kong could afford to smile at rainfall returns however meagre. But it certainly cannot afford to do so now that the scheme is in abeyance—and, as it is understood, abandoned so far as the present Governor's policy is concerned.

The reason for dropping the scheme is stated to be that the ground in question is in leased territory and that if in 1999 it is

returned to China it is as well that as little expense as possible be incurred. But the present works supplying Kowloon with water are also in leased territory and subject to the same possibility. Put on a proper working basis, there is no reason why, in 70 years, works for supplying the island with water from the mainland should not have paid for themselves, besides having been a guarantee against any possible shortage. That is putting the case at its worst, assuming that at the end of the leased period the land and works on it would function no more; but such would hardly be the case. In any event, the pressing necessity for assuring a water supply sufficient for needs in any emergency is so patent that it does not need stressing. We have certainly managed in recent years to supply a growing population on the island from island sources. But these sources are limited and have been developed to their utmost and it must be borne in mind that during the last twelve years we have been exceedingly fortunate in that our rainfall has not dropped below normal to any

great extent. In the absence of a permanent supply such as the Shing Mun scheme could give us on the island, the problem of supplying the island in the event of a year of acute rain shortage would be a serious one. Is not the matter so vitally important that there should be a re-consideration of the abandonment of the Shing Mun scheme for supplying Hong Kong? There was a passing reference to the matter in the Finance Committee's discussions this week and the Budget debate will provide our Unofficial members with a further opportunity of pressing the futility of pursuing the present policy of abandonment.

headline: SKETCH IN DUTCH.
text:
MRS. DICK NORTON SPEAKS ON CHINA.

"NOT FOR ALL THE TEA."

The Globetrotters open their season at the Star Theatre to-night and judging from the bookings, they are in for a record season. Mr. Dick Norton's popular company promises Hong Kong theatre-goers an entirely new programme.

Speaking to a representative of the “China Mail” yesterday, Mr. Norton said that, in response to the request of a large number of friends, he would endeavour to include an up-to-date version of his former great success, “The Midnight Train to Alabamy.”

This number has been revised since the departure of Miss Betty Norton and, according to Straits papers to hand, is more side-splitting than ever.

Mr. Norton's company now comprises the Misses Peggy James (soubrette), Billie Conway (soprano), and Gladys Cathie (ballroom and specialty dancer). On the male side, Mr. Norton is supported by Messrs. Lee Brooker (light comedian) Ralph Lynne (who partners Miss Cathie and appears in a number of solo numbers) and "Bucky" Morris (accompanist and solo pianist).

Laugh in Wrong Place. Mrs. Dick Norton (Miss Lolla Forbes), who has been on a visit to New Zealand, is due in the Colony on Friday next when she will rejoin the company.

Interviewed recently by the Sydney, "Sun," Mrs. Norton said "I would not live out here if you gave me all the tea in China" and went on to reveal something which will come as something in the nature of a surprise to her many friends in Hong Kong.

To quote the "Sun": "Their versatility is such that they translate their sketches into Dutch when occasion demands: "Very bad Dutch, I'm afraid," said Mrs. Norton laughingly. "The audience roars, in the wrong place, of course, at our mistakes and not at our humour. But, still, they love us."

headline: BUS SQUABBLE. / EUROPEAN TO PAY $10 COMPENSATION.
text:
Finding that a charge against Capt. Weston, of the U.S. "Ling Nam", of assaulting a Chinese had been proved, Mr. J. H. B. Nihill, at the Kowloon Magistracy, yesterday, ordered Capt. Weston to pay $10 compensation owing to the Chinese in question having been put to considerable expense and loss of dignity. The case arose out of an incident which occurred on one of the Kowloon Motor Bus Co's vehicles leading to a charge of assault against the Chinese being brought by Mr. T. S. Jeffreys who in turn brought counter-summonses against Mr. Jeffreys and Capt. Weston.

Capt. Weson and Mr. Jenneys were passengers in the traffic bus on Sept. 14 when the Chinese, who is an employee of the Telephone Company, got into the bus and (it was alleged by the two European passengers) dropped a coil of rope about the feet of Capt. Weston. Words followed between the two European passengers and the Chinese and according to Capt. Weston, the Chinese when asked by him to produce his ticket refused to do so, eventually producing it and "flashing it across" his (Capt. Weston's) face. An Indian constable who boarded the bus in the course of the dispute, in reply to the His Worship, said that the Chinese produced his ticket on the ordinary way and did not flourish in the face of Capt. Weston. He saw Capt. Weston strike the Chinese who in turn hit the captain. His Flourish found that assault against Capt. Weston has been proved but not against Mr. Jeffreys and ordered him to pay compensation as stated above.

They succeeded in getting the Hankow ricsha coolies to strike as a protest against the British for one day, after which the men all went back to work.

The Chinese generally are very apathetic to the whole movement, whilst among those Chinese who have habitual dealings with foreigners there is not the slightest trace of anti-foreign feeling, unlike during the troubles of last year which all classes of Chinese displayed resentment and suspicion.

Any trouble which may occur in this direction at present will be purely artificial, and as such cannot last, remarks the "North China Daily News" of this Tuesday.

British Ships Searched. Shipping people are reported to be much incensed at permission given by the Consular authorities to Chang.Kai-shak for his men to search all shipping at Kilometre 10, a point a little way below Hankow.

The excuse given for this search is that the Cantonese, have to take every precaution against the importation of arms and ammunition and general contraband of war.

Actually it seems to be but another instance of the Cantonese fendish delight in annoying the foreigner in every possible way.

The searches thus carried out are perfunctory and irritating in the extreme.

On one British vessel a few soldiers came on board to conduct the search without even an officer. Asked where their officer was they replied that he was asleep and had given orders that his men were to carry out the searching and were not to disturb him unless anything wrong was found on any of the ships.

Dangerous Precedent. Another vessel, also British, was held up for three hours while waiting for the searchers to come on board.

Feeling is running high on this subject among the merchants.

They point out that by allowing Chang Kai-shek's men to search foreign ships in this manner a most dangerous precedent is being established and one which there is now no logical reason for denying to Marshal Sun Chuan-fang. They point out further that Marshal Sun in all his dealings has shown every courtesy to shipping, unlike the Cantonese, and they fail to see why Chang Kai-shek should not do the same. Furthermore, if there is any genuine desire to search ships, there was nothing to prevent this being done by a Cantonese officer in the presence of the usual Customs search party. If Marshal Sun should care to demand that all foreign ships be searched by his men, shipping might be subjected to these delays at every port between Shanghai and Hankow.

headline: “UNEQUAL” TREATIES!
text:
It does not greatly matter to the Powers what kind of Government or Governments are installed in China, save and except any that are determined to flout international Treaties and menace the lives, and property of foreigners. In the latter case it is, and always will be, the bounden duty of the respective Powers to take all adequate measures to bring such a Government to their senses, and to teach them that Treaties are made to be respected by both contracting parties thereto. If any particular Treaty or Treaties are regarded by any section of the Chinese to be "unequal" or unfair the blame therefore cannot wholly be laid on the shoulders of the Powers; equally culpable must be those Chinese statesmen who put their signatures thereto. To condemn certain Treaties as "unequal" is merely to castigate China herself. Why should the "foreign Imperialists" — that catchword of the pro-Bolshevist party in China—alone have to bear all the brunt and be singled out for venomous attacks? Those Chinese who indulge in such claptraps as "hunting dogs of the foreigners," the "foreign Imperialists," and so forth are atrociously poor students of China's own past history. Treaties are made for a purpose. They are framed in accordance with the exigencies of the moment. If certain of the terms are harsh, that in itself implies a previous falling from grace of one of the contracting parties. But Treaties can always be reviewed. They can be abrogated, repealed, amended, or modified at some later date. Under altered circumstances no civilised nation would stand for the continuance of Treaties the terms of which are obsolete and, therefor, "unequal" by the virtue of altered circumstances. Moreover, what does

the League of Nations exist for if it is not to examine such grievances as “unequal” Treaties?

In the scrapping of old Treaties and the framing of new Treaties, however, regard must be had to the prevailing mentality of both contracting parties and the will and the ability of both to ensure the due fulfilment of all obligations undertaken. If it takes two to make a quarrel it likewise takes two to keep a Treaty. Is China to-day in a fit state to be given new Treaties—Treaties, that is of a nature that she could regard as an improvement on the old? The whole country is disrupted by civil war. There is no strong Central Government. The North and South are at daggers drawn, each endeavouring by hook or by crook to gain the ultimate permanent mastery. And yet, in the height of all this welter of blood and amid all the "buying" of Generals by the opposing factions, certain sections in China can find time to repeat the parrot cries of "unequal Treaties," "the yoke of the foreigners," "the hunting dogs of the foreigners," etc., and to pour out on the Powers volleys of verbal abuse! That, surely, is a very ill-advised way in which to plead for the abolition of "unequal" Treaties!, The violation of existing Treaties, at the bidding of the emissaries of Moscow, surely cannot strike the most sagacious of China's leaders as an ideal method of securing relief from "unequal" Treaties. The threat of not abstaining from the illegal boycott of foreign goods for a single day is not likely to impress outsiders with the sincerity of China's case in her relations with the Powers! If "unequal" Treaties do exist, it looks as if the greatest cause for grievance lies on the side of the Powers by the continuous and provocative breaches thereof by the Chinese.

headline: H.K.-CANTON RELATIONS
text: Sir, — Your correspondent, G. K. Chang, says in his letter in your issue to-day that the Canton Government is "our undesirable neighbour." In my opinion, the contrary is the truth. Canton is our most desirable neighbour because Hong Kong has on numerous occasions expressed its friendship and goodwill towards Canton. Everybody in this Colony, except of course G. K. Chang, wants to call off this boycott and to resume normal relation and traffic between us and that city.

These are the undeniable facts. If Canton is an "undesirable neighbour," why not let the present condition remain, where it is? We mind our own business, and Canton takes care of itself. But facts show that the continuation of "friendly terms between Hong Kong and Canton is desired by all save perhaps your correspondent, G. K. Chang.

Your correspondent is unduly alarmed in saying that with the resumption of intercourse between the two ports, there will be a tremendous amount of 'Red' element pouring out from Canton into this Island to conduct their mischievous service.

Assuming for the sake of argument only, if there are "reds" wishing to start trouble here, they should come now. They can come here now with as much ease as after the "settlement of the boycott. Why wait? What evidence has your correspondent in supporting such statement? No suggestion has been made to Canton asking that no Reds be permitted to come to Hong Kong. The truth is that Canton has no more Reds than New York or London. The Hong Kong Government knows how to handle the situation, and your correspondent's Red advice serves no other purpose than to create ill-feeling which sensible persons like to avoid.

[To the Editor of the "China Mail"] Sir Y our correspondent "Monitor" raises an interesting question and, synchronising as his letter did, with Captain Cobnam's return from his flight to Australia, provides material for much study.

In the course of this speech when introducing the air estimates in the House of Commons last February, Sir Samuel Hoare, Secretary of State for Air, said that his air policy was to provide Home defence against air attack: to provide air defence in suitable parts of the Empire to undertake the required air work for the Army and Navy: to develop civil air routes over the face of the Empire and to "help the British people to become a people of the air".

Sir Samuel, Hoare is certainly to be congratulated upon his policy as regards the promotion of civil flying and the expansion of air knowledge. The growing safety and controllability of aeroplanes has an important bearing upon the newest and most significant of all developments in aviation—that of the popular State-aided flying club. There are, I understand, already five light aeroplane clubs in Britain with over a thousand members. A sum of £30,000 is being spent by the Air Ministry in the encouragement of this scheme and it may be anticipated that further grants will follow. That State aid is well justified may be judged from the fact that each pilot trained by the clubs will be expected to join the Royal Air Force Reserve, and this means that Britain will be building up that human reservoir of air power which will be all-important in any emergency of the future. In another great world struggle, should it come, aeroplanes of metal will pour from the factories upon a mass production plan and the great problem will not be machines, but airmen; hence the national importance of any movement which produces pilots in times of peace. Yours, etc. Hong Kong, October 5.

headline: WEDDING BELLS / UNION INSURANCE MAN MARRIED: / SOMMERFELT—BIRCHALL
text:
St. John's Cathedral was the scene of a pretty wedding yesterday afternoon, the parties being Mr. Allister Sommerfelt (of the Union Insurance Society of Canton, Ltd.), son of Mrs. Sommerfelt and the late Captain Sommerfelt; and Miss "Edith" Dorothy Lillian Birchall, daughter of Mr. C. Herbert Birchall, J.P. and Mrs. Flork Birchall, J.P. (of Wallacey, Cheshire, England).

The Rev. G. H. Hewitt, Naval Chaplain, officiated.

The bride, who was given away by her mother, looked charming in a dress of champagne lace over georgette with hat en suite. She carried a bouquet of crimson roses. The bride's mother was attired in black marocain with pink under-dress.

Mr. J. W. Alabaster was best man.

Mr. F. Mason, at the organ, played the "Bridal" March from Lohengrin.

Following the ceremony, which was attended by many friends of the bride and bridegroom, a reception was held at "Hillcrest," the Peak, following which Mr. and Mrs. Sommerfelt left for Fanling, where the honeymoon is being spent.

The bride travelled in a beige crepe de chine jumper suit.

The bride's gift to the bride-groom was a gold wrist watch and that of the bridegroom to the bride a string of peanuts.

headline: TO SUPPRESS PIRACY.
text:
There will naturally be considerable misgivings in regard to the latest piratical outrage that resulted in a China Merchants' steamer being controlled by pirates for over nine hundred miles and taken to the usual rendezvous at Bias Bay. It may well be asked how much longer are these outlaws to infest the China Sea and interfere with merchant vessels? Is it not high time that the Governments of Hong Kong and Canton made common war against the pirates and rooted them out once and for all from Bias Bay?

In the course of an interview with a Press representative Mr. Eugene Chen is reported to have declared that he hoped that "arrangements for the termination of the boycott would proceed smoothly, after which "we shall then be able to tackle the piracy question, perhaps with the help of the British Government." This, like his utterances in respect of the ending of the boycott, is a definite statement. There is not the slightest qualification. It is a bold declaration of policy in the campaign against the pirates, and, as such, it is one that must be respected but never forgotten. The pessimists, who—like the poor—are always with us, have been sceptical about Mr. Eugene Chen's boycott statements and about his ability to keep his word. He himself, it is reported, has admitted that he was unaware that the boycott movement was so deep-rooted—hence the delay in giving effect before October 10 to the Canton Government's resolve to terminate the boycott. Unless steps are taken without further, and to wipe out the pirates and their stronghold at Bias Bay Mr. Eugene Chen may likewise have to confess that he did not realise how deep-rooted are these pests and that the "tackling" process may take much longer than he imagines.

If Mr. Eugene Chen is in earnest in his desire to tackle the piracy queen he is placed in a position of immense advantage in that Bias Bay is in Kwangtung territory. Moreover, ninety-nine per cent. of the victims of these

piracies are Chinese subjects, and in any measures directed toward the suppression of piracy Mr. Eugene Chen can count without the slightest doubt on the moral and material support of every law-abiding man and woman in Kwangtung, as well as throughout the whole of China itself.

In the matter of the help of the British Government Mr. Eugene Chen knows full well already that this has always been available and will continue to be available without the slightest scruple. We have the men and we have the ships only too eager to embark on a punitive expedition against Bias Bay. As a constant reader of the newspapers of this Colony Mr. Eugene Chen knows as well as anybody else that he shall never seek the co-operation of the British Government in vain. And there is no need to tell Mr. Eugene Chen that unless the question of "tackling" the piracy question is accelerated by the Kwangtung Government the work will be taken out of its hands by the British armed forces. However, co-ordination and co-operation between the Kwangtung and the British Governments is naturally the best course to pursue, and, on the settlement of the boycott, we shall await the next move by Mr. Eugene Chen and his colleagues in the way of "tackling" the piracy question with considerable interest. He has promised to do so. We look to him to fulfil his promise in the same hope and faith as we now regard his word of honour regarding the termination of the boycott on October 10.

headline: VAUDEVILLE / GLOBE TROTTERS AT THE STAR. PEGGY JAMES ILL
text:
Mr. Dick Norton certainly deserves the sympathy of his many friends in Hong Kong. The typhoon is responsible for much. Dick, himself, nearly lost his voice and now vivacious Miss Peggy James, who partners Mr. Norton in a number of items, is laid up with fever and was unable to appear last night.

In the circumstances, the second programme of the season suffered considerably, and particular credit is due to the remainder of the Company for "keeping the "flag flying." This would particularly apply to Mr. Leo Brooker, the light comedian of the show, who worked like a Trojan. We are glad, however, to note that there is every prospect of Miss James appearing this evening. Mrs. Norton, (Miss Lolla Forbes) is due to arrive from New Zealand to-morrow, and will appear both at to-morrow's show as well as on Saturday evening.

The concerted numbers last evening were quite entertaining, one or two numbers being really clever — notably “alphabetical poker.” Ralph Lynne in a couple of female impersonations scored heavily, and Herbert Morris received quite an ovation for his rendering of Dvork's “Humour-esque.” Mr. Dimoff's playing on the balalaika remains the outstanding attraction of the show.

headline: Confidence in Future.
parent_headline: CARMI THOMPSON. / DISTINGUISHED VISITOR IN HONG KONG.
text:
When asked as to his opinion as to "Whether the Philippines were ready for independence, and the economic conditions of the Philippines, Colonel Thompson refused to make any statement and said: "It is apparent that I should not discuss matters to be considered in my report until I have presented it to President Coolidge, but without violating my instructions, however, I can say that the Filipino people in all walks of life are hungry for education.

“I have noted with great satisfaction a desire among the Americans and the Filipinos alike for some constructive policy, with will ensure the economic development of the country. I have said on many occasions, and I will say it again, that the Philippine Islands are on the threshold of the most prosperous era in their history. They have just begun to understand the wealth of those islands, and to realise that the world is waiting for the production of its soil, metals, and its minerals from the mountains and the priceless lumber from the forests. When this prosperity is accomplished, it will result in a higher standard of living for all the people; better working conditions for labour and higher wages. This development will innure to the benefit of the Filipino people and will fix them on that firm foundation where they can compete with the commerce of the world.”

headline: AN END OF MARKING TIME.
text:
Marking time is not at the best a profitable proposition. In the case of the Government essential public works are held up; votes are trimmed down to the uttermost; and a general state of vegetation creeps in that works to the detriment of the Colony as a whole. Retrenchment may to some have something of a glorious, self-sacrificing ring about it—dear to the hearts of those who would like nothing better than to be regarded by posterity as Apostles of Economy. But it is not always proved by subsequent hard facts to be real economy. A certain municipality once upon a time was "hard up." It had got into the hands of municipal spendthrifts, and, to save the ship, it resolved to raise a loan to pay its debts and at the same time to suspend all work on roads, bridges, and public utilities for a period of two years. But it reckoned not with the Minister for Public Works for the State. However you economise, however you retrench, however you raise funds to pay your debts, provide a sinking fund, and secure your financial future, it is imperative that you continue the legitimate maintenance and repair of your roads, bridges, and public utilities, or your last state will be immeasurably worse than your first." And that dictum had to be obeyed—merely to prove the wisdom of the Minister's words.

Here we have retrenchment and economy, dinned into our ears since the flat went forth at the instance of Sir Reginald Stubbs. The Government has fallen down and worshipped the ideal. Retrenchment has been converted from a panacea into a mania. "Money, money everywhere and not a cent to spend" on ensuring that the Colony shall progress with the times and be in a position to cope with the turning of the tradal tide on the termination of the boycott. But—it may be said—have not votes by the million been passed right throughout the period of depression by the Government? True! — votes essential only to save the ship and prevent it becoming a complete wreck. There is not a single Department but has been in a state of financial starvation during the past sixteen months, when a little less of the previous doctrine of retrenchment and a little more of the genuine policy of true economy might have saved thousands in the long run.

Now there can be no longer an excuse for the obsession of retrenchment. There can be no more marking time at the expense of the ultimate benefit of the Colony. There must be no more spoiling things for the lack of a halfpenny worth of tar. The financial administration of the Colony has got to be galvanised. Rip Van Winkleism must go. The need for a bold and progressive policy will be greater after October 10—the date of the termination of the boycott—than it has ever been since the close of the Great War. In the framing of the Budget shortly we look to the Government to take its courage in its hands and to display at long last a stroke of real financial genufs. The Colony is ready for it. Let it not be disappointed!

headline: MR. POULTER SHOT? / BELIEF OF RELEASED LADY MISSIONARY.
text:
When a naval communique announced that the captured Customs launch "Kongmoon Chai" had been found and Miss Leonore Scarlett, a missionary, taken back to Kongmoon, nothing was said as to the fate of Mr. Poulter, the Customs officer in charge, or of the three loyal seamen.

From later reports it appears probable that these were murdered out of hand when the attack took place.

The launch is reported to have been captured as the result of connivance of certain of the crew, new men who had not long been with the boat; these also smuggled two members of the gang on board who emerged on a given signal.

Soon after the launch left Kong-moon shots were heard on deck and the engineer and fireman were confined in the engine room, Miss Scarlett later being taken from her cabin and placed with them. Although neither of them saw the events on deck they are of opinion that the shots were fired at Mr. Poulter and the loyal crew on deck in order that possessions of the vessel might be secured.

headline: REPUBLIC ANNIVERSARY.
text:
[To the Editor of the "China Mail"] Sir,—After reading the doings which took place in celebration of the Anniversary of the Republic of Portugal on Tuesday, it strikes me to enquire if the two members of Council representing as they do the Chinese of this Colony, are to hold any function on the coming Sunday to mark the 15th Anniversary of the Republic of China.

What I mean is, will there be a reception, say at the Chinese or at the Merchants Club, where East meets West in a spirit of concord amidst feelings of sincerity and warm friendship?

The opportunity should not be missed, as the day is free to all, and I am sure that H.E. the Governor will be delighted to attend, as it was he who spoke of the high values that will bring about the formation of a Concord Club in this Colony, the membership of which, of course, was to include Chinese.

If I am not mistaken, the Chinese Ambassadors at the European Courts hold this annual function which is usually attended by a distinguished gathering. The two Chinese representatives, enthusiastic as they are, continued at foot of next column.

headline: TO BE HELD IN.
text:
GOVERNMENT HOUSE GROUNDS

The pity of it is that the Prime Minister has seen fit to wait so long before speaking on behalf of his Government. Long before the Wanhsien incident outrages against Britons were becoming of far too frequent occurrence right throughout China. Valuable British lives were lost and all that the public heard of any official action came in a round-about way through the Consular Corps or Press correspondents. Not a word was uttered by responsible Ministers "in Downing Street. They were too absorbed, apparently, with the coal stoppage and the League of Nations, to pause and give expression to their attitude and policy in regard to the murders of Britons in China. There was little wonder that the irresponsible Chinese were given ground for the suspicion that the series of outrages against British life and property could go on indefinitely so far as the British Government cared. As was recently pointed out, in effect, by the United States, one outrage, fatal or otherwise, against a foreigner in China does not necessarily create a causus bellum, nor does it call for intervention in the affairs of China. But one, two, and three instances of brutality in which foreigners are the victims do cry aloud for the most vigorous denunciation and the exercise of the national right of the foreign Powers individually to protect the lives of their own nationals.

headline: MOTOR DRIVERS CLAIM.
text:
In the Summary Court this morning, a Chinese driver claimed a month's wages in lieu of notice from Mr. J. H. Mitchell by whom he alleged he had been engaged as a chauffeur.

Mr. Mitchell said that the man had only been engaged on trial and that when, being dissatisfied with his driving, he (Mr. Mitchell) asked the driver for his licence he refused to produce it, became insolent and the next morning did not put in an appearance. Holding that as a driver on trial plaintiff was not entitled to pay in lieu of notice, His Honour made an order for payment of amount outstanding on his wages only. This amount Mr. Mitchell had previously indicated his willingness to pay.

headline: Too Much Business.
text:
When the national legislative body reconvenes for its second session on December 6 it will find 140 bills and 33 resolutions on the Senate calendar awaiting action and 230 bills and 15 resolutions on the House calendar. Administration leaders agree that it will be impossible to dispose of this volume of business in a session lasting only seven weeks. The belief is gaining ground that President Coolidge will be compelled to summon a special session beginning March 5, as a continuation of the session which closes March 4, in order that long delayed matters of legislation may be considered.

The Senate will reconvene November 10 for the impenchment trial of Federal Judge George W. English, eastern district of Illinois, who was charged in the House with misuse of his official position. Under a special rule adopted at the close of the last session the rivers and harbours bill will be taken up December 14 and will probably be out of the way before the Christmas holidays.

Five Railway Bills. The steering committee already has agreed on five railroad bills for consideration before March 4, including the Cummins measure for compulsory consolidation; also a bill to lease Muscle Shoals to a fertilizer company; the Copeland bill to prevent future coal strikes; several farm relief bills; 13 bills to amend and strengthen national prohibition enforcement; and the complex problem of the French debt.

"We expect loud growls from those who have been demanding action on the Philippines," said one prominent figure on Capitol Hill, "but we will toss them the Thompson report and let them fight over it in committee."—"United Press."

headline: A FREE RIDE. / PASSENGER WITH AN OLD TICKET. / A TRAMWAY CASE.
text:
With an old tramway ticket stuck in his hat, a Chinese had a free ride in a car last night until an inspector with keener sight than the conductor discovered the fraud. Evidence of this was given when the man was charged before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Central Magistracy this morning with attempting to evade payment of fare. Mr. A. Gillard, of the Tramway Company, said that the ticket was one issued three days previously.

Defendant was fined $10, or 14 days' hard labour.

headline: A GOOD SIGN. / TRADE UNIONISTS AND AMERICA.

headline: MINISTERING CHILDREN'S LEAGUE
text:
A SATURDAY CAUSERIE.

This week has seen continued assurances on the part of Canton as to the capacity of the officials to deal effectively with the pickets and enable normal trade relations to be resumed between Hong Kong and Canton as from tomorrow. It is to be hoped that their confidence is justified and that the declarations of other leaders in Canton that the pickets will undergo reorganisation and will continue their activities in intensified form are unauthorised outbursts unfounded in fact and uttered merely with the object of fulfilling that almost sacred necessity in China for "saving face" even if it be at the expense of all truth and reason.

That there are directors of obstructive tactics in Canton who do not see in recent developments in Canton the end to their regime is apparent from the fact that there have been sent to Hong Kong quite recently agitators who are charged with the duty of introducing their insidious doctrines into certain of the Chinese schools here—doctrines which are far from introducing that element of peace and harmony in the relations between Hong Kong and Canton that the new era is said to be ushering in Mr. Eugene Chen and any other responsible officials who may be anxious for a settlement in order that a trial may be given to the proposed institution of taxes—to be paid by the Southern Chinese people themselves—have an unenviable task if the policy of the several factions in Canton is as opposed as it would appear from recent declarations.

text:
FIRE-WINDSTORM-MARINE INSURANCE.

It is extremely doubtful if the Government's intention, ascertained this week, to rebuild the Government Civil Hospital on a site adjoining the present will commend itself to the general public and it is probable—if provision for the work of rebuilding is included in the estimates for next year—that Unofficial members will have something to say on the matter at the Budget debate. With negotiations proceeding with regard to hospital accommodation on the Peak, the outcome of which will be either that the present Peak Hospital will be very much enlarged and improved or that work will be put in hand on the War Memorial Nursing Home, there would appear to be sufficient accommodation for Europeans, at any rate, on the Peak or at the French Hospital. Would the need be such, then, that the Government would be justified in putting in hand a scheme which it is stated will cost something like three million dollars?

headline: NEW CHINESE GRAMMAR
text:
A new Chinese grammar, with copious illustrations and quotations from the best works, styled ("A Grammar of the Chinese Language"), has been published by the Chi Hua Book Room, No. 31F (2nd floor), Wyndham Street, Hong Kong.

The author' Mr. Hu Kun-chi, formerly senior Anglo-Chinese master at the Diocesan Boys' School, has endeavoured to exhibit the structure of the Chinese language in a clear and logical manner.

The book will prove useful to non-Chinese students of the language as well as to the Chinese and should prove a decided acquisition to libraries.

headline: BANDIT TERRORS. / MACHINE-GUN FIRE ON A SHOP.
text:
[From Our Own Correspondent.] Pakka: Kongmoon Oct. 6

Famous now for its achievements against bandits, the 13th division of the Nationalist Army has been transferred to Shekki where outlaws are active.

Since the withdrawal of part of the garrisons for Canton's war against the north, robbers have been coming out into the open. Only recently the 18th division shot a good many alleged pirate chieftains. Major-Gen. Chu King-tong and Brig.-Gen. Chan Cheung-po are the heroes of this part of the delta.

At Kowkong, one gang brought up a machine-gun in daylight and opened fire at point blank range into a shop which had refused to pay blackmail.

Hardly an inmate escaped. Everybody from master down to the lowest foki was either killed or wounded.

Since this incident, over a hundred shopkeepers in the same district have received similar threatening demands.

The military are co-operating with the volunteer militia in keeping order.

headline: NEW FLAVOURS
text:

We have simply taken Mr. Eugene Chen at his word—his first word "fearless of the consequences of being "let down." In most circumstances it is a poor old policy to cross a bridge before it is reached. Into the circumstances actuating the Canton Government to reverse its policy and to resume communications with Hong Kong we have not entered. We have been simply content to regard it as a matter of fact—with nothing to add except to urge local merchants to prepare themselves for the day on which the boycott has been actually and officially declared to be a thing of the past.

headline: TURNING OF THE TIDE.
text: At the moment of writing, no definite news has come through from Canton recording the actual formality of terminating the boycott. Messages received in the Colony, dated Canton yesterday morning, however, leave not the slightest room for doubt that the official programme was duly carried out to the letter as arranged by Mr. Eugene Chen. In that event it may be proclaimed from the hill tops in Hong Kong, as it was on the East Parade Ground in Canton yesterday at noon, that the anti-British boycott is at an end.

Even until the news comes through officially that the boycott was terminated yesterday, there is not the slightest ground now for scepticism. It is a good old British axiom to hold a man innocent until he has been proved guilty;—in other words, hold every man to be an apostle of truth until there is convincing evidence of “terminological inexactitude.” On at least four distinct and separate occasions Mr. Eugene Chen, in his capacity as a responsible member of the Canton Government, declared his intention to call the boycott off on or before October 10. That should have been quite sufficient to ward off scepticism, pessimism, and controversialism—until midnight on October 10. If to-day—October 11—Mr. Eugene Chen has been found to have “made good” and kept his promise, not one word more can be said. On the contrary, in the most improbable event of the slightest hitch in the pre-arranged programme in Canton yesterday, then naturally Mr. Eugene Chen will be the cynosure of the eyes of the whole world demanding to know the reason for his breach of faith and his departure from the truth. But this seems too great a stretching of the imagination to be laboured further. All the signs point to just the opposite. Even after these words have been written and before we go to press, an official intimation of the actual termination of the boycott may come to hand through the usual channels. So—why worry meantime? headline: NOT A REVOLUTION. / COMMENT ON CHINESE REPUBLIC.
text:
Speaking at the dinner of the Central Union of Chinese Students in Great Britain in London, yesterday evening, in celebration of the fifteenth anniversary foundation of the Chinese Republic, Dr. Hu Shih declared that the Chinese Revolution failed because it had never been a real revolution—only a superficial change in the form of Government.

"We have been too conceited to understand the modern world and its new civilisation, and we never earnestly prepared our young men for the great task. We have been fifty years behind Japan in coming to a willingness to accept modern civilisation."

Chinese were sent abroad merely to acquire technical education, and almost none studied philosophy. The revolution found China with no leaders and had only given rise to many unscrupulous opportunists. He hoped that the students would become leaders in the new revolution and make China a great modern nation.—Reuter.

A very high-sounding phrase, indeed! But just on a par with the touching "gesture" implied in the presentation of a Red flag to the chief malefactor among the pickets!

No matter when or in what manner China's civil war ends Borodin and Co. will assuredly find that they will be numbered among the great unwanted in that great country. They have been tolerated so far where toleration merely meant the influx of the almighty dollar from Moscow's apparently bottomless exchequer and an inflow of Soviet arms and munitions and "ready-made" Generals. Money has been doing a lot of talking in China in these latter days. But the mist of Moscow cannot hang for ever before Chinese eyes. It will lift—it is rapidly lifting now in some parts of the country. Then shall Borodin & Co. be told in the plainest of language that their room is preferred to their company if they persist in their pernicious Bolshevik propaganda, which is as alien to Chinese ideals as to British

Borodin may expect praise in Canton as the power behind the recent strike and anti-British boycott "that was intended to " ruin Hong Kong"; but he has lived "to learn that even the Canton Governmentment as at present constituted has a mind of its own—that when it wills a thing not all the gold of Moscow can turn it from its purpose. And so it will be even if the Southern forces subjugate a large portion of the rest of the country, for the greater the sphere of influence of the Southerners the less will become the domination of Borodin, Karakhan, and all the other emissaries of the Soviet. Hence, it may be repeated, the latter have nothing to gain but a mighty lot to lose by a really strong Nationalist Party with its ramifications extending from Canton to Manchuli.

headline: Hong Kong, Tuesday, October 12, 1926
text:

Although the wish may be father to the thought there are certain signs showing that Bolshevism has been found out by the best Chinese leaders and moulders of Chinese thought. Bolshevism may not exactly have shot its bolt entirely in China, but assuredly its days are numbered. Its death rattle can be distinctly heard. The day and hour of its demise depends on the ability of the Chinese "captains" of politics to assist in the reconstruction of a New China that will have nothing in common with Moscow. According to unofficial and unauthenticated reports that archenemy of Great Britain, M. Borodin, was present at the demonstration in Canton on Sunday when the boycott was formally declared at an end. As advisor to the Canton Government he could not well have excused his absence.

The Chungking correspondent of the “Central China Post,” writing under date of September 20, states:—

Night Watches

The British men on the compound have "formed themselves into a British Defence Corps under an elected" Commandant who works in conjunction with the American S.N.O. We are keeping night watches with a view to anticipating any attacks from outside, and intend to hold on as long as it is possible. Last night, the compound was surrounded by about 200 of the T'uan, and we are reliably informed these men considered the possibility of making an attack. These people seem to have returned to their hills, and we hope they will not return here. It is generally thought the T'uan have definitely abandoned that part of their programme which referred to this compound since it was noticeable that the American gunboat was taking an active interest in matters.

Officials in Sympathy. City military and civil officials have informed the American Consul that they are in sympathy with the present anti-British agitation but will, they say, do their best to preserve law and order. This merely means that they will not definitely act against us—more than that is unlikely, and we need not expect any help from them. The most that has been done up to now by responsible officials on our behalf was the despatch of two military officers from the city "to preserve order." As a matter of fact, these men were themselves afraid of the local people, and asked to be allowed to stay inside the compound, which request was refused. From this, a fairly correct estimate of the situation as far as the officials intend to interest themselves can be made.

All office staffs are absent from British offices, and it is problematical when they will be able to return, hence, for the time being, it is quite impossible for us to handle cargo if sent up by outside steamers. The present position is that we are practically besieged inside this compound, and while we are able to smuggle out an occasional telegram, or get hold of mail, nothing like ordinary business, is possible for the present. The local Telegraph Office folk are making difficulties by refusing to accept telegrams except those accompanied by cash, and the Telephone people to-day called to collect September subscriptions under veiled threats to cut us off. I have not seen the Compradore nor any of his people for more than a week now.

headline: CARNIVAL
text:
BACK TO THE PARISH'PUMP!

With the passing of the boycott the parish pump will have a chance to come back into its own. Purely local affairs have been more or less under a cloud for sixteen months. The Colony has been content to "carry on" with the least possible attention to the local problems that matter—and many that do not!

on SATURDAY, 30th October, 1926.

headline: AT THE HONGKONG OR REPULSE BAY HOTELS
text: The easiest thing in the day's life here is to find a complaint or a grievance. The Colony is simply swarming with them. But all eyes have been centred so much on Canton that may "handy annuals" have almost withered. Many, indeed, are sadly faded for lack of the necessary attention. It is a moot point whether this is all for the good. Goodness knows the community is not so articulate as it should be in years in which wars and strikes and boycotts play no part. Spasmodic efforts are made to create and sustain public interest in vital local problems; but the talk and the action are generally confined—like everything else here—to a select few who do not seem to mind shouldering other people's troubles and airing other people's grievances. The bulk of the community—and we write now only of the non-Chinese portion—are content to drift along in a happy-go-lucky fashion, hearing not and heeding not the turning of the parish pump handle. The call to real citizenship, sad to confess, apparently is heard by few.

headline: COLGATES BEAVING SOAP.
text: Outside the Unofficial members of the Legislative Council and the Sanitary Board there is surely work for citizens of the Colony and citizens of the Empire—to make their influence felt; to stir up the dry bones in a too apathetic community; to arouse in them a sense of duty and of responsibility as residents of a British Colony and of the great Empire to whom they owe allegiance.
