headline: A SATURDAY CAUSERIE.
text:
With a history dating back to the earliest days of pioneering effort in China, Macao has every reason to be proud of the part she played in the opening up of trade relations with the West. It is a hopeful augury for the future that the spirit which animated these intrepid early explorers and traders should have found, such striking reflection in the united efforts of all sections of the community in connection with the trade Fair and Exhibition which has attracted so many from Hong Kong this week. The Macao Fair should serve a useful purpose—apart from the "fillip" it should give to local industries—in directing attention to aspects of Macao's life which are too often overlooked.

The world-tourist or the Hong Kong's tripper who spends his time at Macao at the fantan tables and claims to have "done" Macao has concerned himself merely with superficialities. The lifting of his standard of judgment to a higher plane would reveal much of historical interest and much in the harmonious relations existing between those of differing nationalities. This reflects the spirit of the place far more truly than the limited spheres with which most visitors to Macao concern themselves. On an occasion which marks the introduction of a new phase of industrial development for a neighbouring port with whom our relations have always

been of the friendliest, we join in the cry of her patriotic citizens.—“Viva Macao!”

This year has witnessed no diminishment in the interest evinced in the most important event of the year in the realm of local sport—the interport cricket match with Shanghai. The minds of some of our local enthusiasts, yearly engaged upon the self-imposed task of rendering advice to and divining the intentions of the selection committee, have been more keenly exercised this year than ever by reason of the evenly divided chances of many of the candidates. The Committee's choice will not, of course, fit in with the views of all—it would need a mind gifted with superhuman powers to evolve a team which did. However the team is one which preserves a sound balance between the requirements in all departments of the game and may be depended on worthily to represent the Colony. From the point of view of the spectator there has been a welcome innovation in the way of more comfortable accommodation. Another outstanding feature of interport week will be the excellent programme arranged by the A.D.C. whose nightly entertainments will serve to mark the week as a notable one both in the realm of sport and of dramatie art.

The announcement in the “Government Gazette” today that Mr. J. P. Braga has been appointed a member of the Sanitary Board during the absence of Dr. W. V. M. Koch will give general pleasure. The appointment is without precedent in the history of the Colony, as this is the first occasion on which a member of the Portuguese community has been appointed to the Sanitary Board. It is very, fitting that the honour should fall to Mr. Braga, whose position in the Portuguese community is acknowledged, and whose public spirited work for the Colony on many occasions has won him the respect and goodwill of the entire British community. The Government is to be commended on its choice, and Mr. Braga is to be congratulated on a notable distinction.

Odessa, Nov. 12.—Full ceremonial was associated with Rushdi's arrival. A large "crowd" cheered vociferously.—Reuter.

Rugby, November 12.—Lord Grey at the League of Nations Union last night expressed the hope that though it continued in name, Armistice Day would always be associated with the ceremony which commemorated no great victory but rather relief felt by the country when fighting ceased. Referring to the work of the League, he said the real test as to whether it succeeded in making a sense of security prevail was whether it prevented competition in arams. British Wireless Service.

headline: AMERICA & THE BOXER INDEMNITY.
text:
[To the Editor of the "China Mail"] Sir—Apropos of "Ionides" allusion in his letter to-day to the above subject perhaps you will find enclosed cutting from the "British Weekly" of October 20 of interest.

More than enough has been heard about America's generosity in the matter of the indemnity. Let us hear the other side. The European war debts afford an opportunity for justice, not to mention generosity, which America seems not too eager to embrace. That is a subject on which the world at large is saying less than it thinks, but some day the flood-gates will be opened.

Dear Sir,—In last week's issue of "The British Weekly," under the paragraph, "Does China Understand Anything but Force?" I notice you say: "For refusing to exact her indemnity from China after the joint advance to Peking under Graf Waldersee, the United States of America secured from the Chinese a moral prestige which could be stated in terms of money, influence and opportunity, is beyond all calculation."

By this time I expect you to have heard from others correcting this statement. Who your informant may have been, I don't know, but he has misled you. So far from America claiming no indemnity, she claimed more than was her due, with an ulterior motive in view. When the opportune moment came she magnanimously offered to forego the unpaid part of the indemnity; but on conditions. These conditions were that the money should be used for educational purposes, but the education to be in the hands of Americans, and that each year so many students (about 100, I believe) should be sent to America to complete their education. These conditions were agreed to, and the plan is being carried out, as everyone who is acquainted with Chinese affairs knows.

Only two missions in China declined to accept indemnity—the China Inland Mission and a small independent mission called the Show Yang Mission, with which I myself was connected. After the Boxer outbreak my wife and myself were the only two survivors of this latter mission, the other eleven members, with their children, being among the many martyrs of Shani.

headline: GUMLEY—HALL
text:
The marriage was solemnised at the Union Church yesterday morning of Franc Stewart Gumley, son of Mr. and Mrs. John Tait Gumley, to Elizabeth Margaret Hall, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Robert Hall. The bridegroom is with Messrs. Butterfield and Swire. The Rev. J. Kirk Maconachie conducted the ceremony. The bride looked charming in white brocaded satin deeply Van-dyked, and hemmed with pearls over a white lace slip. She wore a veil of white embroidered silk net sewn with pearls, and carried a wreath of white heather and orange blossom.

Miss G. Nicholls was the brides's maid. Her dress was of powdered blue flowered georgette, with that of blue taffeta and velvet. Her bouquet was of chrysanthemums, blush roses and maiden hair.

The matron of honour was Mrs. C. R. M. Young, who wore an attractive dress of nigger brown marocaine, trimmed with tangerine. Her hat was of velvet to match.

The best man was Mr. J. Petrie, of Davie, Boag and Co., Ltd., and the bride was given away by Mr. C. R. M. Young, of Messrs. Butterfield and Swire.

The reception was held at No. 549, the Peak.

The honeymoon is to be spent at Fanling. The bride's travelling dress is a fawn two-piece costume with crepe de chine hat to match.

The girl in the drama said more than once: "What a pitee." We said it more than once as we saw some empty seats. Hong Kong may be hard up, but Monday is often much more in evidence than on Saturday night.

It, is indeed, a reflection upon the general education of the community that the house was not crowded. It is the duty of every citizen that claims to be educated to support art such as the A.D.C. give us.

Some of us will attend more than once or twice. We sincerely hope that every reader of "The China Mail" will see this "Dramatic Medley." It is a good show and it is well worth the money. Messrs. headline: Shipping Boycott.
text: The news that the shipping boycott at Canton has been called off is of the first importance, alike for the immediate impetus it will give to trade between Hong Kong and Canton, and for the hope it holds out that all obstacles to trade between the two ports are about to disappear. There has been no doubt for some time now that the Canton Government has been sincerely trying to end the boycott. That it has not succeeded before this has been due in large measure to the strength of the pickets. The Canton Government has felt it wiser to play the waiting game rather than to take any drastic steps which might be interpreted as an affront to Labour. The waiting game has paid up to the point that the shipping boycott has now been called off. Let us hope it will prove as affective with the remainder of the pickets. Once these gentry have been removed, there will remain no further obstacles to unrestricted trade now that ships of all flags are at liberty to trade to Canton once more. That unrestricted trade is what both ports require needs no saying—the greater the prosperity of Hong Kong, the greater the prosperity of Canton, and vice versa; is a local axiom that becomes clearer every month. The intelligent classes in both ports realize that fully, and it remains only to impress it upon the minds of such pickets as are still active at Canton, or if that cannot be done to remove those pickets without further argument. headline: [From Our Own Correspondent.] Peking Nov. 8.
text:
China's abrogation of the Sino-Belgian treaty is almost the sole topic of conversation in Peking to-day, though the last half-week has not been without other incidents of interest and importance.

The Koo Cabinet was undoubtedly in disfavour with most of the Press and public before the treaty was abrogated. The radicals felt that Dr. Wellington Koo had not been vehement enough about Wanhsien, and that the dragging on of Belgian negotiations would lead no place.

Then, without warning, came the abrogation of the treaty with Belgium, and at a stroke of the pen all Belgians and Belgian interests in China lost extraterritorial rights. The resultant chorus of approval for Dr. Wellington Koo, Foreign Minister and Acting Premier, and for the Regency Cabinet, has been tremendous. Young China feels that a beginning has been made toward ridding the nation of the "unequal treaties."

But there is another side to the picture. "The more sober-minded Chinese, and all of the Legation Quarter, feel that the Chinese Government (so-called by courtesy) has made a grave mistake. The trouble is that China is a signatory to treaties which put her under obligation to submit to the Hague Tribunal precisely such disputes as that which resulted in the abrogation of the Belgian pact. Naturally the Legation Quarter, and of course the Home Governments of all countries having Ministers here will interpret this step to mean that China has decided upon a course of treaty-breaking, and that, since the majority of the people approve of it, no agreement made with China will be held binding."

Another view widely held is that Belgium made a grave mistake in ever negotiating with the present government. The Tariff Conference will not be resumed until China has a responsible Government, and it is felt that Belgium made a mistake in negotiating with a Cabinet that has no real power outside the walls of Peking.

The Peking, Government to-day, in the eyes of most of the Powers, is nothing but the archives of China in which to deposit the proper series of notes and protests. The present Cabinet, in international standing, is of no more importance than a post box in which to drop letters for a certain distant destination—only in this case the destination seems distant in time instead of in miles.

headline: CHINESE MUSIC. / WESTERN AND EASTERN TEMPERAMENTS.
text:
Chinese music is certainly a fascinating subject at the present moment; and the human voice, for the love of which every artist helps to intensify, will always form a matter of human interest.

That Chinese music of the best quality, vocal or instrumental, is becoming popular among Chinese, may be seen by a visit to local ten-houses, which the majority of patrons day and night, frequent more for the music than for the refreshments offered.

In many homes gramophones are replacing regular instruments:

Chinese music is welcomed by merchants, students, workmen, shopkeepers, at marriage core-monies) entertainment and social gatherings.

At the "West Point restaurants, where European and American visitors are welcomed," Chinese music is also introduced, though some of it cannot be said to be creditable reproductions of the genuine thing.

According to the really accomplished Chinese musicians, the ordinary professional's do not represent the best type of musician. Usually the ordinary Chinese will have no more respect for music than the ability of the musicians to render it. Skilled Chinese musicians, however, crave the art of employing sounds as a medium for artistic expression.

They aspire to impart through the medium of melodious sounds, all their inner feelings and emotions as is the aim of other arts like painting and architecture.

Many instrumental musicists have now the habit of playing to the accompaniment of singers of their own selection; usually these singers are blind girls from Canton.

These blind girls, well trained to love the art rather than simply to fall an engagement, differ from the restaurant singers in that their songs are soft and sweet and better still, very harmonious when heard to the accompaniment of the strains of true musicians.

An Important Question.

The careless players of so-called music so often appearing in public are really speaking, not musicians. Those players on Chinese stages and popular halls also fail to interpret the Chinese music of the highest order.

It is also obvious that Western and Eastern musicians differ in temperament and it is a little backward on the part of the Eastern musicians for that they have been sadly lacking in standard composition for the whole Chinese people.

Music in China is not universal; playing of one class of musicians does not coincide with that of another, though the clapping of hands and the stamping of feet to mark the rhyme and time are similar. Why should not standard music be composed and taught like other subjects in all Chinese schools is an important question.

This question is being taken up by some musicians in Hong Kong; and the matter now lies in the hands of the executive committee of the Chinese Amateur Musical Association. "In order to raise funds for this noble purpose this Association is going to give its third Grand Concert before the end of this year.

It might be recalled that this Association gave a Concert some years ago for the benefit of the Kwangtung Flood Fund. Some of these musicians have had many years' experience in the study of music as amateurs in Hong Kong, Canton, Swatow, Shanghai, and even in London and Chicago. It is certainly well worth while again to see and hear some of the members of this talented troops.—“Contributed.”

headline: PIRATES
text:
To the hundred and one comments on the hundred and one piracies during the past few years it seems impossible to add one fresh comment—at least one fresh comment of an original nature. That in itself, however, need not preclude us from sounding a note of gratification that the latest piratical effort on the s.s. "Sunning" has not met with the usual measure of success from the viewpoint of the fiendish "crowd from Bias Bay. Until full details of this latest outrage are to hand it is impossible to envisage the whole scene enacted on board the "Sunning"; but "sufficient is known (or, at least, surmised) to conclude that but for the gallant resistance offered by the Captain and his officers the "Sunning" would have been burned to the water's edge and her passengers and officers either drowned or borne off by the pirates as hostages for ransom. For once the pirates appear to have mistimed their diabolical attempt to seize and burn the ship. They evidently could not have calculated on the presence of other merchant vessels in the immediate vicinity, nor on the possibility of British warships being summoned by wireless in good time to prevent their full pre-arranged programme being carried out to the bitter end. It is really splendid news to learn that the escape of a number of the pirates was cut off by H.M.S. "Bluebell," and that nine others of the piratical crew were captured on board the "Sunning." It cannot be regarded as irhumane to hope that the fate of the captured desperadoes will be such as to strike an effective blow at piracy in Chinese waters for years to come. If not for all time. Whilst numerous measures have been put into operation to frustrate piracy, and whilst some other ideas have been suggested, it remains quite clear that the best preventative of all is a thorough search of all Chinese passengers at the port of embarkation. This was strongly em

published newspapers in China at the time of the "Tung 'Chow" piracy in the latter end of December last year, when Captain Macintosh was wounded. In that case, it may be recalled, the pirates boarded the vessel at Shanghai and seized the ship between that port and Wei-hai-wei. Armed guards are useful only up to a point, as was proven by the "Hanoi" piracy only last week when an Annamite guard was shot and thrown overboard. Wireless installations were once held up as the only deterrent to a successful coup by the pirates, but events have amply proved that wireless installations can be and have been damaged or put out of commission by the ruffians from Bias Bay. In the systematic search of all passengers at the port of embarkation lies the best possible hope of preventing piracies. The delay of steamers for a few hours may impose certain hardships on shipping companies, but these must be borne with in the interests of themselves, their passengers, and their cargoes. In certain cases such a systematic search may involve the co-operation of the local Chinese authorities at various ports en route; and that, in turn, may involve a display of moral suasion.

headline: Contracts for Britain.
text:
The people who will tell you that the country is going to the dogs, Sir, have received a jar by the news from Home to-day. A single message announces three huge contracts—one of £10,000,000 for the Buenos Aires tubes, another of £1,200,000 for the Singapore floating dock, and a third of £1,000,000 from Melbourne for cotton machinery. These contracts, besides providing work for British workmen for many years and putting over £12,000,000 into circulation in the country, have great importance as showing the faith that it is still held in British brains and British industry. The contract for the Singapore floating dock would be let in the United Kingdom, as a matter of course, perhaps, but the contract from Melbourne might easily have gone elsewhere, since it is offered by a private, not a State, enterprise, which presumably sought the best terms it could obtain. Even more gratifying is the contract from Buenos Aires, with the flattering requirement that the city's new tube system must be a copy of London's. There are other cities besides London with tube systems—New York, for example—and it is a distinct compliment to British industry that the contract should have gone to London. These three contracts, one from the Homeland itself, another from a Dominion, and the third from a foreign country serve to illustrate that Britain, while it may no longer be the workshop of the world, is yet more than able to hold its own with its rivals.

headline: THE WORLD'S RUBBER.
text:
[To the Editor of the "China Mail."] Sir,—The two latest of Reuter's telegrams dealing with the question of the world's supply of rubber cannot fail to have interested a number of local residents who have invested their hard-earned dollars in the rubber-growing industry.

It will, I think, come as a great surprise to most people to learn that Sir Ernest Birch, an ex-British Resident of Perak and Selangor, who, having spent so many years of his life in the service of the Malay States Government, and who, since his retirement, has identified himself with so many "rubber-producing companies in the "Golden Chersonese," should now come forward as Chairman of a company in Brazil which it is said to own 415,000 acres. This is significant, to say the very least, more especially having regard to the fact that the total area under rubber cultivation in the Malay States is just over 2,400,000 acres.

Now, whilst it is generally admitted that the known tin-bearing lands of the Malay Peninsula are becoming rapidly denuded of their metaliferous contents, it is conservatively estimated that the amount of land available for the cultivation of plantation rubber is sufficient to supply the world's needs for at least a century to come—even taking into anticipation the discovery of a new use for the product capable of absorbing a quantity such as is at present absorbed by the motor-car industry. Moreover, experts are unanimously of the opinion that the quality of the Malay product is far better than that of Brazil. Then there is the labour question, which, undoubtedly, is an important factor. Why then does so prominent a personage connected with the rubber-growing industry embark upon this new enterprise. Apart from the economical aspect of the question, one can hardly imagine Sir Ernest Birch associating himself with a Brazilian enterprise for purely pecuniary motives. Has one is tempted to ask, Sir Ernest lost faith in Malaysia? The other matter to which I would refer is the somewhat astounding news that the Secret

tary of State for the Colonies, was unable to supply Mr. F. G. Penny with figures which, I venture to think, most people who know anything about the industry, would have imagined the Rt. Hon. gentleman to have had at his finger tips. Mr. Penny has spent many years of his life in the Straits Settlements and can be credited with knowing something about the subject. It does not require the genius of an Einstein to surmise that there is something wrong somewhere. Has the Rubber Advisory Committee been allowed to lapse since the lamented death of Lord Stevenson? Let us hope that such is not the case.

headline: “YOLANDA.” / HIGH CLASS PICTURE AT THE QUEEN'S.
text: There are some pictures that, generally and not purely locally speaking, are boomed to the skies by picture producers and are sheer disappointments. headline: DEAD UNDER BED. / SEAMEN'S CLUB CARETAKER MURDERED.
text:
A Chinese caretaker of a Sem-men's Club at No. 19 Cheong On Street, Kowloon City was found dead under a bed on the second floor of the premises, the circumstances indicating that the deceased had been murdered.

The tragedy was discovered by a neighbour who, being unable to gain admittance to the Club, called the Police who broke down the door. The matter is being investigated by the C.I.D., but no arrest has been made up to the present.

The appeal in Hong Kong for the fund in aid of the relatives of those who lost their lives at Wanhsien in September has not been maintained so fully as the promoters had reason to hope would be the case from the sympathetic and immediate response which greeted the launching of the appeal. This is a pity, as there could be few better causes. First there was the distinguished bravery which characterised the conduct of those who took part in what has come to be known as the epic of Wanhsien—in itself sufficient to commend the claims of the dependants of those who lost their lives. Then there was the nature of the cause in which those lives were laid down, viz., the protection of shipping and of the lives and liberty of British subjects in foreign waters. There should therefore be no lack of support for the fund among any foreign community in the Far East, and it is to be hoped that an impetus may be given to the appeal locally so that Hong Kong's contribution may adequately represent the appreciation that is felt locally of the action of those who made the supreme sacrifice.

The loss of the interport cricket match with Shanghai has led to the "what-might-have-been" reflections which are usual on such occasions. The comment of the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird at the interport dinner might be read as a reflection on young men in the Far East in that, in Mr. Bird's opinion, they exhibit a preference for the Roof Garden and such places, where they may perfect themselves in the latest "fashions" in dancing. Such criticism, however, is a little unfair in view of the fact that most young men do not leave their offices until five o'clock. By that time in the cricket season there remains but half an hour or so of daylight—a period which in many cases would be taken up in arriving at the

ground and getting into suitable clothes. Debarred from active outdoor sport, it is surely not an indication of femininity that the young men in question turn to the most healthy form of indoor relaxation which is possible to them? A wider adoption of the "summer time" policy in operation in a few local offices whereby; in return for attending office earlier in the morning, the staff is allowed a corresponding period off in the afternoon would be as welcome to cricketers or would-be cricketers as it would be beneficial to the standard of local cricket. Many heads of local business firms were present at the dinner at which Mr. Bird's comment was made, and applauded the sentiments he expressed. Is not the remedy very largely in their own hands?

The traditions of the sea have been enriched by the epic defence of the “Sunning.” Hereafter, whenever piracy in the China Sea comes up for mention, the “Sunning” exploit will be recalled with pride and pleasure. Landsmen find it difficult to picture the scene on the “Sunning” during that terrible night. Could there have been three greater perils at one time than the terrific sea, a burning ship and a pirate horde? Darkness only was required to intensify the ordeal—darkness to give cover to the lurking ruffians who were ready to shoot at sight. Little wonder the captain of the “Sunning” was “all in” when he stepped ashore at Taikoo, after the further anxiety of a long tow through dirty weather into Hong Kong harbour. The sympathy and admiration of the entire community will go out to Captain Pringle and his men, especially to the Chief Engineer, Mr. Cormack, who had the misfortune to be the only one to suffer serious injuries at the hands of the pirates. The opinion is strongly held in Hong Kong that the admiration of the community for the “Sunning” heroes should not be permitted to stop short at mere words. These men, if performing their duty, have also rendered a great service to the Colony—indeed, to every port in the Far East. They have taught the pirates a lesson which should have lasting effects and they have given a new inspiration to the measures to cope with an evil that has cost many lives and caused immense losses.

Certain superior people in Hong Kong affect scorn for the world it tourists who periodically invade the Colony in large numbers. That attitude cannot be condemned too strongly. Apart from the fact that the world tourists, to put the matter on its lowest level, spend large sums in Hong Kong every year, and these sums, although going into certain limited channels, yet benefit the whole community in the long run, there is the vital fact that every world cruise does something towards fostering international understanding and goodwill. The visit of the "Ryndam" to Hong Kong proves that as it has never been proved before. Not only have the 500 travellers of the Floating University seen most of the places of interest, and beauty that the Colony has to offer, but they have come into contact with a section of the community with whom they have a great deal in common—the educationists who are so well qualified to give them an insight into the life and problems of Hong Kong. Admittedly their two days' stay here, as Professor Heckel said last night at the dinner aboard the "Ryndam," has not made them competent, "to determine the wisest policy for the British Government to pursue in this part of the world," none the less they have been able to realize the extent and the complexity of our problems. They now appreciate the fact that there are problems, and these problems cannot be settled with a mere gesture. Therefore it is not surprising to find Professor Heckel declaring further that many of the "Ryndam's" students will return to their own country more tolerant and with greater understanding. Last it be inferred from this that we consider Americans are the only ones who can so benefit, we hasten to add that we feel sure British University students could adopt the floating university experiment with equal profit. Hong Kong's European

community, for the most part is a community of travellers — we have all all seen at least a part of the world, if it is only the beaten track from Hong Kong to London via Suez. Consequently most people here have that broader outlook and wider tolerance which come from travelling. But so many of our people have never left their island home—they are those of whom Kipling wrote "What know they of England who only England know?" Perhaps these people, on the whole, are not quite so parochial as the stay-at-homes of America, whose vast country, remote from Europe and Asia, seems to swallow them up altogether. None the less the Britons who have never been further than Brighton, for all their country's traditions of Empire, are parochial enough, and we would gladly see them acquire the world cruise habit. Especially would we welcome such voyages for our university students—the leaders and teachers of to-morrow. The present cruise of the "Ryndam" is an experiment, we have been told: it is an experiment that has justified itself already — if its success persuades the organizers to make it an annual event and encourages the British universities to follow their example, it will have become one of the historic voyages of the world, for it will have begun a new era in the fostering of understanding and goodwill among the nations.

headline: WAR DEBTS FOR EDUCATION.
text:
(To the Editor of the "China Mail") Dear Sir.

Many prominent Americans have stated that they believe their country will be harmed economically and in other ways, by itself using all the War debt money, and various suggestions for cancellation or re-adjustment have been published.

A suggestion of considerable interest has been sent me by Mr. R. Cameron Beadle, Editor of "Combustion," and I forward copy of his letter in the hope that you will publish it.

His suggestion recalls the fact that higher education and research in Scotland have been greatly helped by money from an American source, namely the Carnegie Trust; also, the indemnity due to America on account of the Boxer Rebel.n, was given back to China and used by the Chinese Government for education.

I know Mr. Beadle well enough to say that he uses the word "education" in its very broadest sense, and this includes knowledge gained by travel, which is perhaps the best form of education.

By means of grants, thousands of American teachers and students are benefited by visiting this country and Europe every summer, and the sending of deputations of our workers to study "conditions in America and other countries, were education of, first rank.

If Mr. Beadle's suggestion could be carried out, it would mean, a great uplift for people of the Nations concerned, and help bring about better International understanding.

E. KILBURN SCOTT. 84, Kingsway, London, W.C.2.

Copy of letter from Mr. R. Cameron Beedle, Editor of "Combustion," is as follows:— Dear Kilburn Scott,

I write in reference to my feelings as to the War debts, and the European attitude towards America, because it is well for our friends to know that there are some Americans who appreciate the difficulties of the situation.

The money was borrowed in good faith, with intention to pay, and America expected it would be repaid, but in the stress of War, no one had time, or inclination to consider the ultimate economic results incident, to re-payment of such vast sums.

headline: CANTON'S MOVE. / OFFICIAL PEKING GREATLY
text:
POWERS "IN A BAD HOLE"

Official Peking," and the Legations, too, are upset by Canton's new attitude over the surtax problem.

Canton, by boldly returning to the Senior Consul-General at Canton the joint protest of the Treaty Powers over the surtax with the assertion that Canton "does not recognise the senior Minister of interested Powers" at Peking, puts both Peking and the Powers in a bad hole.

If the Powers negotiate direct with Canton over the surtaxes, such negotiations will be held, tantamount to recognition. If they simply permit Canton to continue collecting the surtaxes after they have protested they will lose a great deal of face.

The Cabinet is much concerned at Canton's boldness, and at the phrase in the return note which declares Peking to be powerless and adds that 'Canton controls more than half the area of China proper.' Neither of these statements can be refuted.

headline: PEKING FARCE. PENNILESS GOVERNMENT'S GESTURES.
text:
EDIFYING SPECTACLE.

[From Our Own Correspondent.] Peking, Nov. 15. Peking is being treated to the edifying spectacle of a "government" arrogating powers to itself for the abrogation of solemn treaties binding a nation of 400,000,000 people, when that same government cannot even pay its university or its grade school teachers.

The $300,000 of Russian Boxer Indemnity Yunds released "during the week for educational purposes did not help the situation at all. Instead of pacifying the teachers it merely increased rancour and ill feeling, for each group feels that all other groups received more than should have been given to them.

The universities continue closed or on half time," and the teachers in the lower and middle schools remain on strike because they declare that the university teachers received more than their share of the Russian money. All in all no one received even one month's full pay, and the university teachers are nearly two years in arrears, while the public school pedagogues have more than six months pay coming to them.

Suggested originally in the "China Mail" it is gratifying to find the Chinese General Chamber of Commerce deciding to recognise the gallantry of the officers of the pirated "Sunning." Mr. Ho Iu, in his letter to the Chamber on the subject, struck the right note when he stated that the heroism of the "Sunning" officers, in fighting as they did against such overwhelming odds, had dealt a staggering blow to the activities of the pirates. He considered that the commercial community, who would ultimately reap the benefit, should mark their appreciation of the bravery shown. Another fine note was struck when he expressed the opinion that their gratitude was also due to the officers and men of the British gunboats for their ready assistance at all times in making the coast of China safe for shipping and thereby making trade possible. Coming from such a source, this excellent sentiment—fully endorsed by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce—will undoubtedly be much valued by the British naval authorities. It places the greatly maligned "British Imperialism," of which the Bolshevik crowd make so much, in a light entirely different

from that which has been ventilated in certain quarters of China within the past eighteen months. In itself it is fresh evidence of the oft reiterated statement that the best Chinese thought—whether that be in Hong Kong, Canton, or Peking—recognises the worth of British friendship and British policy in regard to Chinese questions.

To return, however, to the Chinese merchants' appreciation of the "Sunning" officers' heroism, the Chamber is to be commended in striking whilst the iron is hot. It has promptly decided to open a fund and, moreover, expressed the belief that the Shanghai merchants, who have equally much at stake, would wish to co-operate. Of the success of the fund there should be not the slightest doubt. When the Chinese give to such a cause they give unsparingly. When the invitation to co-operate reaches the European General Chamber of Commerce the seal should be set on a splendid community effort to recognise the heroism of those on whom is dependent our communication with the outside world—on whom we rely for our trade in the China Sea.

headline: BUTCHERS ON STRIKE.
text:
[From Our Own Correspondent.]

The activities of "Red Spear" and other bandits in various parts of the Province are proving a menace to many. However, the Officials are on the watch and some of the bandits have been caught and summarily dealt with. There is still much room for improvement, but for every effort made, however small, the people are thankful. The Y.M.C.A. have been holding a campaign against "Oplum and allied Drugs, and we trust their efforts will" be crowned with success.

During one of the many storms which have visited this coast this season, two fishermen were drowned despite the efforts made by their fellows to save them.

Kao Taoyin has been away on a visit to Mukden to solicit help from Marshall Chang, and it is reported that large quantities of ammunition are now on their way to this Province as the result of his visit.

Several residents have left us since I last wrote, among them being our genial Consul, Mr. J. L. Smith, who is leaving for a well earned furlough. His successor, Mr. C. F. Garstin, has arrived and taken over duties at the British Consulate.

The last of the series of Lectures which have been given at the C. I. M. Memorial Hall this Term, was delivered by Mr. P. A. Bruce, B.A., his subject being "Racial Problems." The lecture was most interesting and instructive, Mr. Bruce dealing with many sides of the question, and closing with a stirring appeal to all to face and share the problems of the land in which we live in a true spirit of brotherliness and thus be helpers the one to the other.

The Rev. A. H. Faers was Chairman and introduced the Lecturer. We regret to note that after many years of faithful and unremitting service Mr. T'an T'ai has resigned from the Chairmanship of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. This will not only be a great loss to that body, but will have its effect on the whole of the business world of this port.

The Officials of the Chefoo Club are doing their best to cater for the amusement of the public during these long evenings by showing some high-class cinema pictures once a week, and we are glad to say that their efforts are being much appreciated.

A tax upon the local butchers by the Chief. of Police has resulted in a meat strike. We hear that arrangements are being made to meet the demand by considerably raising the price of meat.

Another tax is being levied on the Postal parcel service of two per cent. on all parcels, both inward and outward, going through the mails.

The new building which has been erected in Beach Street for the postal service is now ready, and the opening day is fixed for the 16th instant when the officials will be "At Home" in their new premises for the transaction of business. The building is a fine one, being imposing in size and graceful in appearance. It is one of the very best buildings in the port. Mr. A. P. Dowglass, the Architect, and Messrs. Wang Teh Cheng, the builders are to be congratulated on the completion of their work.

A serious fire broke out in the Chinese city during the early hours of Wednesday morning, and despite the efforts of the Fire Brigade, much damage was done, three shops being completely gutted. We hear that all three shops were insured.

headline: THANKSGIVING DAY. / TO-MORROW'S AMERICAN ANNIVERSARY.
text:
PRESIDENT'S PROCLAMATION.

To-morrow will be observed by American citizens throughout the world as "Thanksgiving Day"—a day set apart by Presidential proclamation as a day of thanksgiving for the blessings of the year then ended.

Thanksgiving Day may not be observed in Hong Kong on such lavish scale as is the case in the United States or even in Shanghai, where there is a large American community, but, generally speaking, local Americans will observe the day as an unofficial holiday. Most of the business houses will be closed, whilst only one official will be on duty at the United States Consulate-General for the purpose of dealing with urgent matters.

There will, of course, be many dinner parties both in private homes and at the local caravan series in the evening, whilst special arrangements have been made to give the American sailors and marines a good time on board their ships.

President's Proclamation. In accordance with time-honored custom, President Coolidge has issued a Thanksgiving Day Proclamation. This, which we publish by courtesy of the United States, Consul-General, reads as follows: "As a nation we have passed another twelve months in the favour of the Almighty. He has smiled on our fields and they have brought forth plenty, business has prospered, industries have flourished, and labour has been well employed."

headline: A SATURDAY CAUSERIE.
text:
Although the Colonial Government of Hong Kong and the Embassy at Peking are answerable to different departments of Empire administration, the need is none the less apparent for the fullest possible co-operation in the matter of safeguarding British interests in North and South China. Mr. Miles Lampson, the new Minister to Peking, showed his appreciation of the need for such cooperation when, at some considerable personal inconvenience, he transhipped at Hong Kong in order that he might hold informal conversations with H.E. the Governor. This visit should enable him to grasp the peculiar problems with which British administration is faced in its relations with South China and to understand the patience and sacrifices of the British communities in the south in the endeavours that have been made to overcome these difficulties. Mr. Lampson will leave Hong Kong today with the best wishes of all sections of the community for a successful term of office. He has already voiced at Home the Government's deep sympathy with the difficulties of the Chinese people; its impartiality towards the contending factions; and its duty to protect the lawful rights of British subjects. Pending the establishing of a national government the British Government is bound to accord its nationals the fullest possible protection and exact reparation where no Chinese authority exists, a policy which cannot be misinterpreted as indicating an attitude of unfriendliness or a desire to interfere with internal politics of China. Our Volunteers are at present undergoing a series of week-end camps for the various units in connection with the winter training season of the Corps. Everyone realises the value of such camps in affording opportunities for more concentrated training.

香港中環五十六號

time at the disposal of instructors on the occasion of the monthly parades after official hours. There is a danger, however, of too much being crowded into the two days by officers — actuated by the worthiest motives—endeavouring to increase the efficiency of their Companies by acquainting them with the true significance of various field operations. From a short cross-country run and P.T. exercises early in the morning, followed by, say, one field operation during the day, nothing but benefit is to be derived. But in the extension of the programme to include extended order and other drills and two field attacks on each day, (taking, for instance, the opening camp of the Infantry Company), there is a possibility of increased efficiency being obtained at the cost of impairing the health of some of those participating, "the nature of whose sedentary occupations debars." them from indulging in regular active sports to keep them fit. It is a pity that the claims of business do not allow of full week camps yearly, in which event it would be easy to work up gradually to more intensive training. Failing that, a note of warning should be struck which has already found expression in the views of some who did not experience the benefit they expected from last week's camp, but found it rather a tax on their reserve of strength. Exercise is only beneficial when taken in moderation by those who have been unaccustomed to it in strong doses.

That society is made up of a number of units, mutually dependent, and that the inceptive to labour is enjoyment of the fruits of the labour—individual effort and individual reward—is being gradually recognised by the Soviet rulers, who may be devoid of common humanity and justice but are certainly no fools. Hence the New Economic Policy, the change in the law relating to inheritance, and the effort to secure outside aid in repairing the ravages of the past eight or nine years of destruction. The last mentioned they will not get, we hope, until guarantees are given that they recognise the law of commerce and reliance can be put on their promises. The world in general recognises this and laughs at the Communist-inspired fables about the purchase of millions and millions of pounds worth of machinery, payment to be deferred, the security being the promises of the Communist minority. Later on, perhaps, ready cash will be offered for machinery and goods, but only as a way of lining the pockets of the 0.08 per cent. of the Russians that rule. There are thus two causes at work which give some hope for the future of Russia, one internal which may result in the formation of real national Soviets, when the power of the minority will be dispersed and weakened among the local people who form national Soviets; and the external force of circumstances resting on the fact that no other nations will trust the Soviet rulers for that international commerce and intercourse which is essential to every country, however apparently self-contained. No mass lives to him self alone and no nation large or small can do it either.

headline: Student Invasion.
text: The "North China Daily News" observes that it is a common saying among those who live in American university towns that "you can tell a group of university students as far as you can see them because of the funny-dressed men and ugly women." Shanghai, not being an American university town, critics of our student visitors, who walked along the maloo and adjacent roads yesterday, voiced their opinion of the young ladies as follows: "They are sweet little things, some of whom are entirely too far away from home." With regard to the young men, the general opinion in Shanghai was that their clothes were peculiar. Loud vested youths, coloured like something that Shanghai has seldom seen, paraded through the hotel lobbies. "Other peacocks in plus-fours and latest model collars and ties gave all an ample opportunity to visualise the more sombre variety of clothing.

headline: The Shipping Strike.
text:
The latest move of the strikers is characteristic of Canton. Yesterday afternoon, a number of pickets, arriving in motor-cars, boarded a China Merchants' steamer lying at the French Bund and attempted to stop work by violence. Police investigations show that the cars came from the Chapel district. At the time these steamers are loaded, there are hundreds of people about the wharf, and therefore the pickets had little difficulty in getting aboard the vessel. A squad of Annamite policemen was sent to the wharf, but in the meantime the efforts of the police had proved sufficient to put an end to the trouble.

headline: TROUBLE AT HANKOW.
text:
Feelings akin to despair will be caused by the news, from "Hankow. That trouble should occur there again is bad enough: that it should occur at this juncture is particularly unfortunate. The Nationalist Government, by its efforts to suppress the boycott at Canton, has gained much credit in the eyes of the world. This credit, it is hoped, will be greatly enhanced, during the next few weeks, by "the cleaning up" of Bias Bay, with the aid of the British Navy. After that the Nationalist Government, but for the threatened trouble at Hankow, could have stood before the world with a claim for new consideration, based not merely on words, but on a record of actual achievement. The Nationalist Government, we are prepared to believe, is not in full sympathy with the threatened trouble at Hankow—from the sincere efforts it has made to suppress the boycott at Canton, we are ready to believe, indeed, that it would end the trouble at once, if it could do that with ease, having learned to its cost how such movements useful as they may be at the outset, can get out of hand and become an intolerable curse. The Nationalist Government, we are sure, would settle the trouble at once if it could do so with ease. But it feels it cannot do so with ease. The student and Labour elements at Hankow are too strong in its opinion to be put in their places out of hand. The Nationalist Government evidently thinks the unruly must be given their heads, and only when they have become tired through the recklessness of the pace, must they be curbed. This policy doubtless has points in its favour for the Nationalist Government, but it can hardly be expected to appeal to the Powers whose nationals' lives and property are endangered as a result. The Nationalist Government, therefore, can hardly blame the Powers for taking any steps they deem necessary to protect their subjects. Nor can the Nationalist Government blame the world for setting the trouble in the North against the efforts to secure better order in the South, and qualifying its good opinion according

香港中環五十六號

ly. The world naturally looks to a government to enforce law and order in the territory it controls. The Nationalist Government is seeking recognition, we are told, as the representative Government of all China. The world does not expect the Nationalist Government to suppress trouble in Peking or Mukden—it will be satisfied if the Nationalist Government can enforce law and order in Hankow and the other parts of China where the Kuomintang flag flies to-day.

headline: The Navy and the Yangtze.
text: The London Times makes the Cantonese invasion of the North a lever for denouncing hesitation in taking adequate steps to protect British interests on the Yangtsze and for having a slap at the Bolsheviks. It states that to trust vaguely to some ultimate Chinese reaction against Bolsheviks is wholly unprofitable, for by the time the reaction comes there may be little left for us to save and the state of China herself will be appalling. On the Yangtsze, our contemporary points out, opportunities for provoking further conflict are innumerable, and the worst enemies of Britain are watching to take advantage of them. It is obvious who these "worst enemies of ours" are. Equally obvious is it that they will continue their insidious propaganda against us in China in defiance of the Russo-British Trade Agreement expressly forbidding anti-British propaganda outside Russian borders. How that propaganda is working may be gleaned from the cables informing us of the serious position in Hankow, where the British community are "in daily expectation of an incident which would involve bloodshed." They now declare that our naval forces are not adequate for their protection, and they ask the Home Government for an assurance that the naval forces will be strengthened. This appeal is under the consideration of the Government, including the Admiralty. Only a few days ago it was stated in Parliament that our naval forces in China were considered adequate; but the new situation in Hankow has altered the aspect. If the Chinese authorities themselves cannot, or will not protect British subjects in Hankow or elsewhere on the Yangtsze the British armed forces have no alternative but to step into the breach.

headline: The Communist Fallacy.
text:
In trade, in politics, in agriculture, in the Army and Navy, in manufactures, in education and in law, the Communists propose to supersede the fit by the unfit. All the trained, experienced and capable directors, organisers, managers, salesmen, architects and engineers, and all the educated professional men are to be murdered or exiled that their places may be filled with the rag-tag and bob-tail of the slums—men ignorant, unskilled, unjust and violent. Such is the plan, such the hope of the apostles of revolution. They desire to establish what they term the dictatorship of the proletariat. Now, apart from the criminal lunacy of the suggested means, let us consider the political idiocy of the end. The dictatorship of the proletariat, as exemplified in the case of Soviet Russia, means the rule of the peasants and soldiers. But that rule would surely be more than a form of political government. It would imply also the confiscation of all public and private property and the control of all industrial and commercial concerns by the proletariat. Once they have abolished law and order, and discipline and business

and common sense once they have successfully blown out the brains of the commonwealth, they will be able to wave the red flag and live happily ever after. It is the most impossible, hideous and absurd delusion that ever betrayed fools to their own ruin. Anyone who has any real experience of popular movements, political or industrial, knows that the rank and file never do anything but listen and cheer and vote. All the real work is done by a few energetic workers. The great mass of the people never take an active part in public affairs. They resent the labour and effort and trouble. They must have leaders. They always did have leaders. Without leaders they are a helpless mob. Do the Communists expect to be able to dispense with leaders? Do they expect the whole mass of the proletariat to develop a common will, a common purpose and a common discipline? We have no hesitation in saying that they do not expect anything of the kind. They intend the proletariat to have not only leaders, but masters, and they intend to secure those posts for themselves. To put the whole thing in a nutshell, the advocates of the dictatorship of the proletariat do not intend to allow the proletariat to dictate. No, they are to be dictated to.

headline: STALIN. / IS POLITICAL BOSS OF OLD TYPE.
text:
$ _{1} $ NEW RULIER OF RUSSIA.

London, September. 13.—Behind the kaleidoscope of Soviet politics, which recently has sent some well-known figures tumbling, stands a new power in the person of Stalin, the name he took which means the "Man of Steel." He is the Russian counterpart of an American political boss, the head of the machine, the power behind the principal actors of the Soviet drama to-day according to reports reaching England!

He sent Trotsky into exile and called him back again. He directed Djerjinsky, the head of the ferocious Cheka, the secret police, who recently died under mysterious circumstances. He sent Zinoviev down from power and was behind the dismissal of Kamenev from his place as chief of the Commissariat of Trade. His name is Josef Djugnashvili, but he calls himself Stalin.

He is a big man and dour. He is a blustering, rough and impetuous leader, who wins through discipline. Lenin was his first idol and still is his example. But Stalin is a practical man of politics, who does not let fine theories stand in his way. He recognises facts when he sees them, yielding here and pushing forward there according to the facts.

In his hands, Soviet Russia probably is on the edge of many changes, which will make it fit more smoothly into the society of other nations, for Stalin is neither a bigot nor a fanatic. He does not beat his head against stone walls.

He has made himself deliberately a man of greatest mystery. For years he boasted that he had never given out an interview for newspapermen, nor allowed any newspaper stories to be published about him if he could prevent them. He is the most difficult man in all Moscow to meet and now he is the most important. But Stalin is the despair of newspaper correspondents.

He has been a revolutionist since 1905 when he took active part in bloody fighting in the Caucasus, for which he was arrested by the Tzar's police and axiled to Siberia. But he came back with Lenin and worked for several years, quietly and smoothly, in the second rank of the leaders. He has only recently come forward to the front of the Soviet directors. His work until now has been almost unseen and wonderfully successful.

It was his task, when the Soviet Union was formed, to placate the so-called "outer nationalities," the states surrounding the fringes of central Russia which were declared free and independent by the Soviets but which had, above all else, to be kept within the Soviet circle. By adjolery, by adept leadership, by wise concessions and softness where softness was needed, he kept all the surrounding states except his native state of Georgia loyal to the Soviets. He used no force. The people chose to be loyal.

Then Stalin was promoted to become secretary of the Communist Party, which controls the Soviet Government, and there again his fine diplomacy, good judgment and political sense won for him a conspicuous success. He is gathering the fruits of it now, for his secretaryship gave him control of the Soviet political machine, the "steam roller" which he has now steered over the earlier leaders.

headline: IRISH COURTSHIP.
text:
SYSTEM THAT CLOSELY RESEMBLES THE JAPANESE.

Courtship in Ireland is not the simple affair that it is in some countries. For Paddy, always a politician, has an eye to the main chance. And somewhere he has read that beauty is only skin deep. Rarely does he become engaged to a girl who has nothing but looks in her favour. In fact, his courtship is hedged round "by preliminaries that would cool many a girl's ardor.

Having noticed a girl whom he would like to marry; Pat does not proceed to make love to her. That would create a scandal. Instead; he usually seeks a go-between to plead his cause and to approach the father, whose consent is always necessary before a young man may even walk out with a young girl. This go-between or matchmaker often called the "mountainy-man," is found in every village and is almost invariably endowed with unlimited audacity and speech, as though he had kissed the Blarney Stone.

The matchmaker first insidiously creates an atmosphere. He talks with the girl, telling her what an "iligant feller" Pat is and what a nifty cottage he has on his two acres, "wid'a new thatch o nut, so it has." Also the cow, the pigs and the hens. Then he talks about it in the shop and in the saloon till at the countryside knows that Paddy wants to marry Bridget Malone. Then certain that Bridget's father has heard the rumour and has had time to think it over, the "mountainy-man" sallies forth with the swain to the father's house, a large bottle of best Irish, provided by the prospective bridegroom, in his pocket. He begins by reminding the father that it is high time his daughter got married and follows it up with the suggestion that if she doesn't hurry about it, he will surely have to keep her all her life.

“Sure Bridget will soon be on the shelf if you don't watch out,” he warns the father.

"And what way would she be lavin' this house, yet," retorts the father, "with her only a slip of a girl only just 20? It'll be a sorry day for me when she goes, for there's not the likes of her at making butter or cakes this side of County Tipperary."

Then, over many glasses of whisky and much good-humoured banter, the matchmaker cleverly ascertains how many cows and pigs the father is likely to give with his daughter when she does marry, and pointing to the young man who has remained silent throughout the conversation, he indicates what a fine son-in-law he would make and what a grand home his farm would make for the cows, the pigs and, incidentally, the girl. Finally, if both father and matchmaker are satisfied that they can strike a good bargain, they clinch the deal over another glass, and the father goes to the door, behind which the daughter has been listening all the time, and brings her in, protesting and giggling, to a seat near her sweet heart.

And so the two become engaged and after a short courtship are married, the wedding festivities providing a further occasion for bouts of merry-making, after which the bridegroom and his friends leave the bride in her father's House till the morrow, when with his best horse and cart he goes back to fetch her to her new home. At the same time his friends bring carts to take away the cows and pigs that form her dowry. An Irish country marriage is rarely improvident, and woe betide the father who fails to carry out any part of his verbal contract concerning the marriage settlement. An attorney in County Kildare not long go received a visit from an irate husband one week after his marriage. The latter wanted the father-in-law informed that the daughter would be sent back immediately if the promised cow was not delivered within three days. The animal was handed over.

headline: LEFT CHUNGKING
text:
SEVENTY-SIX REFUGEES REACH HANKOW.

EXCITING TRIP DOWN RIVER

Hankow, Sept. 24—That matters are not all well up river was evidenced yesterday morning by the return to Hankow of a party of seventy-six residents of Chungking, who had been obliged to evacuate that city. This party consisted of Dr. and Mrs. Anderson and family, Mr. and Mrs. Irish and family, Mr. and Mrs. Bayne and family, Dr. Birke and family of the Canadian Mission. Mrs. Burcell and children, Mrs. Frier, and Miss Perkins of the same mission were also members of the party but remained in Ichang. Of the Chinn Inland Mission there were Dr. and Mrs. Parry, Mr. and Mrs. Batstone, Miss Shoering, Miss Cecil-Smlth, Mr. and Mrs. Burgess.

Mr. A. Davidson and Miss Hutchinson of the Friends Mission. Of the business people evacuated there were Mrs. Lewis and G. Lewis of the A.P.C., Mr. and Mrs. Pennyard of Mackenzie and Co., Mr. B. Hicks of Arnhold & Co., Ltd., Mrs. Donelly and three children, Mackenzie & Co., Mr. and Mrs. Wilson and child, A.P.C., Mr. and Mrs. S. B. Starling, of B. and S. remained in "Ichang" Mrs. Moying and Mrs. Hughes of Barry and Dodwell also remained in Ichang, Mrs. Jones of the Standard Oil Company also remaining in Ichang, Mrs. Bollard, of Brunner Mond and Co., to Hankow.

These people were warned on Friday night, the 17th inst., that they would be required to evacuate Chungking on the following day. It appears that a large demonstration was expected to take place that day in which it was feared that anti-British feeling might get beyond the control of the authorities and at a meeting it was decided to evacuate the place.

Previous to this, General Wang who was in command, had been able to give all assurance for the safety of foreign lives and property; but apparently there had arisen a difference of opinion between General Wang and two other Generals in the district, and the former had become a little uncertain of his powers.

The demonstration as planned, was to consist of the entire student body supported by the local militia from the surrounding districts; but in the event it is reported that the militia did not turn out in the numbers expected, and in consequence the demonstration did not reach the heights of violence expected.

During the absence of the British Consul, who was at Wanhaien, the United States Consul in the port arranged the evacuation, and is still holding bouts in case the Americans should eventually have to evacuate as well.

The evacuation was not quite the simple matter it would at first sight appear to be. Conditions down river were not definitely known, and in the first instance two steamers belonging to Jardine Matheson and Butterfield and Swire, respectively, with the refugees aboard, dropped down to the A.P.C. installation, some eight miles below Chungking.

The Journey Down.

The journey however was not continued on these boats as it was by "no" means certain that the Chinese, knowing that the "chung-king party, were on board, would not commence hostile demonstrations en route.

The following day, therefore, the steamers anchored at a point away from all villages on the banks, and were transferred to the Standard Oil tanker 'Mei Chuan,' and on this boat they proceeded on their journey.

headline: COSTS
text:
AVOIDANCE OF REGULATIONS When Sir Frederick Lewis, in the course of his annual address to the shareholders of Messrs. Furness, Withy, and Co., spoke of the saving in operating costs resulting from transferring a ship to a foreign flag, it is perhaps a pity that he did not go into greater detail. Presumably he was referring both to the saving in wages and the avoidance of many of the regulations that are imposed on British shipowners. The economy in wages would not necessarily infer a reduction of individual wages, as the law entails the upkeep of a larger crew in British ships than is required abroad. I believe that no country in the world, except our own Dominions and the United States, insists on the maintenance of as large a crew on board ship as is required under British law, and many shipowners hold very strongly that the law could be relaxed without any danger to life or limb and with pronounced benefit to our sea-carrying trade. Apart from regulations as to crew, not even the United States has such an elaborate code of shipping laws as Great Britain. A number of our regulations have been strongly criticised—as, for example, our timber-carrying regulations, which have been condemned as being very much more costly than Continental regulations but not as effective in their purpose. Such a prominent shipowner as Lord Kylisant has argued that in the present emergency the Board of Trade would be well advised to review all our shipping regulations with a view to curtailing them temporarily until such time as the industry can afford to carry a heavier burden than is imposed on their foreign competitors. It seems clear that Sir Frederick Lewis's views cannot be very different from Lord Kylisant's.

The actual saving that Sir Frederick Lewis quoted in the particular case of a steamer that was recently transferred to a foreign flag amounted to $247 a month, or round about $3,000 a year. From these figures one gathers that the steamer is not a very large one, as the saving of foreign regulations

In comparison with British regulations is known to be substantial. He quoted a number of examples of speedy dispatch abroad. In the United States one vessel recently loaded 9,000 tons of cargo and 1,500 tons of bunkers within twenty-four hours. On the Continent a grain cargo of 7,100 tons was discharged in two days. These are two examples out of several showing performances that are rarely equalled at our own ports. Sir Frederick Lewis pointed out that ships are probably the highest valued instruments of commerce, and it would make an enormous difference if they were all handled in port with the speed and economy that is achieved abroad.

It is interesting to notice that efforts are now being made to bring down the cost of loading coal—that is to say, of loading coal when British coal is once again on the market. At the time of the Coal Commission shipowners, contended strongly that a big impediment in the coal export and bunker trade was the high cost and difficulty of loading coal. They particularly complained of the trimming charges, on which a reduction is at present being sought. After several meetings it is announced that the National Joint Trimming Committee has been unable to arrive at any agreement, on future wages, and that notice has been given of a reduction of the present tariff that is to be put into operation on Monday week.

It may be recalled, however, that in addition to the question of charges, shipowners found themselves in difficulty, according to the evidence given before the Coal Commission, with the refusal to coal trimmers to work a third shift. The absence of night work since the war was proved to lead to serious delays not only to coal ships, but also to general cargo vessels, resulting in a bill of expenditure that ought to be avoided. The difficulty arose out of a somewhat complex situation, and the Coal Commission suggested that a conference of all the parties concerned ought to be able to tackle the whole matter and find a convenient solution. So far it does not appear that any steps have been taken towards calling such a meeting. All in all, it is only too clear that before the shipping industry is rehabilitated much work still remains to be done. Unfortunately, so many of the difficulties are contributed from outside the industry. They are not alone adding to operating costs, but many of them are responsible for diminishing our export cargoes, and thus making a double difficulty to always.

headline: COBHAM HOME.
text:
A vast gathering of people lined both'sides of the Thames at Westminster', being reminiscent of Boat Race days, to welcome Mr. Cobham. There were tremendous outbursts of cheering as he passed and repassed Parliament. House's prior to landing at the spot facing the House of Parliament.

headline: TRUST / STEEL / GREAT INTEREST SHOWN IN
text:
HOOVER MAKES A MOVE.

Great interest is being taken in the formation of the European Steel Trust. Mr. H. C. Hoover, Secretary for Commerce, it is reported, has ordered an investigation of the matter.

The opinion is generally expressed, however, that the new combination will not menace the American home market, but will possibly considerably influence the world market.

Mr. Gary, Chairman of the United States Steel Corporation, says he hopes that the Combine will be a great success. "He thinks that its managers will be friendly toward America, whence the sentiment will certainly be reciprocated."

The spokesman of the leading manufacturers at Pittsburgh expresses the opinion that the influence of keener competition as the result of the Combine will be chiefly felt in the Far East and Latin-America, where the cheaper labour transport enjoyed by the Trust will give it an advantage.— Reuter's American Service.

French Socialists' Anxiety.

The Socialist leader, M. Blum, intends to interpelate the Government on the exact tenor of the Steel Convention, the conditions under which the Government controlled the negotiations, and the measures to be taken for the purpose of watching its economic and social repercussions and the possible consequences in regard to France's foreign policy.—Reuter

text:
September 80. being the day mentioned by Mr. Eugene Chen as the date on which the boycott would be most probably terminated, it is interesting to observe that there is no reference in that day's "Canton Gazette" to the possible withdrawal of the pickets.

Relations" is published. “Swear Not to Stop.” The circular concludes:—

The. "China Mail" wishes to be distinctly understood that the foregoing is reproduced merely to clear, if possible, some of the obscurity enshrouding the position at Canton.

"Resumptions Likely" It is not undoubted that a large section of the responsible unofficial classes are anxiously awaiting the settlement. Latest news will be found elsewhere in this issue.

The following paragraphs are translations from the Canton vernacular press:—

The representatives of foreign firms, who had left Shameen on the commencement of the strike, are now beginning to return to Shameen, as relations between Canton and Shameen are likely to be resumed after the termination of the strike.

On Sept 27, the Municipal Council of Shameen, finally cancelled all martial law restrictions and published a special notice that henceforth boats may anchor off Shameen and land passengers, says a Chinese news-agency report. headline: IN A DILEMMA.
text:
MINERS RETURNING IN THOUSANDS.

BUT REJECT PROPOSALS.

An anomalous position has been created in the coal fields, where the miners are returning to work in thousands daily, whilst the districts generally are overwhelmingly rejecting the Government's plan for district settlements and a National Appeal Tribunal.

This is explained by the fact that only in Lancashire has there been a ballot vote and there the men who have returned to work are excluded.

The decisions of other districts were reached at delegate conferences or by a show of hands at Lodge meetings, some of which were only poorly attended.

The Miners' Executive at their meeting in London to-day, are faced with the difficult task of deciding whether to advise the miners' delegate conference to-morrow to continue the struggle or to advise the districts to make the best terms possible without any calling off of the stoppage nationally by the Federation.

The position of the miners' leaders is further embarrassed by the fact that whilst the drift back of the miners threatens the existence of the Federation in South Wales, the miners are demanding the adoption of a militant policy. —Reuter.

Government's Last Word. London's Late

On the eve of the miners' national delegate conference Mr. Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister, has sent a letter to Mr. A. J. Cook stating that the Government's proposal's of September 24 regarding a National Arbitration Tribunal must either be accepted or refused by the conference. If they are accepted the Government will introduce the necessary legislation at the earliest possible moment. If they are rejected the offer, "which has obviously failed in its primary purpose, must" be withdrawn.

headline: No Recommendations.
text:
'Mr. Cook, at the conclusion of the Miners' Executive meeting, announced that the Committee are not making any recoromendations to the delegate conference.—Reuter. $ ^{9} $ Rejection: Foreshadowed:

The latest reports from the mining districts afford further indication of the likelihood that the Government's "offer of a National Arbitration Tribunal" to be set up after the resumption of work on district settlements will be rejected at tomorrow's meeting of the National Delegate Conference. If this negative result is reached the newspapers assume that it will be tantamount to the abandonment of any attempt at a national settlement, as there is no other proposal before the parties to the dispute.

The drift back to work on terms offered by the mine owners, on a basis of a longer working day, continues and to-day it was authoritatively reported that over 193,000 are now employed at producing coal. This figure does not take into account the safety men in the under qits or those engaged on various other duties at the mines. To-day's increase exceeded 7,000.—British Wireless Service.

headline: GERMANS KILLED BY FRENCH OFFICERS.
text:
Berlin, September 28.—The German press demands a strict and impartial investigation of the slaying of two German civilians by French army officers at German-sheim yesterday. The shooting, in which two other Germans were wounded, followed a dispute over lights. The records of the two officers show that they were principals in a similar affair last July and that they were allowed to go unpunished.

The German press is no longer over-the-matter but it claims that there should be a fair and open trial and the editors point out that this incident emphasizes the need for a better German understanding. If the French will keep the letter of the Locarno pack they will withdraw at once all their troops from German soil, so the papers insist.

headline: BOYCOTT END.
text:
British goods would be suspended October 10.

It is understood that the announcement means the complete suppression of pickets and the lifting of all bans against normal communication and trade between Canton and Hong Kong.

There is considerable diversity of opinion as to the reasons for this sudden change of attitude on the part of the Canton authorities and it is thought in many quarters to be a prelude to a movement for obtaining international recognition of the South China Government.

Mission Going Abroad

A report is current that a mission has already been sent to foreign capitals with this end in view.

Another view is that the new British policy of regarding all pickets as pirates, to be hunted down when found operating on the waterways, has been a deciding factor in the case. In this connection it is thought that recent official intimation that 14 British warships, of a type suitable for "river patrol" work, have been ordered to China, "has impressed the Canton Government".
