headline: No Armistice.
text:
To the danger from lurking foes was added that of fire, the pirates lighting large quantities of waste under the bridge in the hope that the officers would be smoked out. The set of the wind was against the object, however, and the pirates themselves were in it inent danger from the flames which spread to the quarter where they had taken up their stand.

The officers on the bridge, strengthened by those who had joined them below through the searchlight, were in a strong position and, recognising the helplessness of their case, the pirates endeavoured to treat with the officers through Mr. Lapsley, the European passenger who is still unaccounted for—having, it is believed, been taken away by the pirates.

The pirates indicated their willingness to cease hostilities if the officers would give up their arms and combine in ences to get the flames under. The overtures were ignored and the pirates then left the ship, as already detailed. This was about 4 a.m.

It was subsequent to the departure of the two boat loads of pirates that the two officers and wireless operator left the ship in the remaining boat with the Russian lady passenger, the fire being at its worst at the time and the action being taken as a result of a consultation between the officers who deemed it the most advisable course. The boat was being threatened by the flames and the opportunity to place the lady passenger in safety might not have arisen again. It was also intended to place on board the Chinese lady passengers, but the half burned painter parted and the boat drifted away.

“Sheep” And “Goats.” The subsequent events consisted of the arrival on the scene in

the early hours of "Tuesday morning of the "Kalyo Maru," the first to wireless the report which was picked up by H.M.S. "Bluebell," the standing by of the "Kalying" and "Suiyang," the quelling of the flames and the boarding of the victimised vessel by an armed party from the "Bluebell" which "sorted out the sheep from the gouts" and put the suspected pirates into irons (they were met in some cases with resistance and had to use force).

In connection with the arrival of the “Kaiyo Muru” and other vessels which stood by, the officers of the “Sunning” report that prior to the arrival of the Japanese vessel, a ship loomed up about three miles away at a time when the ship was blazing and the officers still engaged in defending the bridge against the pirates. This was the hour before dawn. To their astonishment and bitter disappointment, the “mystery vessel,” after heaving to at the sight of the blazing “Sunning,” from which frantic signals of distress were made, proceeded on its course, leaving the stricken ship tossing and burning in the heavy seas.

The tug from Taikoo arrived on the scene at 9:20 p.m. on Tuesday night and within three quarters of an hour was able to hitch up securely and get under way. The tug averaged 7 knots an hour on her way to Hong Kong, a remarkable achievement considering the high seas running and the heavy burden.

Five Thrown Overboard. Among the Chinese crew, there were but minor casualties, a few having received superficial wounds in pluckily resisting the pirates. Five members of the compradore's staff are said to have been thrown overboard, this being due to their loyalty to the No. 1 compradore whom the pirates are reported to have been desirous of securing for the purpose of holding him to ransom.

Compradore's Escape. At the first sign of trouble, the compradore, having blackened his face with oil and coal dust, joined with the members of the crew and escaped observation. Enquiries by the pirates among the compradore staff and crew, and threats used towards the bo'sun failed toicit information as to his wherebouts and the pirates had to be satisfied with leaving the ship without having secured

the ship without having secured him.

One Annamite (third class) passenger is also stated to be missing. It is stated by other passengers that he was thrown overboard by the pirates for resisting search.

headline: Loss By Fire.
text:
The other officers on board, apart from the marks their uniforms bore of their struggle with the flames, and their unshaven appearance, bore few signs of the terrific strain through which they had passed. The flames had not left a vestige of their equipment, papers and personal effects, or of those of the two European passengers. "We have nothing other than we stand up in," said one officer whose uniform had been so badly burned that he had discarded it for a sweater.

The 2nd Officer and Third Engineer, Messrs. J. W. Hurst and A. Duncan respectively, the only other European officers not already mentioned, were those "picked up by the Norwegian vessel which stood by and later conveyed them northwards, together with Mrs. A. Prokofiers. They were the officers who were lowered into the one remaining bout for the purpose of ensuring the safety of the lady passenger. The Norwegian vessel landed them at Swatow.

In addition to the personal effects lost, two mail bags were burned. These were despatched from Amoy for Hong Kong and Canton. The bulk of the mail carried was from Shanghai and this was untouched together with the cargo.

Cargo and Engines: Untouched. This was due to the fire being entirely confined to midships, the most remarkable thing striking the observer being the suddenness with which all traces of the fire ceased on either side. The cargo engine room and other parts of the ship were entirely unaffected. The "Sunning" could, in fact, have come to Hong Kong without tow had it not been for the fact that, having lost steam, she could not get it up again.

headline: RIGID SEARCH.
text:
Chinese opinion in Hong Kong is unanimous that rigid search is necessary at all ports of call on river and/or coastal boats bound for Hong Kong

At the same time, the local authorities are praised for their vigilance in having scared away

piratus gangs from Hong Kong so that they must ship at other places. Criticism of the alleged unwarranted rigour exercised by searchers on Hong Kong wharves has considerably moderated. Sympathy is expressed with the officers crew and passengers of the "Sunning" for their terrible ordeal, but they are thought lucky for not having had to abandon the ship in the confusion of the night when beset by flames as was the case with the "Tai On."

Chinese engaged in the shipping trade are still against suggestions to segregate native passengers while under way on account of possible dangers at sea and making too many innocent sufferer for the sins of the few.

The principal of a firm of Shanghai merchants in Hong Kong said: "It is impossible at present to expect our (the Chinese) Navy to perfect a system of patrols or convoys which foreign warships are put to considerable trouble in maintaining over even a small area.

"Every gang has been traced to Bias Bay except the outlaws on the West and East Rivers (of Kwangtung) who are also bandits and robbers and these are scattered over hills in the adjoining territory."

Novel Chinese Solution. "Bias Bay will provide the solution. A precedent exists, as extradition treaties are provided to help friendly nations in arresting prisoners. Therefore the only cure is for the Nationalist Government to provide the troops and to ask for the co-operation of foreign Navies in a campaign at Rias Bay.

The object, however, should be solely the hunting down of the pirate gangs, and not the bombarding of the vicinity at random. "After that the local military commanders could hold the elders and headmen of each community responsible for their respective clans not having any pirates, at home or abroad. Severe penalties for clansmen would have sufficient deterrent effect on the erring brethren, or the others would see to it that the offenders were delivered to justice."

"This practice was followed with conspicuous success in the latter years of the Manchu dynasty, when Kwangtung was free from robber bands."

A former compradore on a Jardine boat in North China said he very much doubted if the killing and arrest of part of one gang would serve as a lesson to others

His experience of pirates was that they did things on a very businesslike scale and took the expense (including purchase of passages, possible loss of their weapons) as being more important than the risk entailed.

headline: CANTON ADVANCE.
text:
In the House of Commons, to-day, in answer to questions, the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Sir Austen Chamberlain, said that the advance of the southern forces in Central China did not appear to have adversely affected the personal security of British residents or to have involved any serious danger to British property, though inevitably there had been some disturbance to British establishments in the army zone.

The anti-British agitation in Szechuan had led to the destruction of some British property at Chungking, and it had been considered advisable for the women and children to leave that port. Conditions in mid-China were still uncertain, and it would be premature to pass judgment. Questioned as regards the "Sunning" incident, Sir Austen Chamberlain asked for notice of the question. He also requested notice of the question whether he could assure the House that there was a sufficient naval force at Hankow to ensure the safety of British residents there in case of need.—Reuter.

In an article in the "Financial News" on the Chinese crisis, Mr. Hilton Young says, the establishment of the rule of Southern Nationalists throughout China, which recent events have made by no means improbable, would result in a vast area inhabited by nearly one fifth of the world's population erecting between itself and the rest of the world the same impenetrable barrier of suspicion, distrust and dislike at present isolating Russia, and thus the basis of credit would be destroyed and international trade would languish. He says that recent events in Java show how infectious Moscow's propaganda is among an ignorant Oriental population, and opines that Britain's best policy is to approach the Canton Government, giving it some qualified form of recognition, and seek to guide it away from the path of repudiation, so ruinous to China herself.—Reu

The Foreign Office hitherto has not replied to the Belgian Legation concerning the proposal to submit the question of treaty abrogation to the Hague, but certain Chinese and foreign papers to-day state that preparations are being made for an anti-Belgian boycott if Belgium does so.—Reuter.

Senator Borah's View's.

Senator Borah in the course of an address to Jewish women said the present turmoil in China furnished the acid test of the world peace programme.

He opined the real trouble in China was nationalism coming into contact with imperialism. "Any nation which adopted a policy of forcible intervention, there will become the assassin of justice in the Orient."—Reuter's American Service.

The Court of Justice at Median has sentenced a Japanese, Kozo Oriuchi, accused of ill-treating coolies on the Peoloe Mandate state, to 2½ years imprisonment.

"Note the nonchalanee of the Chinese arrested for alleged implication in the sensational piracy of the "Sunning" this week. Crouched in the attitude typical of the average coule, each man against the steamer's railing is handcuffed, either two hands together, or one hand to the next man. Standing behind are Indian members of the Hong Kong Police. The light clothing of most of the suspects, as compared with the thick wadded garments of the Chinese in the lower photo point to their being Southerners."

"Another scene on the deck of the 'Sunning' after the authorities had taken over control. Among the confusion of baggage and lifebelts strewn everywhere, a group of Shanghai passengers of the poorer class are seen bitterly weeping over their misfortune in having been robbed by the pirates. The features and clothing are typically those of North China's emigrants. A bluejacket of the boarding party from H.M.S. "Bluebell" is on the right. The figure in the centre foreground (in the spotted coat) is an extraordinarily fat Chinese girl who refused to be comforted.

headline: STRIKE NOW OVER.
text:
Pakkai, Kongmoon, Nov. 16. Five...secessionists from the Sunning Railway employees' union have been killed and the strike has ended.

Trains are now running again. It will be recalled that as a sequel to the strike for better pay, some of the workmen formed their own union of "Five Districts Railway Engineers."

Six of the leaders were “arrested” by pickets from the central guild in Canton. After five of these were killed the new union was abolished.

The question of increased pay, has not been settled but a truce was brought about by the media-tion of the local authorities and other labour unions.

Pirates Captured.

There has been another primitive expedition against pirates at Ku-cheng. Two pirates were captured and a number of bamboos hits were burned out.

headline: CABLE & WIRELESS / CHEAPER PRESS RATES SOUGHT.
text:
INFLUENTIAL DEPUTATION

London, Nov. 19. A deputation of the Empire Press Union, headed by Lord Burnham, chief proprietor of the "Daily Telegraph," waited on the communications committee of the Imperial Conference this afternoon and submitted a memorandum emphasising the necessity for reduction in cable and wireless press rates within the Empire.

Besides Lord Burnham the speakers included Sir Robert Donald, Chairman of the Empire Press Union, Sir Roderick Jones, the head of Reuter's, Sir Stanley Reed, Editor of the Times of India," Mr. Corsbie Roles, Hon. Secretary of the Empire Press Union, and a Director of the Times of Ceylon" Co., and Mr. Taylor Darbyshire.

The Secretary of State for the Colonies, Mr. L. M. S. Amery and the Prime Minister of Australia, Mr. Bruce, responded very sympathetically and promised most careful consideration of the representations.—Reuter:

headline: SIR PAUL CHATER. / A MEMORIAL TABLET UNVEILED. / YESTERDAY'S SERVICES
text:
Yesterday was observed as Victoria, Diocesan Sunday in all the local Anglican churches when large congregations filled the various places of worship and the collections were devoted to the building fund of the new church at Yamwadi.

The preachers at St. John's Cathedral were the Rev. N. V. Halward M.C., M.A. (Diocesan (Chaplain) at 11 a.m. and the Bishop of Victoria (Rt. Rev. C. R. Dippuy D.D.) at 6 p.m.

The Bishop also preached at the morning service at St Andrew's, Kowloon, after which His Lordship unveiled and dedicated to a memorial tablet to the late Sir Paul Chatter.

The inscription of the tablet, which is at the West end of "the church on the left of that of the late Rev. Spinks, was as follows:

Elected by the congregation. in memory of

Chater, C.M.G., LL.D., etc. Born in Calcutta Septem- ber 8th, 1846

Died in Hong Kong May 27th 1926.

A regular worshipper at the church of which, with both the "Intech Hall and Vicrage, he was the generous donor.

A genius in Finance, a Prince in Charity and with a humble servant of his Masterm

"You, though I walk through the Valley" of the Shadow of Death, "It will fear no evil" for thou art with me."

Taking his text from St. John, 1 v 17. His Lordship said:—

Our Lord is correcting a wrong idea: the idea that God's work in the world has ceased. The work of God He teaches goes on throughout the ages; creation is a continuous process; moment by moment God is working in this Universe; and He give man the privilege of working in this creative work.

You and I are called to be fellow-workers with God in creating the world of tomorrow. Everyone of us has been put into this world to be a creator; to do something which if we fail to do perhaps for ever will remain undone. Each generation as it comes stands for a moment at the centre of time, its work is to create the world of tomorrow.

And to despair of human nature is against the facts. The action of Christ who is Risen on mankind whom He has redeemed fails not but increases" said that eminent historian the late Lord Acton.

I know the world is in disorder, that it is an open question whether the discoveries of the 19 century are to be used for life or Depth. But I know too the world is redeemable; has been redeemed by Christ. Go and evangelise the whole creation, was His command and this is the biggest thing you can ever set your hand to in the world. Utterly unattainable men will tell you. Yes, but it is the mark of the saint that He busies himself with that which is remote and unattainable. Again and again it has been proved that the saint is right, that what is impossible with man is possible with God. The prevailing sin of man is that he is of such little faith, he will not believe that human nature can be redeemed.

And yet it is more apparent today than ever before that it is with Christ that the hope of the world of to-morrow lies, that He is the hope of the nations.

People are beginning to see that you cannot get a new world by having half the nations in it for as Tolstoi so tellingly puts it—“We constantly think there are circumstances under which a human being can be treated with

There is one way by which this world can be put in order, it is the way of Christ, all other ways are deemed to failure."

There are many signs to-day that the time has come, and that men know that the time has come, to make the experiment of applied Christianity on a world scale:

For of spite of all men say—and rightly say — about the Church's failure it is the Church of Christ that holds the key of humanity's unsolved problems and is the steward of what the world supremely needs.

"All mankind is seeking God." Hi, G. Wells says somewhere. "There is not a nation nor a city in this globe where men are not being urged by the Spirit within them towards the discovery of God. The kingdom of God on earth is not a dream nor an uncertain project, it is the thing before us, the close and inevitable destiny of mankind."

Christ, we say, is the hope of the future. You and I are living in a diocese which is supposed to contain something like 70 millions of people and where literally millions have never heard of Christ. Are we doing what we can to evangelise the whole creation, to spread Christianity, to make Christ known?

You may say that this diocese epitomises the history of our branch of the Church in China. As I think about it all I marvel both at what has been done and at the vast undone.

I marvel at what has been done. Eighty years ago, when Sir Paul Chater was born, you may say our branch of the Church did not exist in China. To-day there are twelve bishops and over 180 Chinese clergy. (We have thirteen connected with this diocese.) It seems to me that those 180 clergy are the harbingers of great hope for China.

I marvel too at the vast undone. What are 180 clergy among all the millions of China? Let me take two illustrations to show you the hugeness of this diocese. During the past week I have been speaking with two workers, one going to Nanning and the other to Lungchow. These places are 500 miles away and within the diocese. It is three years since any clergyman has been there to give the Christians Holy Communion; we have none to send. Then a few days before this I was welcoming a new worker for Yunnan-fu, 1,000 miles away, also within the diocese. In a province our Church has only one congregation in the whole area larger than Great Britain. You may travel mile after mile in this diocese and you will find no single messenger of the Cross, literally millions have never heard of Christ. Do you wonder there is disorder? I don't.

Can you I ask, do more than you are doing; to spread Christianity amongst the millions who have never heard of Christ? It is the biggest thing you can do do with your life.

You have an opportunity given you to-day of helping to build a Chinese Church at Yaumati. You can join the Victoria Diocesan Association and get more knowledge of actual needs and join a fellowship of prayer and service.

headline: NICARAGUA.
text:
The statement of Mr. F. Kellogg, Secretary of State, with regard to Nicaragua has brought to the forefront the burning question whether the United States or Mexico have the predominating influence in Central America.

Whilst at present no decision has been reached in regard to President Diaz's invitation, it is understood that Mr. Kellogg will first endeavour to induce the Nicaraguan Liberals who are said to have the support of Mexico, to co-operate with the new Conservative Government. If he is unsuccessful, it is suggested that the United States should lend Marines in order to assist President Diaz to restore a stable government in Nicaragua whose disturbed state is claimed to be due to Bolshevik agencies in Mexico, and the ambition of the Callies Government to increase its sphere of influence to the South.

Ex-President Obregon, in sum- ming up' Mexico's point of view.

Do not complain of lack of power. There is plenty of power in this universe only we do not know how to use it. headline: SIR J. W. JAMIESON.
text:

headline: $11,000 THEFT.
text:
SWEETHEART SHADOPED.

An assistant accountant of an import and export office at 49"Deau Vaux Road appeared this morning before Mr. R. E. Lindsell charged with larceny of $11,100 from his employer.

Sub-Detective Inspector Fallon, who prosecuted for the police, said that on November 16 Mr. Leung Lau-po (master of "the firm"), left his shop with defendant in charge. An hour later, complainant returned, and found missing from his drawer $1,000 in bank notes and a note receipt of $10,000 from a native bank. Inquiries were made at the bank who informed the police that the amount had already been withdrawn.

Defendant was constantly shadowed by the police who were later led to his sweetheart residing at Whitfield Street. The place was searched and $10,300 was found.

Defendant pleaded guilty when the charged was read to him and was sentenced to six months hard labour.

headline: THE BIG WAR. / CHINA HOSTILITIES NOW IMMINENT.
text:
CANTONESE V. FENGTIENITES.

few days, the two strong-est political parties in China will soon be meeting the most determined opposition that each has yet encountered.

A stubborn campaign is certain. In this latest phase of the nation-wide conflict there may lie a solution to the confusion of so many governments, but events in China have taken the least expected course in the past and a prediction is futile at the moment.

Both General Chang Kai-shek and Marshal Chang Tso-lin have won signal victories before. Each has in turn crushed formidable adversaries but not eliminated them.

No Unification Yet?

Wu Pel-fu and Sun Chuan-fang have been stripped of their power but they still have a following. They still count as adversaries of the Nationalists. The Christian general was put to rout by the Fengtienites, but he still has many troops in the north-west.

Even if one of the two major factions is totally removed, when this threatened struggle is over, what is going to happen to the others now remaining in the background? If history is repeated, one side will be trounced but not wiped out. And in this light I venture to think that the time is not ripe, or the field is too vast, for unification to be attained by military conquest.

Chang Tso-lin's Wealth. As to the chances of the rival camps, it is difficult hazard a guess.

Observers with "the Armies point to the Manchurian warlord as being the stronger in men, munitions and money.

To counteract Russian help for the Southerners, Chang Tsolin has his division of White Russians.

Within the last few years, the Fengtien party has amassed considerable wealth — estimated at $10,000,000—with which to equip their army to great advantage.

Against Wu Pei-fu and Sun Chuan-fang, the Cantonese had a telling superiority in a united command whereas these two Northern leaders were dependent on the goodwill of overgrown subordinates miscalled allies. No so with Fengtien.

The system that started from Mukden savours a good deal of feudalism, and each general is personally responsible to the Marshall. More than once subordinates have rebelled but never with success.

One point in favour of the Nationalists, even before the vanguards are at grips, is that some of the people are on their side.

This statement needs to be qualified. The middle and upper classes are partial to nobody, being weary of all disputes.

8he lower or artisan masses are more apt to declare, in their own roundabout way, for the Southerners than for Fengtien.

Very briefly the explanation lies in the Kuomintang policy of taxing merchants and property-owners heavily, while the wage-earner pays little in proportion. Not so, the Northerners. All is grist to their mill.

So much as to conjecture. In territory, the adversaries are fairly evenly matched.

To start with, Chang Tso-lin had three provinces forming Manchuria (known as the three eastern provinces), Chihli and Shantung.

Although constantly offering aid to the Northerners, Fengtien maintained a policy of masterly inactivity against Canton and practically ceased war as soon as the other Nationalist Army that of the Christian general (Feng Yu-hsiang) was removed to a safe distance.

Meanwhile, the Southerners wrested Hunan and Hupeh provinces from Wu Pei-fu. Kiangsi was captured from Sun Chuanfang and Fukien is partly overrun.

To prevent losing everything, Sun Chuan-fang sought. Chang Tao-lin. At this stage, a very recent incident

headline: RUSSIAN HOLIDAY. / CIGLEBRATED BY SWATOWRADICALS.
text:
Swatow, Nov. 8.—The Ninth Annual Versary of the Russian Revoluion was celebrated here yesterday. The celebration included a public open air meeting with a fairly large attendance, the majority being of the Labour classes. The students were in the minority. The programme was made up largely of Communistic propaganda with the most decilled "Red" sentiment that has yet been expressed in Swatow. One young Russian spoke and about twenty Russians were on the platform and sang the Red National song. They then marched through the streets yelling the usual radical yells.

However, the day passed off without any violence and business seems to be progressing. The strike trouble with the employees of the medicine shops has been settled and the men are back at their work. The British boycott is off and the British boats are coming and going and are getting and unloading passengers and some cargo. The pickets are no longer working openly at least and one is not molested in the least in handling incoming or out-going cargo.

The schools and other organisations are celebrating Dr. Sun's "birthday this week and it promises to be a lively week for most of the people.

From the best report we can get the Southern forces have pushed right on into Fukien and will not stop until they have taken the province. In the meantime things seem to be settled here in Swatow and there seems to be no uneasiness whatever that there will be a change within the near future.—“China Press.”

headline: SALT FIGHT / HISTORIC EXEMPTION DE: FENDED BY VILLAGERS.
text:
Huangyen, Chekiang, November 12.—An ugly incident occurred in this district a few weeks ago. While salt is an object of taxation in most parts of China the districts of Huangyen and Taiping on the Chekiang coast are, and have been exempt from this tax from time immemorial. "Attempts have been made by the authorities from time to time to collect this tax, but in every ease it has been the signal for a miniature rebellion of the peasants and salt workers. The last attempt was made unsuccessfully about 60 years ago."

Just a few weeks ago, another effort was made this time under the guise of measuring some land just recently reclaimed from the sea, but still too salty to be of much value. The peasants in this area are still feeling pretty sore because the supineness of the gentry (not to call it an uglier word) in neglecting to have a floodgate built (for which funds were in hand) has caused the destruction of a lot of crop this year. And now come along the officials, trying to impose this new burden of salt taxation. Perfectly legal, but most important. A clash occurred between the peasants armed with hoes; spades, etc., and the soldiers with their rifles. The honours of the day rested with the peasants, six soldiers dead and four peasants. The city magistrate went out to investigate but, it is reported, even his life was threatened! The whole countryside threatened to rise and all the pirates flocked in to the cause of the peasants, who removed live stock and provisions out of the reach of the military. Never! never!! would this district submit to a salt tax. The officials, not liking the look of things, called a palaver. The peasants won; the tax is not to be imposed. The gentry have had to pay an indemnity to relatives of deceased; it is said $600 for a soldier and $400 for a peasant. Surely China after all is a democratic country.—"N.-C. Daily News."

headline: NEW YORK BEAUTIFUL.
text:
London, November 18.—New York has become within recent years "a thing of beauty, fit for the brush of a master artist," Sir John Lavery, R.A., who has just returned from the United States, declared to-day.

"The city which not so many years ago was a succession of prison-like blocks has changed," he said. "Newer and beautiful architecture has appeared, which has completely altered the monotony of the buildings."

Sir John attributed the intensity of New York's inhabitants to "the sparkling and exhilarating ir."—"China Press." STUDENTS' STATEMENT TO CHILD OF POLICE.

The Shanghai Chinese Student's Union on November 14 sent the following letter to the Chief of the Woosung and Shanghai Constabu-lary:

This Union is a public body working for the welfare of students. The activities have been undertaken for the benefit of students only, and it has never committed any lawless acts. Since the May 30 incident this Union has been guiding the students and advising them not to resort to extreme measures. This can be proven and must be within your knowledge as well. Now the general situation is very critical. People in various walks of life have expressed their views, and we have also to voice our opinion in order to show that students are keeping in close touch with the general situation of the country. Unexpectedly, on November 9, a large batch of police suddenly called out the office of our Union, sealed it up and arrested two officers of the Union who are still in prison. The people know that you are doing your utmost to maintain peace and order in this locality, but it is not proper for you to punish those innocent of any crime. Since this unfortunate incident the students of the various local educational institutions have become restless and their minds are greatly disturbed. Despite the advice of this Union, the attitude of these students is in no way reassuring. Thus your measures to maintain peace and order have had just the opposite results. We, therefore, most earnestly request you to order the removal of the seal from the office, the release of our officers and the return of the documents seized so as to show your broad-mindedness. It would be unwise of you to reject our request, because it would lead to constant disquietude. We hope you will give this matter your careful consideration.

headline: NO MORE CABINET MEETINGS?
text:
___

Peking, November 18. — Dr. Wellington Koo's Cabinet has resolved to resign en bloc on the ground that it is very difficult to control the political situation. The resignation of the Cabinet is expected to be announced after the Cabinet meeting which is to be held either on the 20th or on the 23rd.

Resignation was contemplated before the Tientsin Conference was opened, and the Ministers have finally agreed to day. It is generally observed that after the wholesale resignations, no Cabinet meetings would be held, that it would therefore, be impossible for China to open negotiations as to the revision of the Sino-Japanese Commercial Treaty; and consequently negotiations would be deadlocked pending the stabilisation of the situation.—“Toho.”

Mr. W. H. Edmonds of the Water Works, who, is a musketry expert, has received the substantive appointment of Regimental Sergeant Major in the Defence Corps, having held "acting" rank for some time. He goes on leave till July 31 next year.

The programme of the Feast of Our Lady of the Holy Rosary at Nosary Church, Kowloon, on Sunday is as follows:—First Mass, 8.30 a.m.; Second Mass, 7.30 a.m.; Third Mass, 8.30 a.m.; Solemn Pontifical Mass, 9.30 a.m. Evening Service is at 4:30 p.m.

The late Mr. Andrew Adam Bolton, an engineer at the Talkood Dock who died at sea whilst on a homeward voyage by the s.s. "Montclare" on June 16 of this year, left property in Hong Kong, amounting to $10,200. He left everything to his widow, Mrs. Mary Isabella Bolton.

"The Feast of the Little Flower," St. Theresa of the Child of Jesus, — who was canonised last year— was solemnly celebrated at the Roman Catholic Cathedral yesterday. The celebration of the feast consisted of a solemn High Mass sung at 7:30 a.m., and a solemn Holy Hour with sermon and Benediction from 5:30 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Special music under the direction of the Rev. Father A. Riganti was sung in the morning as in the afternoon service.

Hong Kong is shortly to have a distinguished visitor in the person of Dr. John Allison, M.A., LL.D., J.R.S.E., who recently retired from the Headmastership of George Watson's College, Edinburgh. He is at present on a world tour of Watsonian Clubs and is due here on November 22. Old Watsonians who wish to join in extending hospitality to Dr. Allison are asked to communicate with Mr. John Fleming, of Messrs. Lowe, Bingham and Matthews. Paris, Sept. 18.—According to "Le Petit Parisien," Krassin is to proceed to London during the week end, and will become the Soviet Charge d'Affaires.

Do not forget the opening show by Dick Norton's Globetrotters at the "Star" Theatre, Kowloon, at 9.15 p.m. to-morrow.

Shanghai, September 16.—General Liu Tao-lung, commander of the Hankow-Hanyang Defence Forces, yesterday said a visit to the Japanese Consulates at Hankow and formally apologised for the recent firing incident wherein the Japanese warship "Katada" was attacked by Chinese troops.

SHEWAN, TOMES & CO., General Managers HONGKONG.

Näuen, September 9.—According to a dispatch from Moscow, the Chinese Chamber of Commerce at Harbin has demanded that Russia turn over to China 66 villages situated on the left side of the Amur river, which were occupied during the Boxer Revolt. Russia is said flatly to have refused the demands.

headline: REPULSE BAY HOTEL
text: Peking, Sept. 18.—According to a recent census made by the Ministry of Interior, the statistics for foreigners in Peking according to occupations read as follows: Students, 683; those engaged in commerce and industry, 566; missionaries, 121; teachers 50; doctors, 6; prostitutes, 59; those engaged in communication, 37; in mining and fishing, 11; in agriculture and forestry, 5; and lawyers, 2.

headline: CARNIVAL
text:
SATURDAY, 2nd October, 1926. DINNER $4.00 PER HEAD. (FANCY OR EVENING DRESS OPTIONAL.) LATE BUS TO THE HONGKONG HOTEL 12.30 a.m. TABLES MAY NOW BE BOOKED

San Diego, California, September 16.—Vico Consul Fukuoka, a Japanese Vice-Consul of Los Angeles, has arrived here to investigate the machine-gunning of the Japanese schooner "Iwate" by the Mexican fisheries patrol steamer "Tecate" recently. It is reported that the Japanese Government will lodge a protest against the capture and firing happened outside Mexican or American territorial waters.

headline: THE HONGKONG & SHANGHAI HOTELS LTD. / KOMOR'S KOMOR & KOMOR
text:
Moścow, September 16.—The Commintern (Headquarters of the Third Internationale) issued a manifesto to-day, strongly expressing its opposition to any reinforcement of forces in China on the part of the Powers, especially of Britain. Meanwhile, in view of the recent development of the situation in China, various anti-foreign agitations are going on in Russia under the watchword of "Non-interference with Chinese internal politics." Anti-British agitation is particularly active.

Art and Curlo Experts (Established 1869) beg to announce the Opening of their new Show Rooms at: ST. GEORGE'S BUILDING, CHATER ROAD Ground Floor: (Former Cafe Wiseman Promises).

We invite our Patrons and all lovers of Art to inspect our superb collection of Ornaments, Vases, Ivory; Bronze and Crystal Figures, fine Porcelain Teasets and Cups.

For those who are interested in something dainty and exquisite, yet not too expensive, we have the latest patterns in Imitation Pearls, also Crystal and Bead Necklaces.

You will admire our nice variety of Silk Goods and find many Articles suitable for Wedding and Birthday Presents, as well as Prices for Mahjong and Bridge Parties ranging from 50 cents upwards.

London, September 22.—Lord d'Abernon is leaving the Berlin post on October 6. He will give a banquet before leaving at which President Hindenberg will be the guest of honour.

text:

Berlin, Sept. 18.—Dr. Shurman, American Ambassador to Berlin, is going to Washington via Cherbourg to participate in a financial conference with President Coolidge and the British and French Ambassadors to the United States. The Paris Press believes that this may foreshadow a revision of the American policy regarding the French war-debts.

Peking, Sept. 20.—Mr. David Fraser, Peking correspondent of the London "Times," who has been home on holiday, returned to Peking to-day. He came by way of Russia and Siberia, making the trip from London to Peking in thirteen days. Mr. W. H. Donald, Director of the Government Bureau of Economic Information, who has been substituting for Mr. Fraser during the latter's absence, will leave Peking for Shanghai to be gone for two weeks.

headline: Keep BLOOD-POISON Out!
text:
Hankow, Sept. 24.—While two ladies were getting into ricshas yesterday a long-gowned Chinese of the student type came up and spoke to the coolies. As it happened one of the ladies knew the language and was interested to hear the intruder state that the ricsha pullers had promised at the mass labour meeting held on Wednesday not to have foreign passengers in future. He then requested the two coolies to keep their promise. Needless to say they did so by refusing to take the ladies.

text:

It has been found impracticable to continue the weekly launch trips to Stonecutters Island, under the auspices of the Easma Club, owing to the extensive damage caused by the storm this week at the bathing beach.

Mr. Brookes, an English assistant employed on Petatel estate at Batoebahra, was attacked by a Javanese estate labour with a knife when the former attempted to separate two Javanese who were fighting. Mr. Brookes received three wounds. The matter is being taken up by the police.

Singapore, Sept. 22.—On Friday, the Hon. Mr. J. Lorne is to be presented with a valedictory address by the personnel of the local Land Office on relinquishing the post of Commissioner of Lands, S.S., to be acting Resident of Selangor. He will be in Kuala Lumpur for the opening of the Federal Council on Monday. His locum tenens, Mr. Bartlett, will come from Kuala Lumpur after his departure.

Orders for photos can be placed with our representative at Cheung Chau, MR. JACKSON LOWE.

The Japanese Government is reported unofficially to have decided to grant financial assistance to the extent of Yen 10,000,000 per annum for the next 10 years to the proposed aerial transportation company which is to come under the Department of Communications and Commerce operations in 1928.

Employees of the Chinese telegraph Administration are opposing the appointment by the Ministry of Communications in Peking of Mr. Sun Ying-pu as Hulpan (Associate Director) of the local Administration. They say that their wages are at present in arrears and that it is useless to appoint a new man with a salary $240 monthly.

London, Sept. 13.—The Australian Ladies' Pipe Band, which is visiting Scotland in connection with the Braemar gathering, was involved in a motor accident at Bowling, near Glasgow. The party were enjoying a trip in five private cars, when the stering gear of the leader went wrong. The motor behind crashed into the first and both were wrecked. Two men and one woman were killed, while two women were injured.

Madras, Sept. 14.—There was a tragic sequel to the broken engagement of Milly Figeredo, an Anglo-Indian girl of 20, who was hacked to death by Gonsalves, an unemployed Anglo-Indian, who is alleged to be her lover. It appears that the accused had paid attentions to the girl for some time, but the engagement was objected to by the girls' parents. This morning, while on her way to the M.S.M. Railway Stores, where she was employed, the girl was attacked by Gonsalves with a big knife. After the murder he escaped, keeping at bay his pursuers on the road by brandishing his knife. The Police arrested him later.

The movement of a large quantity of military supplies for the Allied Army of Marshal Sun Chuan-fang occurred during the week-end, when 120 chests containing pistols and revolvers, 600,000 rounds of small arm ammunition several cannon, and a load of food stuffs were sent to, Nanking.

Shanghai, September 18.—Great consternation was caused in local Chinese circles by the decision of the Mixed Court to hand over to the Chinese authorities the eight youths who were arrested during the demonstration on September 7, as well as the Cantonese General who was arrested lately on a charge of alleged conspiracy against the Nanking government.

Although “White Australia” is the slogan of that country, it is yet fair-minded enough to realise that whatever race subject to British rule has settled there and become eligible for citizenship, is entitled to a fair deal. The law in Australia provides that for every child born the mother is to receive five pounds sterling. A bill has now been passed providing that this maternity allowance should also be extended to Asiatic women who are British subjects living in Australia.

Autumn sacrifices will be offered on October 6 to Kuan-ti, the God of War, and to the spirit of Yoh Fei, a famous general of the Sung Dynasty, who is regarded as the most famous warrior in Chinese history. Dr. V. K. Ting, Director of the Port of Shanghai, will be represented by Col. Wang Yah-chi, commander of the 18th Chekiang Regiment, as master of ceremonies and he will be assisted by General Yen Chun-yang, Commissioner of Shanghai and Woosung Police. Local officials and leading merchants will attend.

The All-Ceylon Motor and General Engineering Exhibition, organised by the Automobile Club of Ceylon, will be opened on January 6, 1927, by His Excellency the Governor, and it will continue for ten days. Arrangement for the coming Exhibition, which will be held on a site opposite the Public Hall, are on a far larger scale than in any previous year and the Shows is likely to prove a record in every respect. The 1921 Exhibition, held in Victoria Park, was the biggest of its kind held in Ceylon, but the forthcoming Exhibition will be three times as large as the 1921 Exhibition.

Marshall Wu Pei-fu has telegraphed to the Shanghai Chinese General Chamber of Commerce expressing his full support of their demands for the cancellation of the old treaty between China and Belgium and stating that "if China is to be saved all unequal treaties must be cancelled.

The forthcoming weddings are announced of Bernard Crowley, assistant, Butterfield & Swire, residing at No. 1, "Woodside," Quarry Bay, to Augusta Crowley, of Staines, England; and Carlos Antonio Remedios, clerk, residing at No. 37, Granville Road, Kowloon, to Eulalia Christina Sousa, residing at No. 584, Nathan Road, Kowloon.

Nauen, September 16.—The Chinese Ambassador to Rome, Mr. Tang Tsai-fu, who is representing China at the meeting of the League, offered a special greeting to the German representative, an act of courtesy which is accepted in German circles with much satisfaction and as a happy initiation of successful co-operative work in the League of Nations.

Madrid, Sept. 28.—For the first time since the close of the World War, a large party of German tourists is visiting Tangier. The party is composed of wealthy men and their wives and has had special accommodations on sea and land. The Germans, who formerly formed a big factor in tourist trade, stopped all visits here during the war. The return is the occasion for much show of hospitality.

Mrs. Gensen of Kobe died peacefully at sea, aboard the "Empress of Canada," on September 12 at 4 o'clock in the afternoon. She was on her way to the United States for treatment of cancer, having just come from Karuzawa, where she had been under the care of Dr. N. Gordon Munro, director of the hospital at that summer resort. Mrs. Gensen was accompanied by her daughter, G. Grindow,

headline: A WEEK'S PAPERS IN ONE OVERLAND CHINA MAIL / OUTSTANDING EVENTS
text:
This week's events of outstanding interest were the disastrous typhoon and Canton's official announcement of the termination of the boycott.

Folks at Home often see and hear a great deal about the havoc of cyclones in this part of the world. What better than to send them a realistic account of your experiences on Monday, coupled with the vivid descriptions in the “Overland China Mail”? All the articles in the daily edition of local interest are reproduced. Instead of having to write a tiresome letter about what actually happened the best alternative is to send a copy of the paper specially designed for the use of friends, relatives and former residents.

headline: IS THE BOYCOTT OVER?
text: In a few days it will be possible to tell whether the boycott has ended. All the steps leading up to the decision by the Canton Government—together with official communiques—are included in this week's issue. Readers are also told about the effects in Canton and Hong Kong and what is being done in anticipation of the return to normal conditions.

The forthcoming wedding is announced of Cezar Outairies Baptist, banker, residing at "Alpha," Hart Avenue, Kowloon, to Elfrida Maria Gomes da Silva, residing at No. 23, Jordan Road, Kowloon.

Dr. Wu Chi-lin, formerly Chinese Minister to Peru, arrived in the Colony by the s.s. "Empress of Asia" yesterday. Dr. Wu has lately been practising in North China and has come to Repulse Bay for a short holiday.

Through the courtesy of Mr. H. W. Ray, the manager of Hong Kong Amusements, the students of the Sacred Heart English School will give a stage performance for students of the schools managed by Rev. Father G. M. Spada, at the Tai Yat Theatre on October 10, at 10 a.m. In the development of fighting aeroplanes driven by powerful engines and capable of very high speeds the United States authorities, in conjunction with medical experts, have been investigating the physical effect upon pilots of swift dives and sudden accelerations. In some trial movements carried out at extreme speeds, pilots reported a sudden feeling of blindness. This, in the doctors' opinion, was due to the fact that the blood had been driven temporarily from the head.

Mr. Verhomal Shewaram, the proprietor of Pioneer Silk Store, who has recently been in Japan for a pleasure trip is returning by the French Mail s.s. "D'Artagnan," on or about the 12th inst. During his stay in Japan, he was entertained by all his friends in Yokohama and Kobe.

Admiral Sir Robert Harris, whose death was recorded recently, was a great sportsman, and hunted game in all parts of the world. In China, one of his largest "bags" was secured on the banks of the Yangtze. In 14 broken days shooting a party secured 794 head of game, Sir Robert's contribution being 109 wild pheasants, nine hares, 22 anipe, 17 quail, 13 pigeons, five ducks, and five various, 180 in all.

Singapore, September 28—Mr. Tessensohn, who died at Singapore on Sept. 26, was admitted to the General Hospital about six weeks ago and although his illness took on a serious complexion and necessitated an operation being performed, it was not expected, in spite of his ripe age (71 years) that there would be a fatal termination. His mother, who survives him, is 93 years of age. He leaves a widow and several children, grandchildren and great grandchildren, with whom much sympathy is felt. The funeral of the honourable gentleman took place at Bidadari Cemetery on Sept. 27 and was very largely attended. The deceased gentleman's relatives, including his sons, daughter, and many grandchildren, were amongst those who were present at the cemetery. Fourteen grouse from the Scottish moors were despatched from Southampton recently by steamer for New Zealand, where efforts will be made to rear them.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL NEWS.
text:
Berlin.—The Duke of Hohenberg, eldest son of the murdered Archduke Francis Ferdinand of Austria, has become engaged to the Countess Elizabeth Wolfegg-Waldburg. The duke was a boy of 12 when the assassination of his parents at Serajevo led to the world war. Of the total number of 1,318 opium smokers and eaters who underwent the treatment by the Singapore medical authorities for curing them of the habit 580 absconded without completing the treatment. It is in the early stages of the treatment, during which the patients suffer from great discomfort, that patients abscend, states the annual medical report for last year. The mental effect is very pronounced and in bad cases when the craving is at its height they literally roll about and groan in agony. The reasons for admission for treatment are stated to be financial in practically every instance and not to be rid of the supposed ill-effects of the drug. As regards the starting of smoking, the reason appears to be equally divided between pleasure and sickness.

Winnipeg.— The Duke of Leuchtenberg, a relative of the late Czar of Russia, who fought in the Russian Imperial Army during the war, intends to settle in Canada and is selling his estate in Bavaria. He is at present touring with a party in Western Canada.

Mr. T. H. Woo, who has served for 30 years as Senior Accountant Clerk, was the recipient last week of a presentation from the staff of the Civil Engineer in Chief's Department of the Naval Yard. Mr. Carothers, in presenting him with a token of esteem from the European staff, expressed regret at the loss of an able and efficient officer.

The Hong Kong A.D.C. are exceedingly busy these days; rehearsing their productions for "Cricket Wcek." According to the experts, the programme will be a very fine one and present indications point to the entertainments being some of the best and most amusing ever staged by the Club. Full houses and a record success are confidently anticipated.

The many friends of Mr. E. L. Matteson, late general agent of the Dollar Line in Hong Kong, will regret to hear that his 16 months' old daughter died after a brief illness, from bronchial pneumonia in San Francisco on September 6. Mr. Matteson and family left here on leave in April last and the bereavement occurred while on a visit to Mr. Matteson's mother, Dr. Susie Frasior. The funeral took place on September 9.

Marshall Sun-Chuan-fang has issued a proclamation addressed to the people of Shanghai reiterating his sympathy for the sufferings of the nation in general and the local Chinese in particular. He adds that he will do his utmost to keep affairs running smoothly and peaceably in the provinces under his control, and to that end he has given instructions to his troops to come down on trouble makers with the utmost severity. Also, all undesirables will be expelled from his territory. The South Australia House of Representatives has passed a vote of appreciation of the services of Mr. Gunn on his resignation of the Premiership. Mr. Gunn resigned to become a member of the Migration Commission.

headline: GREEN ISLAND CEMENT CO., LTD.
text:
Nairobi.—After many years of sporadic research a serious effort is to be made to exploit the coal discovery on the Kenya coast. Following the completion of negotiations with the Government for better concessional terms, an influential South African mining syndicate has taken over the prospecting work and a gang of drillers has been employed. There is every geological indications or a workable coal bed and coal veins have actually been discovered. If coal is found in paying quantities it will have a remarkable effect on the railways and industry of Kenya.

Sir Tiruvalargudi Avargal, a member of the Legislative Assembly of India, who is at present visiting Canada, declared that the feminist movement was spreading in the East. In India, he said, the bobbed hair fashion was making inroads on the customs of antiquity.

Dr. Franklin Stewart Harris, prominent chemist, arrived in Japan on September 20 from San Francisco on the Dollar Line steamer "President Wilson," to attend the Pan-Pacific Science Congress to be held at Tokyo. He represents the Brigham Young University Provo, Utah. Dr. Harris is to deliver a lecture on alkaloid soil and also on various problems of the subject.

Johannesburg. — A athletic coaches here have declared war on the Charleston dance, which had become extremely popular. They assert that the dance bunches the muscles and checks runners speed. Prominent athletes confirm this. There is now a decided drop in the popularity of the Charleston. One coach holds that several modern dances seriously affect athletics and that the Charleston “is the limit.”

Hankow, September 27.—Presumably most people are aware that Dr. Aird is leaving the port for good at the end of October, and there is a very general feeling that he should not be allowed to depart without receiving some outward proof of the Community's appreciation of the unstinted service he has given for over twenty years and the very deep regret they feel that those services have come to an end.

Boys of Scarborough. Seh Training School, during a holiday cruise in their schooner, "Maise Graham," have had a hostile reception in Germany. Lieut. Heather, the headmaster of the school, writing from the Kiel Canal, says:—We all went into the town of Kiel, but we soon came back: Children and young men and girls openly jeered at us, the younger kiddies running alongside with what were evidently insulting remarks.

Orders for photos can be placed with our representative at Choung Chau, MR. JACKSON LOVE. House No. 11, or from— LEE FONG, artistic photographers, Phone: C. 4028. 7, Wyndham Street.

The Municipal Council of Batavia has considered a big scheme for the improvement of the lighting and sanitation of the town. The plan includes the filling in of the Molenvliet "kali," better street lighting, and the erection of wash-houses for laundrymen. At present all Batavia wash clothes in the "kali."

Osaka, September 29.—A collision between a submarine and a schooner, in which the former knocked her head against the latter from under, occurred yesterday afternoon near Kure. The submarine ("Ro-18") was slightly damaged, but the schooner loaded with copper ore, was seriously damaged and sunk. The crew was rescued.

Peking. September 28.—The Telephone Administration faced with numerous applications for the installation of telephones, has sent out "a general letter to all telephone users in "arrears with their bills that unless complete payment of old bills is made at once the instruments will be removed. It is stated that great numbers of telephone subscribers have failed to pay their bills for months past.

Ottawa—Owing to a shortage of 20,000 harvest hands in Western Canada wages have been increased from 14s. to £1 a day, all found. An influx of harvesters from the United States is hoped for and extra trains are being run from all Canada east of the Great Lakes in the hope of gathering last-minute crews. Emergency calls from the west, especially from Saskatchewan and Alberta are reaching the Government.

Alcoholic delights have a strong appeal for the natives of Raratonga, the principal island of the Cook group, according to a description of South Sea Island drunkenness by Mr Robert Keable, the author. There are certainly many stories of the strength and potency of the home-brewed intoxicants most favoured by the islanders, and it is said that the drink is usually made from the roots of a certain tropical plant. After partaking too freely of this native "fire water" one night, a certain Scotsman returned to his shipmates and, in reply to their questions as to the quality of the liquor, replied—"Man, it's enough to make a rabbit sit up and spit in the face of a bulldog!"

Passengers arriving by the U.S. "Sabarbruecken from Europe included Mr. and Mrs. A. Fothergill and Mr. G. Boediker.

Among the passengers arriving yesterday by s.s. "President Jackson" was Miss "B. Woods, daughter of the Governor of the Philippines, en route for Seattle.

Sir H. H. J. Gompertz, Chief Justice, F.M.S., and formerly Puisne Judge at Hong Kong, is expected to arrive in Kuala Lumpur to-day. He returned from Home on the a.s. "Mantun."

The forthcoming wedding is announced of Franc Stewart Gumley civil engineer, of Humphreys Buildings, Kowloon, to Elizabeth Margaret Grey Hall, of Selkirk, Scotland.

It is reported that the Chinese Customs Administration proposes to send a score of members of the Chinese staff to Europe, America and Japan to study customs systems in those countries. Those who have been in the service for seven years will be qualified to go.

Superintendent T. I. Vaughan, of the Shanghai Municipal Police, has been appointed to the post of Chief Superintendent. This promotion follows the retirement from the force of Chief Superintendent Wilson, who left the force last Thursday after 43 years' service. Superintendent Vaughan is a very popular officer and for some time has been doing special work often appearing in court as prosecutor for the Municipal Police.

Friends of Mr. Ralph A. Cooper will be interested to know that his mother-in-law, Mrs. A. T. Smith, was the leading speaker at the Liberal meeting at Portage-in-Prairie, Manitoba, on Sept. 4. The meeting was in support of Mr. Evan McPherson, Liberal candidate, who defeated the Hon. Arthur Neighen, former Premier of Canada, Mrs. Smith is an experienced public speaker, having been President of the Canadian Presbyterian Women's Society for some time. Both Mr. and Mrs. Cooper have been active workers for the Liberal party in Canada for many years.

"The Colony had a clean bill of health on Wednesday when no cause of notifiable disease was reported."

We are informed by Messrs. Chellerum & Co. that their grand Autumn Sale will close on Saturday, the 9th instant.

Adelaide. — The South Australian Government has granted half an "acre of the grounds of Government House, with a frontage of 105 feet on the north terrace, for a war memorial which is to cost £25,000. Competition for the design is restricted to South Australians who are British. The Returned Soldiers' Association are taking an "enthusiastic interest in the project.

By order of the Soviet Government, a Russian medical Corps, consisting of a number of doctors, chemists, and 16 nurses, left Moscow for Urga on September 21. Their object is stated to comprise the study of health conditions in Mongolia, as well as the furnishing of medical treatment to the Mongolian people, and their headquarters will be established in the western suburbs of Urga. The Medical Corps took with it a large quantity of medicines and surgical instruments.

Negotiations are being carried on between the Soerabayapostal authorities and the manager of Messrs. Whiteaway, Laidlaw and Co. Scerabaya branch with a view of establishing an auxiliary post office on the branch premises. These negotiations have so far been unsuccessful but the manager of Whiteaways has cabled to his head office in London for further advice.

London, September, 22.—A sensation has been caused by the London Stock Exchange posting up an official notice prohibiting its members from taking out bookmakers' licences or from using the Stock Exchange or members' office as betting premises. The prohibition applies to clerks also. There are at present many bookmaker members of the Stock Exchange and the Committee has so far winked at the practice, but, as all bookmakers must now be registered, the Committee has stepped in to point out that the articles of association do not allow a bookmaker also to be a member of the Stock Exchange.

Aneta reports that there has been considerable activity in Java in an illicit trade in pre-war German bank notes, particularly the brown 1,000-mark notes. The chief centre appears to be at Singapore, and the victims are generally native Hadji's travelling via Singapore to the Dutch East Indies.

Peking, September 27.—According to reports published in the "Shih Chieh Jih Pao," a large unit of Cantonese troops is now beginning a campaign against Anhui Province from south-east Hupeh, with Anking as the objective, for the purpose of cutting in two Sun Chuan-fang's forces. Their immediate objectives are Yingshan, Taihu and Sosung.

Johannesburg. — The brothers Ratshosa, "Chiefs of the Bamangwato tribe in Bechuanaland, are appealing against the sentence of ten years' hard labour passed on them for an attempt to murder the regent of the tribe, Tshkedi, on Easter Monday. The appeal is being heard at Mafeking. The appellants' counsel addressed the court for 24 hours, a record speech for South Africa.

A "Daily Mail" reporter who set out to find a tall policeman, had only a few hundred yards to go before "hearing of Police-Constable Nichols, of the City of London force, who is the tallest policeman in England. He is 6ft. 8in. in his socks." A Manchester rival is a mere 6t. 6½in. In addition to Constable Nichols, the City of London police claim to have several taller men than the Manchester giant in their ranks. The Metropolitan Police say that they can produce a number of police officers more than 6ft. 7in. The City Police are generally regarded as the tallest in the world.

Peking, September 30.—The resuscitation of the old Peiyang military party is foreshadowed in a telegram from Chengchow published in the "Yi Shih Pao" this morning, which states that Marshal Wu Pei-fu, in a speech before the Commanders, advocated the reunion of the adherents of the party and suggested that ex-President Tsao Kun should visit the various Provinces for the furtherance of the proposed reunion. The telegram states that Marshal Tsao Kun will shortly visit Anhui and, Chekiang in order to interview Marshal Sun Chuan-fang, General Lu Hsiang-ting and other influential persons.

headline: NOW ON / GREAT REDUCTION / A WEEK'S PAPERS IN ONE.
text:
What better to tell people interested in Hong Kong everything about the latest events, than to send them a copy of the "Overland China Mail"—the weekly edition of all "local" and "Chinese" news—accurately representing life out here?

In convenient size and ready for the mails on Saturday, this week's edition has several features worthy of notice:

All the subsequent typhoon reports from last Thursday are included, completing a terrible tale of havoc and loss of life.

The latest piracy is described:

The "China Mail" has made it a practice of adding footnotes and explanations to all articles that present difficulties to non-Chinese. Such are faithfully reproduced in the "Overland." If you are stumped for an answer this edition will help you out, either as news for folks at Home or as a handy reference.

Then again, the daily developments in the "boycott settlement" are recorded. Instead of writing a long letter send a copy instead and thereby get a full narrative, containing all views.

You are also told about the trend of our Naval movements on the Yangtse, about the anti-British demonstration, and about the present war—how the Cantonese met their equals for the first time and how defence is being converted into offence.

Other items are the special "end of boycott" cartoons: the set of photos of all Canton's celebrities: local weddings: correspondence &c.

READY ON FRIDAY. Homeward Mail closes on Saturday at 2.30 p.m. and the Siberian Mail at 5.00 p.m.

Groton, Mass., October 2,—A revolver and rifle battle between the Kn Klux Klan and the Anti-klan forces numbering more than 500 in which more than 100 shots were fired after midnight was under investigation by the authorities today.

Mrs. K. G. Robinson, of Kingsclere Hotel, Kowloon, has reported to the police that she lost a pair of field glasses, valued at $30, on Wednesday afternoon. The article, which bears her initials, was left on a seat at the "Star" ferry wharf on the Hong Kong side.

A Chinese who was recently arrested in Kowloon City with a dagger and two pieces of wire in his possession was to have appeared before two magistrates at Kowloon yesterday afternoon, but owing to the inability of Major C. Wilson to sit together with Mr. J. H. B. Nihill, the case was adjourned until next Tuesday.

Rangoon.—The Burma ruby mines are being offered for sale as a going concern, subject to the approval of the Government of India. The mines, which are at Magot, have been operated by a London company for many years, and have produced from surface working gems to the value of three crores of rupees (about £2,000,000).

"There has been no legislation and no attempt at legislation in regard to flannelette," said Dr. W. Aylmer Lewis, holding an inquest on Anne's Beddow, aged E4, wife of a market gardener at Balmer-grove. Welshampton, Shropshire, who died from burns. Nearly all the coroners in England, said Dr. Lewis, were tired of talking about the dangers of flannelette. The number of inquests he had held on deaths from this material was appalling, but to protest was like the voice of one crying in the wilderness.

Washington, October 2.—President Coolidge gave assurances to day that there would be no material reduction in national defence appropriations for the next fiscal year. This synchronised with the disclosure that the War Department already has taken steps to loop nearly 1,000 enlisted men off the regular army this year to avoid a deficit under the current appropriation in connection with the stop order on recruiting issued September 15. It was explained, however, that the cut in the enlisted strength is temporary and does not mean a permanent reduction of the army.

The Warrant Officers and Sergeants of the East Surrey Regiment are giving a farewell dance in the R.E. Theatre, Wellington Barracks to-morrow evening. The first experiment of broadcasting a film was made from the Manchester station. A film called "The Greater Glory," a story of Vienna during the war, was chosen, and a dramatised version of it was given from the studio, with an announcer relating the story as the scenes changed. An orchestra supplied the appropriate martial or peaceful atmosphere, and a medley of cheering supplied the crowd effects.

The forthcoming weddings are announced of Albert George Martin, engineer in the employ of Messrs. Jardine Matheson Co., Ltd.; to Isabel Emma Louisa Holloway, residing at the Army Ordnance Quarters; and Hilmar Flrenz Sommers, of the Union Building, to Ethel Mary Saffold, of Repulse Bay Hotel.

Buenos Aires, September 28.—The Argentine Supreme Court today ruled that foreign women may acquire Argentine citizenship by complying with the usual formalities. This opens the door for rich American women to obtain easy divorces for the Argentine law will now be more attractive than that of France.

The Bishop of Truro has received from an anonymous donor the sum of £7,000 towards the provision of a new church at Carbis Bay. This help comes most opportunely when an attempt at church extension is being made in the many new places around the coast of Cornwall that are becoming increasingly popular as holiday resorts. The gift was received through the post in seven brand new £1,000 Bank of England notes enclosed in a registered envelope, with a tiny scrap of paper bearing in little characters the words, "For Carbis Bay Church."

In memory of the late Mr. James Oxberry, an inscribed tablet was unveiled at the R.A.O.B. Institute last night in the presence of a large attendance of members. Feeling reference to the work of the "Father of Buffaloism in the Far East" and the loss the Order had sustained in his death was made by Primo Jefferys, P.G.P. of China. Among those present at the unveiling ceremony was Mrs. Oxberry, the widow, who was presented with a framed set of "in memoriam" verses, composed by Bro. Douglas Gibb, Secretary of the R.A.O.B. Institute. An "Open Night" concert followed the programme having been arranged by Mr. Jack Grenham. Cologne.—Train-wrecking attempts continue in the Rhineland and Westphalia. Recently a train from Mayence to Coblenz was heavily stoned and two travellers were seriously injured by glass splinters. Near Plettenberg an electric train was derailed and it was found that the line had been tampered with. Similar reports have been received from other parts of Germany and the State Railway authorities are offering large rewards for the apprehension of the perpetrators.

Amsterdam, September 22.—Serious disorders are reported from Ede, in the Province of Gelderland, but no fatalities have occurred. The War Office statement confirms the reports and says that complete order has now been re-established.

Copenhagen.—A Danish doctor named Vendel believes that he has discovered the cause of foot-and-mouth disease in a fungus of the Monilla family. His theory is that this fungus acts as the primary agent of infection and creates favourable conditions for other bacteria to become malignant. Iodine proved effective against the action of the fungus at an early stage of the disease.

New York.—According to a Billings (Montana) message, Thomas D. Campbell, "known in America as the 'World's Wheat King," is in the midst of what is believed to be the largest thrashing enterprise in the history of agriculture. On the 48,000 acres he has under cultivation on the Crow Indian Reservation he is thrashing, a wheat crop which he estimates "will reach 500,000 bushels." Upwards of 200 men are employed in the actual thrashing operations.

Concord New Hampshire, September, 30.—The Democratic state, convention to-day went on record as favouring the enforcement of all laws "including the Eighteenth amendment," and held the Republican party responsible for the failure to enforce the dry laws. Ex-Senator Thomas P. Gore of Oklahoma in the keynote address to the convention that the farmers of the west were displeased, with the administration which he said promised everything and gave nothing, assailed the Republican claims of prosperity and economy as fictitious.

A unique display of Chinese fireworks will be given at "Lee Garden", East Point, tomorrow and on Sunday, beginning at 3.30 each night. The feature of the show is a "human bonfire dance," not unlike the war gestures of the Red Indians. As far as is known, the performer is decorated with cartwheels and other explosives and he moves around in such a way as to give an impression that a lighted set was going round automatically. The necessary articles for the displays have been brought down from Canton at considerable risk and expense—owing to interference by "strike pickets."
