"It appears that many people in other provinces" (writes the Kueiyang correspondent of the "N.C. Daily News") "think that travelling in Kueichow is very dangerous on account of robbers. I am glad to say that since Gen. Chow Hsi-cheng took over the Governorship of the province, he has been steadily suppressing robbers and it is probably as safe to truvel in most parts of this province as elsewhere.

The Western conception of "the sinister Oriental" it seems is not yet dead. On November 17, says the "N.C. Daily News," a number of "Ryndum" students, anxious to get as much colour as possible in the short space of time at their disposal, but with no ambitions in the way of waking up in the middle of the night with "a fendish yellow devil" leaning over them with a knife, demanding their money or other life, asked a police officer if he thought it would be very dangerous to sleep in a Chinese hotel for the night. We suspect the officer of a sense of humour, for though his reply is not on record, we do know that the students dropped the idea.

General Chen I, Civil Governor of Chekiang, accompanied by 20 of his bodyguards, arrived at the North Station, Shanghai, on November 18, from Hangzhou by rail, and left for Nan-king. He was met on arrival at the station by Dr. V. K. Ting, director of the Woosung-Shanghai Special Administrative Area, General Li Pao-tsang, commander of the Shanghai Martial Law Area, Ning Shao-san, managing director of the S.N.R. and S.H.N.R. stations, and a party of police and soldiers.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL NEWS
text:
One seventh of the human race are Moslems and every one of them should make a pilgrimage to Mecca at least once.

Washington, September 28.—Five thousand special agents of the Treasury Department began the task of checking income tax dodger in all parts of the country. A drive was also launched for the purpose of collecting about $400,000,000 in overdue taxes.

Long Island City, New York, Sept. 27.—An unidentified man ran amuck during a local baseball contest and murdered the umpire Patrick McTavey, before a large crowd of spectators. Several persons had just yelled "kill the umpire" to emphasise their disapproval of his last decision. The man ran from his seat to the centre of the field and struck McTavey, where after he escaped leaving no trace.

Tokyo, Sept. 20.—A "schooner seaplane," equally at home on the waves or in the air, is being tested by the Japanese Navy. The machine carries a light must and sails in its fuselage and in event of a forced landing and a disabled motor can sail into shore just like a windjammer. The hydroplane is of the "R" series of the Naval Aviation Corps. It is equipped with radio and propelled by two Rolls Royce motors of 360 horse power.

Washington, September 28.—The White House spokesman denied reports recently circulating in Washington to the effect that the United States government was about to enter into treaty negotiations with Soviet Russia for the purpose of reaching terms for recognition. It was stated that there was no prospect of immediate change in the relations between the American government and Russia and that certain fundamental obstacles had first to be removed before such negotiations could be undertaken.

Hankow, Sept. 25.—The native press states that over 70 wounded soldiers of Fan Chung-sheu arrived at Liu Kia-miao yesterday, afternoon. These soldiers had been engaged in the severe fighting which had taken place the day before yesterday northward of Sinyang, with the troops of Tien Weiching for a successive day and night. The casualties of Tien resulting from the fighting are stated to be 1,000 odd soldiers killed, and several hundred wounded. The loss was estimated over 10,000 rifles and bombs were in large quantities.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL NEWS.
text:
Mr. M. J. Quist, Netherland Consul-General in Hong Kong, will be away on a month's holiday from to-day (5th instant); during his absence Mr. A. Methofer, Vice Consul, will be in charge of the Consulate-General.

Washington, September 28.— Major General John L. Hines will be relieved as chief of staff of the army and assigned to command the Ninth Corps Area at San Francisco on November 20. He will be succeeded as chief of staff by Major General Charles P. Summerall.

Syracuse, N. Y., Sept. 28.—The Democrats in state convention today unanimously and for the fifth time nominated Governor Alfred E. Smith for governor of New York. There was tremendous enthusiasm after the nomination. Modification of the Volstead act and American adherence to the world court were among the chief recommendations in the declaration of the party principles adopted by the convention.

Kuala Lumpur, Sept 23.—The Methodist Boys' School, Kuala Lumpur, launched an appeal for funds to enable them to enlarge their present school building in order to meet the increased demand for admission. Besides this appeal to the public, the staff and pupils of the school took it upon themselves to explore all possible avenues which would bring them financial help. The result of this united and determined effort was seen, when Mrs. H. W. Thomson laid the foundation stone of the new building.

Formerly, secretary to the Baroness Burdett-Coutta, and to Sir James Brooke, Rajah of Sarawak, the late Mr. Henry Wagner (85), of Belvedere Terrace, Brighton, son of a former Vicar of Brighton, whose will was published recently, left unsettled property valued at £196,824, with net personalty £184,880. Mr. Wagner, who was a barrister, and one of the oldest members of the Alpine Club, left over £38,000 for charity and his numerous legacies included sums of £2,000 each to his cousins, Dean Tage, of St. Paul's Cathedral, and the Rev. Charles Culbertson of St. Giles, Oxford. Penang, Sept. 27.—The death of Mr. J. L. Woodford is announced and the funeral took place at the Western Road Cemetery on Saturday. There was a large attendance and many wreaths were sent. The Rev. Father A. Devals, of the Church of the Assumption, officiated

Geneva, Sept. 29, — Major General Dennis E. Nolan told the missionary disarmament commission to-day that America was unable to accept the national defence budgets and measures of the commission. He said the pay of one American soldier covers 58 French, 41 Italian, and eleven Japanese soldiers.

Hankow, Sept. 25.—The Chinese paper publishes the news that the piece of land located near the cemetery of the six countries near the Japanese Concession purchased by Chao Yuen-hwa, late Chief Executive of the front line under Marshall Wu, at the cost of several million dollars, had been confiscated by the Revolutionaries on the 22nd instant.

Amsterdam, "Sept. 27.—16 is learned in financial circles that the Laras Rubber Estates are making important additions to their holdings in Sumatra and have just purchased a plantation of 2,395 acres, in full coffee and rubber production for the reported price of $4,500,000. The former owners were a Dutch Indian land syndicate. The new concern is preparing to offer 2,000,000 shares, also 7 per cent. first mortgage debentures totalling 625,000 pounds sterling.

Ichang, September 10.—Yesterday the French steamer "Yung-An" arrived from Chungking, bringing the Chinese staff and crew from "Butterfield and Swire's steamer "Wanhsen," which has been held captive at Wanhsen by General Yang Sen. Later in the day another French steamer, the "Yung-fung, arrived from Chungking, bringing Mr. D. H. Davies of the Customs service.

Washington, Sept. 27.—As a result of the resignation to-day of Allan Dulles, chief of the Near East Division of the State Department, several more resignations of persons occupying high positions are expected shortly in protest against the low salaries paid by the government. The resignation of Dulles is the culmination of many months of agitation by assistant secretaries and heads of special bureaus against the scale of salaries which, they declare, are entirely inadequate to meet the present high cost of living and maintain a standing in the community commensurate with their positions. Dulles was recently appointed counsellor to the legation in Peking.

Los Angeles, Sept. 27.—The national convention of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, meeting here to-day, will consider several programmes "for a strong campaign against the activities of wet organisations throughout the country." Delegates are unanimous in declaring that any compromise with the anti-prohibitionists at this time would mean defeat for the cause of prohibition. As one leader said, it would be a "national calamity and a world disaster."

London. Sept. 28.—A royal mystery that had endured since Queen Alexandra's death has been cleared up by the revelations that she left no will, and that her property was divided among her four children—King George, the Princess Royal, Princess Victoria, and Queen Maud of Norway. It is understood, however, that the Prince of Wales is to receive Queen Alexandra's famous pearls, so that they may be worn by his Princess of Wales when he marries.

His many friends and associates will be pleased to learn that Mr. Eric B. Cumine, son of Mr. H. M. Cumine, has just passed his final examination of the Architectural Association. He left Shanghai in the spring of 1922, up to which time he made himself well-known in various lines of sport, particularly in cricket, making his century and playing in the Shanghai Foot-Ball League matches for the final Skottows Cup, and for the Shanghai Public School in 1921. While in England during his studies he found time to captain his school cricket team and to serve on the selection committee for "rugger." He will return to Shanghai at the end of next year to join his father's firm. Consular Body held a meeting to-day, on which occasion it was unanimously decided to lodge a strong protest with the Canton Government.

It is stated that a clause in the ordinance providing for the compulsory search of individuals was given particularly serious consideration at the Consular meeting.

headline: America and Britain.
text: The United States' representative-type alone is still hesitating to show a definite stand on the matter on the plea of her Consul being now absent from Canton. Such being the case, the joint protest which was almost decided upon by the various Consuls will not be sent in until America sets forth a "definite attitude, which will not be for a few days. headline: CONTRAST PEKING1
text:
Now that the Canton boycott have been called off, and that reliable news agencies are reporting the return of normal shipping conditions in Hong Kong, all foreign business men in Peking and Tientsin are casting envious eyes to the South.

For business here simply does not exist. Hong Kong merchants and importers may have considered themselves unfortunate during the months of the strike but in reality they sat in the lap of luxury when compared with the conditions of foreign firms in Peking and Tientsin during the last four years.

The status of affairs here has reached such a pass that many of the great international firms announce that they will forsake North China within the next twelve months unless there is a decided turn for the better.

Legations, Not Shroffs. There are scores of firms here doing almost no business at all—firms which four years ago had a profitable monthly turn-over of $500,000 or more. In addition to stagnation they have, in the aggregate, more than $50,000,000 owing to them by the so-called Central Government which makes no pretence of paying either principal or interest. These great firms have been operating for several years on a basis upon which their overhead and annual outlay far exceeded their gross income. In other words, they have been eating into their capital, and now in many cases they will quit China before their capital is entirely gone. The Legations give no aid, but any they are “not bill collectors.”

headline: IN RUSSIA. / GERMAN DOCTOR'S EXPERIENCE
text:
Two young Germans, Di Kindermann and a student named Wolcht, who on a trumped up charge of plotting against the Soviet regime was solemnly condemned to death while travelling in Russia at the invitation of the Russian Government some years ago, have now returned to Berlin. It will be remembered that these two men, together with a number of German Popular officials, who on equally himay grounds were accused of commercial espionage, were in reality hostages seized by Russia in its determination to enforce by fair means or foul the liberation of the notorious Russian known as Skobolevsky, who was sentenced first to death and subsequently to penal servitude by the Leipzig Supreme Court for organising the Hamburg Communist rising of 1922.

The stratagem adopted by the Soviet Government has now led to the exchange of the prisoners referred to, and the desperado Skobolevsky, whose real name seems to be Kryloeff had the satisfaction of crossing the German frontier on his way to Russia. Both Kindermann and Wolscht have visibly aged as the result of the ordeal through which they have passed. They are very reserved concerning their experiences during the two years' sojotrn in Mogcow prisons. When the death sentence was pronounced they confess that they would be shot, and they wrote farewell letters to their relatives in Germany. Kindermann washed a shirt for himself in prison in order that he might, as he says, die in clean linen. A black cloth was hug out of the little window of their cell as a sign that their execution was impending. After three days of suspense they were told that they had been for the present reprieved, and they were removed to another jail. The walls of their new cell they found scribbled over with thousands of depressing inscriptions, dating mainly from the time of the revolution. Many of these merely contained the laconic statement: "I am about to be shot." Many of the signatures showed that the writers were Cosack officers. Finally the two Germans were informed that their sentences had been commuted to ten years' imprisonment with hard labour. It was not until Sept. 14 that they learned they were to be liberated, an official from the German Embassy bringing the welcome news. That evening, under a strong escort, they were taken to the Moscow railway station and sent to Leningrad, where they were placed on board a German stormer bound for Swinemunde.

The week-end campaign by the miner's leaders in Leicestershire failed. There was no audience or a mere handful at its arranged meetings. The stoppage in Leicestershire is almost ended.—Reuter.

The 12th report of the Shanghai Mission to Rikisha men states:— If in some former years the happy monotony of the peaceful routine of the Mission's work has tended to a measure of repetition in the annual report, this year, with its attendant political and social upheavals and unrest, has provided a sufficiency of alarms and menaces to the peace and safety of the work to provide quite sensational writing if considered desirable, but having weathered all successfully, it seems more fitting to dwell gratefully on what has been avoided.

headline: SINCERE'S. GREAT REDUCTION SALE
text:
NOW IN PROGRESS

In the early Spring of 1925 life was very hard for the majority of rikisha men and their class, and needless to say, the warm, brightly lighted Mission halls, where food, clothing, and shelter by day and night could be obtained by destitute men, were very popular resorts, and the Mission workers had hard work to meet all the requirements of the relief work, in the Mission and outside.

A day memorable in the history of Shanghai is the beginning of the general strike which most seriously affected all the industrial sections of the city for over three months except the rikisha pullers who alone stood untouched by the strike movement, although most determined efforts were made to induce the men to stop work. Strike promoters tried all methods at their command to attain their aim, intimidation, actual violence, inflammatory literature, promises of money and support, etc., but all failed. The rikisha man refused to be threatened pra cajoled.

Director Mr. George Matheson, worked unceasingly during the strike, addressing great crowds in the Mission halls, open air, lodging and tea houses and homes, urging the preservation of law and order, and distributing "the Municipal Council's propaganda leaflets," "Read the Truth," "of which about 24,000 were circulated by the Mission staff along with an abridged account of twelve years work of the Rikisha Mission, which it was hoped might convey a favourable impression of the good feeling towards Chinese on the part of the foreign community. The general opinion of the public during the strike was that "the conduct of the men was admirable, in consideration of which the majority of foreign users of rikisha treated them with sympathetic kindness.

headline: Popular Demonstration: "Rugby, Oct. 5.
parent_headline: SIR A. COBHAM. / PIONEER PILOT OF THE
text: His Majesty has been pleased to appoint Mr. Alan Cobham a Knight Commander of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire. Sergeant Ward has been awarded the Air Force Medal and, Mr. Capel, his other mechabic, has been made a Member of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire. The knighthood for "the famous airman and the distinctions for his companions" were announced by Sir Samuel Moore. Air Minister, to-day, at a luncheon in Sir Alan Cobham's honour given by the Air Council. Sir Alan Cobham was greeted with tremendous applause. Numerous speakers expressed admiration for his achievements, and the Air Minister said that it had brought appreciably nearer the day when London would be within a fortnight of every capital in the Empire. He said that there was no technical reason why that should not be achieved. Sir Alan Cobham is only 31 years old, but he has already flown 300,000 miles. Among his exploits in recent years are his 12,000 miles flight through Europe, Northern Africa, Egypt, and Palestine in 1923. He made a 17,000 miles flight to Rangoon and back carrying the Director of Civil Aviation, in 1924. He flew 1,700 miles to South Africa and back in 1925. He flew 28,000 miles to Australia and back. — British Wireless Service.

headline: AIR CRASH.
text:
CAUSE A COMPLETE MYSTERY.

EXPERTS BAFFLED

Expert witnesses at the Inquest at Tonbridge in connection with the crash of the French aeroplane were totally unable to account for the cause of the fire. They declared that the pilot was most expert; that the machine was equipped with the most complete fire-fighting appliances; and that the wreck was so complete that it was impossible to ascertain even where the fire started.

The jury returned a verdict o accidental death.—Reuter. Public Enquiry To Be Made.

A verdict of accidental death, there being no evidence to show the cause of the fire, was returned at the Coroner's inquest on the seven victims of the crash of the French Air Union liner near Tonbridge. An official of the Company said that all the latest inventions to ensure safety were fitted to their machines. He suggested that ignition of lubricating oil and not petrol may have caused the fire. The wrecked machine had made 100 hours flight between Paris and London, and the pilot had flown 187,000 miles. The Coroner said that a public enquiry would be held by the Air Ministry.—British Wireless Ser.

headline: DOCKERS' STRIKE. / WORK RESUMED AT TILBURY
text:
The dockers and labourers, who struck at Tilbury yesterday, returned to work this morning. on the recommendation of the Transport Workers' Union, pending a meeting with the Port of London Authority, to discuss their grievances. Mr. Attwood has been permitted to enter the docks.—Reuter.

Meeting This Week. Rugby Oct. 5.

Two thousand Tilbury dockers who went on strike yesterday returned to work today, and the differences that had arisen between the Port of London Authority and the officials of the men's Union, who had been forbidden to enter the dock gates, are to be the subject of a joint meeting later in the week. —British Wigless Service.

headline: Acrimonious Discussion.
text:
An acrimonious discussion at the Miners' Delegate Conference preceded the vote on the South Wales proposal to "intensify the struggle, prevent outcrop work, endeavour to place an embargo on foreign coal, and to secure a Trade Union levy to support the

The rejection by the districts of the Government's plan left the Federation the only alternative of continuing the struggle during the Winter and striving to maintain the status quo and secure a more favourable compromise. It is generally agreed that the Conference must immediately decide the Federation's policy. The President, Mr. Herbert Smith, criticised the South Wales proposal amid protests, Mr. Smith threatening to leave the chair. No amendment was submitted to the South Wales drastic scheme.

Henceforth the Executive's policy will be noteworthy. The Federation controls 85 per cent. of the safety men in South Wales, although the proportion in the rest of the country is smaller. The levy proposal will require a special Congress of Trade Unions.

To-day 3,300 more miners returned to the pits, making a total of 197,000.—Reuter.

headline: Chance for Orators.
text:
The coal fields meetings rejected the Government's scheme for settling the coal dispute by 737,000 to 42,000 votes, whereupon the Miners' Delegate Conference to-day decided that the offers should be rejected officially. A resolution was passed by a majority calling for the withdrawal of safety men from the pits and the placing of an embargo on coal imports, ordering miners to cease working outcrops, urging the Trades Union Congress to impose a levy on members to aid the miners, and recommending a speech-making campaign in the areas where the men have returned to work.

The delegates are continuing the conference to-morrow.

Meanwhile the number of miners now working was to-day again increased by several thousands, and is approaching 200,000.—British Wireless Service.

headline: TRADE UNION LAW. / CONSERVATIVES: SEEK AMENDMENTS.
text:
SECRET BALLOT IMPERATIVE

For first time the annual conference of the Conservative Party, which was opened at Scarborough to-day, was presided over by a woman, Dame Caroline Bridgeman; wife of the First Lord of the Admiralty, occupying the chair.

One of the first subjects discussed was a proposal to amend the law relating to Trade Unions, and a resolution, which was carried unanimously, urged the Government to make illegal any strike without secret ballot; to increase the security of the individual worker against victimisation and intimidation on account of this political belief; to make mass picketing and picketing of a man's private residence illegal; and to require national accounts of Trade Unions to be audited by certified accountants. — British Wireless Service.

headline: Definite Decision.
text:
The Executive Council of the National Federation of Colliery Enginemen, Boilermen and Mechanics, which controls practically all the safetymen, has decided not to withdraw the safetymen from the confirries.

How the coal shortage, in consequence of the British strike, is hampering the Continental manufacturers is illustrated by Gothenburg recording the imminence of a fuel famine.

Dealers have so far postponed purchases, hoping for an early end to the dispute.

As it is now impossible to secure coal for November delivery prices for later delivery are bounding daily.

A contract of 5,000 tons has been lodged in America at 54/- a ton. Difficulties are accentuated by the freight rates having been recently doubled.—Reuter.

headline: POLICY OF DESPAIR.
text:
It will not be known until next Thursday if the miners' district Lodges approve of the latest suggestion of the Delegate Conference to withdraw the safety men from the pits.

The proposal is widely criticised as a "policy of despair," and, even if adopted, it is likely to be without effect.

The great majority of safety men are not affiliated to the Miners' Unions, and there is no possibility whatever that they will cease the work of keeping the pits in order, on which they have been engaged throughout the dispute.

Even if the safety workers who are in the Miners' Unions responded to the call, there would be little difficulty in carrying on the work that they have been doing.—British Wireless Service.

headline: AT LOGGERHEADS / COMMUNIST RIFT IN MOSCQW.
text:
Moscow: October 9.

“In view of the violation of party discipline by the most prominent members of the Opposition,” the Political Bureau of the Communist party has resolved to submit to the next plenary meeting of the committee of the Central Controlling Commission the question of imposing due party penalties on Trotsky, Zinovieff and Piatakoff.—Reuter.

An earlier message from Riguestated that the Moscow Committee of the Communist Party has requested the Central Committee to remonstrate with a number of leaders of the Opposition who are, allegedly responsible for many secret meetings and the distribution of much illegal literature. The names mentioned include Trotsky, Zinovieff and Radek.

Rugby, "October 9.

The South African National Memorial at Delville, Wood, on the Somme will be unveiled to-morrow by Mrs. Louis Botha. General Hertzog.-Prime Minister of the Union, and many eminent South Lord D'Abernon, the retiring British Ambassador in Berlin, who is returning to Britain to-morrow, presented his letters of recall to President von Hindenburg yesterday.

Africans will be present, together with Marshall Coffee, representing the French and Field-Marshall Lord Haig representing the British armies.

Delville Wood is piece of France sacred to South Africa and the design of the memorial unites it with the great imperial war grave and cemetery where lie all recovered bodies of those who fell in Delville Wood battles.

The memorial, however, is dedicated to all South Africans who gave their lives in the war, as is shown by the inscription, on it, which is "graven both" in English and Dutch, and reads:—

"To the immortal dead from South Africa, who at the call of duty made the great sacrifice on the battlefields of Africa, Asia and Europe and on sea, this memorial is dedicated in proud and grateful recognition by their countrymen." Many of those attending the ceremony will be taken there and back to-morrow in a Special set of Imperial Airways machines.—British Wireless Service:

A large crowd had gathered outside the palace in the Wilhelmstrasse, and Berlin correspondents state that the Ambassador's departure has provoked a remarkable display of regret on the part of all classes of Germans.

Addressing the President, the Ambassador reviewed the events during the six years of his mission. He mentioned the stabilisation of Germany's currency, after a crisis unparalleled in history, of Germany's passage through financial chaos to financial equilibrium, and the reorganisation of her industry and commerce upon a basis auguring well for the future material prosperity.

He added, "In the sphere of politics the transformation has been no less remarkable, and I leave Germany at peace with her neighbours, her security assured by the Treaty of Locarno, and her place among the nations at Geneva established by universal consent."

The President, in replying, said that the policy of permanent European peace had made an important step forward, and in that evolution Lord D'Abernon had taken a paramount share which would not be forgotten.

The Ambassador was presented by the Government of the Reich with a magnificent antique silver centrepiece.—British Wireless Service.

headline: A Striking Speech.
text:
In the presence of a great and representative gathering, including Prince Arthur of Connaught, Lord Buxton, Lord Gladstone, the Earl of Selborne, General Hertzog, Lord Haig, representatives of Marshal Joffre, the South African Defence Forces, ex-Servicemen, and relatives of the fallen, Mrs. Botha unveiled the imposing South African war memorial at Delville Wood on the Somme.

General Hertzog, in a striking speech, said that the South Africans had marched to the battlefield with all the fervour and determination born of the conviction of the righteousness of their cause. If militarism still stalked the face of Europe the blame was not theirs. It now rested with the statesmen of Europe—especially the victorious statesmen to justify the confidence of the world and realise the high and noble purpose of the war.— Reuter

headline: COTTON PRICES / LOWEST FOR FIVE YEARS IN NEW YORK.
text:
Cotton has dropped 82 points today—the lowest point for five years—following publication of the Government Estimates. Half of the loss was later recovered on heavy domestic selling. The foreign mill buying market closed at 42 to 50 points lower on the day. It is believed that a crop of seventeen million bales is certain with good weather.—Reuter.

President Coolidge has appointed a special committee of Government officials to investigate cotton market conditions and to recommend measures to relieve the situation arising from the slump in prices.—Router's American Service

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
MINERS FORM COUNCIL OF

A NEW PHASE.

It is officially announced that the Miners Executive Committee has now become the Central Council of War. The first meeting will be held at Nottingham on October 10.—Reuter.

The decision on the formation of a Council of War was taken at a meeting of the Miners' Executive which resolved to revert to a demand for pre-stoppage conditions' arangement for it, meeting of the Federation of Engineers, Boilerman and Mechanics and endeavour to withdraw safety men; similarly to meet the Trade Union General Council and press for a levy and embargo; and finally, to conduct an intensive campaign of propaganda in the mining areas.—Reuter. Plans of Despair!

The Minors' Executive, resuming its meeting to-day, considered further action in view of the vote of the districts favouring the withdrawal of safety men, an embargo on foreign coal," a levy on other grades Unions, and a stoppage of work on outcrops.

According to an official statement, it was decided to discuss the withdrawal of safety men with the Secretary of the Union; to ask for a special meeting of the General Council of the Trade Union Congress, in order to place before it a request for a levy and embargo; and to send out a request to miners to remain loyal to the Federation and cease producing coal from outcrops.

It was further arranged that members of the Executive and the miners' members of Parliament should proceed to the different areas to carry on propaganda with a view to bringing out men who have returned to work.

The Executive will form itself into a "Central Council of War." It will hold its next meeting on Tuesday at the miners' offices at Basford, in Nottinghamshire, and will remain in the Midlands for the time being.

These decisions of the Miners' Executive are generally regarded as plans of despair. It has been made abundantly clear at any rate that an embargo on coal imports is impracticable, and that other Unions could not, if they would, help the miners with a levy. There is also little prospect of the men who have resumed work being induced to come out again by the leaders' forlorn hopes.

The increase in the number of men resuming work goes steadily on, there being 6,289 more at work to day bringing the total to 236,892. —British Wireless Service.

headline: Boom in Germany.
text: The textile industry at Krefeld, Munchen and Gladbach districts, West Germany's Lancashire, are booming largely in consequence of the British coal stoppage. Spinning, weaving and other process mills, cotton, woollen and silk trades are running full time, in some instances in double shifts. A similar situation obtains in numerous factories where clothing is made.—Reuter.

headline: LIBERAL LEADER.
text:
LORD OXFORD EXPLAINS HIS RESIGNATION.

Lord Oxford and Asquith has resigned the leadership of the Liberal Party but will continue in public life. In a letter announcing his decision, which is irrevocable, he states that he still hopes to be of some service to the State and to Liberal's.

It will be recalled that acute differences among leading members of the Liberal Party arose during the General Strike, and they have created a situation which Lord Oxford says has necessitated reconsideration from every point of view of his personal relations with the Party. He affirms that he sees nothing to withdraw from his letter criticising the attitude of Mr. Lloyd George, which he wrote soon after the strike was over, and repents that it was with as much distress as surprise that he found his public declarations during the strike were met with a challenge from a quarter which it was impossible for him to disregard, coupled with a refusal at a time of national crises to meet him in council.

Proceeding, he says: "I cannot and will not take any part direct or indirect in sectional controversy. I am now in my seventy-fifth year. I have been for the best part of half a century in public life. I was Prime Minister for a longer consecutive term, and had to face graver responsibilities than any of my predecessors during the last hundred years. For still longer a time I have been leader of the Liberal Party. Though my health is now restored I feel that anxieties and responsibilities of leadership ought not to be undertaken or continued by any one who cannot be reasonably certain that he can stand the strain."

Lord Oxford announcement was made on the eve of his speech at the Conference of the Scottish Liberal Federation, in which it was anticipated that the future prospects of the party and his own relations with it would be fully examined, and the Federation this morning and journeyed when a resolution reaffirming its confidence in Lord Oxford was reached. Newspapers of all shades of opinion pay tribute to the great services to the State which Lord Oxford has rendered during his long Parliamentary career.—British Wireless Service: "Who Will Succeed?

headline: China the Jail / HONGKONG, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 23, 1926. / OVERSEAS EMPIRE.
text:
A STRIKING REVIEW.

Great Britain's Fine Civilising

In the statement by the Secretary of State for the Colonies, Mr. L. S. M. Amery, at yesterday's meeting of the Imperial Conference, a comprehensive survey was given of the progress and development of the British Colonies and mandated territories in various parts of the world.

Referring to the immense growth of the work of the Colonial Office in recent years, he said that the Colonial Empire had, in fact, in last generation evolved as a separate constituent element in the Empire

—different on the one side from the self-governing parts of the Empire, based on democratic institutions, and on the other from the complex of races, religions, creeds, and old civilisations which made up the Empire of India. Inasmuch as the responsibility for their various Governments in the last resort lay with the British Parliament, though they had autonomous institutions in a varying degree and increasing measure, this Empire enjoyed a certain unity, which it also derived from the fact that its units were mainly inhabited by populations of a nonwhite character and were mainly situated in the tropics.

headline: COAL CRISIS. / AN URGENT PLEA FOR SETTLEMENT.
text:
POSSIBLE AVENUE?

Mr. Arthur Pugh, who is preaiid-ing over the General Council of the Trades Union Congress to-day at a meeting with the Executive Committee of the M. ners' Federation to consider the position in the coal dispute, has sent a long letter to the "Times" on that subject, containing an urgent plea for settlement in a spirit of conciliation and mutual agreement. Mr. Pugh expresses the conviction that the only solution lies in the application of the Coal Commission's recommendations, and urges a temporary arrangement enabling the mines to resume work pending the achievement of a national agreement. The “Times” points out such a temporary arrangement would have to visualise facts as they are and take account of areas where work is resumed. The “Times” adds that if Mr. Pugh and the General Council of the Trades Unions can persuade the miners to accept such a plan, they will open up a possible avenue to a settlement worthy of the careful examination by the Government and Parliament.—British Wireless Service.

headline: Special Conference.
parent_headline: COAL CRISIS. / AN URGENT PLEA FOR SETTLEMENT.
text: After conferring with the Miners' Executive all day long the General Council of the Trade Union Congress decided to call a special conference of the Executive and the members of the Affiliated Unions on November 3 to consider the question of a levy on the members of affiliated Unions. It was decided that the question of an embargo on the import of foreign coal must be considered with the principal Unions affected.—Reuter.

headline: No Promise. Rugby: October 22.
parent_headline: COAL CRISIS. / AN URGENT PLEA FOR SETTLEMENT.
text:
The Miners' Executive to-day met the General Council of the Trades Union Congress with the object of endeavouring to obtain an embargo on imported coal and a levy on Unions. Details of the discussion were not officially disclosed, but it is understood that the General Council, whilst expressing sympathy with the miners, did not promise either an embargo or a levy.

The Trade Union leaders took the line that it was time that the parties to the dispute got back to the Coal Commission's recommendations. They were willing to use their good offices to induce the Government, if possible, to permit further deliberations on the lines of the Coal Commission's report, but the two sides to the discussion had not reached a common platform regarding the suggestion when the meeting was adjourned.—British Wireless Service.

headline: MORE 'QUAKES' / OVER SIX HUNDRED CASUALTIES.
text:
A violent earthquake occurred at Lenin'akan, formerly Alexandropol. Three hundred were killed and seventy seriously injured. Half of the buildings in Leninan are wrecked and several villages destroyed.—Reuter.

The Trans-Caucasian Government states that 15 were killed and 30 seriously injured at Leninakan, and 300 killed and 300 injured in the neighbourhood. A dozen villages are badly damaged, six of which are obliterated. The earthquake lasted three minutes. The seismographic station at Tiflis states that it was due to a collision between massive mountain layers.—Reuter. New York, October 23. A cable from Erivan to the Near East relief organisation reports that hundreds were killed, thousands injured, and many thousands rendered homeless by an earthquake in Armenia last night, but that all the American workers are safe.—Reu

headline: SOVIET RIFT. / OPPOSITION LEADERS CENSURED.
text: A plenary meeting of the Central Committee of the Third International and the Central Control Commission of the Communist Party made a resolution censuring Trotzky, Kameneff, Sokolnkoff, Zinovieff and other members of the Central Committee and decided to dismiss Zinovieff from the International and Trotzky and Kameneff from the Political Bureau. The meeting approved the agenda of the Conference of the Communist Party opening on the 26th instant when Stalin will submit a report.— Reuter.

headline: NO NEW TRIAL. / ITALIANS' SENTENCE TO STAND.
text:
Dedham, Massachusetts, Oct. 24. The Superior Court has declined a new trial for Sacco and Vanzetti. --Reuter's American Service.

[A report dated September 1] stated: The Superior Court. at Boston has granted a motion for a new trial of Sacco and Vanzetti, the [Ialians who were convicted of killing a paymaster and bodyguard at South Braintree, Massachusetts, five years ago. The conviction has resulted in much agitation all over the world on the part of sym- pathisers with the convicted men.]

headline: COAL CRISIS. / LORD DERBY OFFERS HIS
text:
After yesterday's meeting, between the General Council of the Trades, Union Congress was the Miners' Executive, it was announced that the General Council had considered the request of the miners' representatives for a special Trade Union conference for the purpose of discussing the question of a levy on the affiliated Unions and of an embargo on exported coal.

The General Council had decided to call a special conference of the Executive of the affiliated Unions to consider the question of a levy. It was explained that this conference would deal only with the question of a levy. Apparently there was no recommendation for or against the proposal, and it was stated that there had been some plain speaking between the miners' representatives and the General Council on the subject.

headline: Mr. Pugh Hopeful.
parent_headline: COAL CRISIS. / LORD DERBY OFFERS HIS
text: Mr. Arthur Pugh, who presided over the General Council, said that whilst the special conference would not deal with the embargo, steps would be taken to get into touch with the Unions concerned on this matter. Mr. Pugh, who yesterday addressed a letter to the "Times", urging a settlement by the application of the Coal Commission's recommendations, said that the General Council had still to consider the general situation in regard to the coal stoppage. He was personally hopeful that something would happen.

headline: Lord Derby's Offer.
parent_headline: COAL CRISIS. / LORD DERBY OFFERS HIS
text:
Considerable interest has been aroused by an offer made by Lord Derby to act as mediator in the coal dispute.

Speaking at Leighin, Lan cashire, last night, he said:—

"I hope with all my heart that some means may be found even now, that will reconcile the antagonistic interests and bring a peace that will be satisfactory to both parties. I know perfectly well that more harm can be done than good by anybody butting in, pretending to be a mediator, but if I can be of any use there is nothing that would give me greater pleasure. But I would not venture to suggest that unless I were asked to do so."

headline: Full Authority Asked.
text:
The General Council of the Trades, Union Congress, after hearing a report made by the deputation which last night discussed the coal situation with the Prime Minister and other Ministers, decided to ask the Miners' Executive to meet them on Friday, Mr. A. J. Cook, the Miners' Secretary, who had been recalled to London from Walsall, subsequently stated that he had called his Executive together to meet the General Council as proposed. On behalf of the General Council it is stated that they hope to be able to induce the miners to give them full authority to begin and

On behalf of the General Council it is stated that they hope to be able to induce the miners to give them full authority to begin and carry on negotiations for a settlement. British Wireless Service.

headline: Mr. Cook and the T.U.C.
text: The summoning of Mr. A. J. Cook to London to meet the Trade Union Council was a sequel to the decision of the Council this morning to ask the Executive of the Miners' Federation to meet them as soon as possible to discuss the reopening of negotiations.—Reuter

headline: Government Nothing To Say.
text:
Members of a deputation from the General Council of the Trades Union Congress who last night discussed the coal situation with the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues at Downing Street this morning gave a report on the meeting to the General Council. It is understood that the Ministers and delegates discussed the whole situation, but that it was pointed out to the delegates that little could be achieved until the latter were definitely in a position to assure the Government that they spoke with the full approval of the

The Premier, in reply to a question by the delegates, made it clear that he was perfectly willing to meet them again at any time but whether a further interview will take place depends mainly upon the trend of conversations which are believed to be proceeding between members of the Trades Union General Council who are extremely desirous of effecting a renewal of negotiations, and the miners' representatives.

Mr. Winston Churchill, Chaucer for of the Exchequer, who accompanied the Premier at the meeting with the delegates, later addressed a meeting at which he referred to the dispute. He pointed out that the Government had acted as mediators, but were not in a position to force workmen down the pits or compel employers to keep open pits at a loss. He declared it was always open for anyone to put forward proposals to the Government who would earnestly consider all suggestions. At the moment the Government had nothing to say. They had made an offer which had been rejected and if any further step was to be taken it must be as the result of sincere proposals from the miners' representatives. Discussing the demand for an amendment of the Trades Dispute Act, Mr. Churchill said great changes had occurred since the measure was passed. Privileges and immunities then given to Trades Unions had been abused in such a way that four main questions had to be considered. There was peaceful picketing which had been abused to the point of intimidation. Secondly, there was immunity of the Trades Unions for serious acts which had been used in the general strike for levelling an attack on society. Thirdly, the question of a political levy must be considered to relieve from his position a man who did not wish to subscribe but could only be exempt by making special application. Lastly, there was the question of a compulsory ballot before a strike could take place. This, he agreed, was a more questionable matter, but the whole subject was under careful examination by the Government.—British Wireless Service

headline: BOMB PANIC. / NEW YORK'S ESCAPE FROM CALAMITY.
text:
Thanks to the accidental discovery of a bomb inside a suitcase on the window ledge of the County Court House, the city has been saved from a possible explosion similar to the one in Wall Street in 1920.

A clerk saw the case, which he proceeded to examine. "His suspicions were aroused by a ticking noise within... A policeman praised it open and summoned the bomb squad of the Fire Brigade who conveyed the bomb to the sea. The suitcase contained sufficient dynamite to blow up the Court House and other buildings. News of the discovery almost caused a panic among several hundreds working in offices.

The Police are of the opinion that the outrage is connected with the Massachusetts Court refusing a retrial of the Italian Communists, "Sacco and" Vanzetti.—Reuter's American Service.

headline: U.S. TRADE. / INCREASES RECORDED FOR SEPTEMBER.
text:
FACTORIES MOST ACTIVE.

The monthly report of the Federal Reserve Board shows that industrial and trade activity increased during September.

Oil and cotton prices declined sharply, but prices of most commodities advanced. The output and factory employment in the basic industries reached the highest point since the Spring, the increase being particularly noticeable in the large textile mills, with increased consumption. Cotton and woollen mills were more active than since January. Iron and steel productions since the late Summer are on a higher level than the same period of previous years. Though slightly below the figures for August the automobile output was greater in September than in

Though slightly below the figures for August the automobile output was greater in September than in the same month last year.—Reuter's American Service.

headline: STARTLING CANTON REPORT.
text:
On Responsibility for Preserving

Coming in the nature of a big surprise is a report received last night from Canton that the Strike Committee has forbidden members of a certain labour union to search shops for British goods! The Chinese merchants responsible for this piece of news say that the Strike Committee feels that it is answerable to the authorities for the preservation of order in labour disputes arising immediately out of the boycott settlement.

"Volunteering" for the work of taking stock at all shops where foreign merchandise is carried, this Union of Fokis actually did start to make the pounds until the order was made by the Strike Committee, pointing out that such duties were the work of the strikers (in conjunction with the Committee for the Severance of Economic Relations).

Trattle has improved and increased but the under-tone of uneasiness has not been dispelled. The principal obstacle is the fear of running foul of those who, until the week-end maintained the common around the Steamboat Co.'s wharves, and of being found out by the andonymous publishers of the street posters enjoining no intercourse with "a certain nation."

Although news has come down from Kongmoon that the Surtax Bureau is now in operation and that cargoes can now be shipped up from Hong Kong, another report says that difficulties still exist. Such, however, are not attributed to the boycott, but to a demand by the cargo coolies' guild of prohibitive wages.

That confidence is felt in the situation at Kongmoon is evident in the announcement of the s.s. "On Lee" to resume the trip this week.

A New Steamboat

A new steamboat will join the Hong Kong-Canton run in a few days under the Chinese flag. This is the s.s. "Yuet On," built locally, for the Fook Yuet Co. Yesterday she proceeded from her anchorage at Cheung-sha-wan to the Po Tak wharf at the Praya.

A representative of the owners is having stated that the boat cost about $200,000 to build. A German will be in command when she sails.

The following details are also given: —length 192 feet, speed 13½ knots, can take 1,000 passengers and 300 tons of cargo. Yet another "outside" steamer is joining the Hong Kong-Canton run. This is the s.s. "Kwong Foon". (formerly on the Canton-Wuchow), owned by the Sai Hing S.S. Co. of Hong Kong. In spite of protection by the Canton Police, there is no increase in the traffic carried by the Steamboat Co. but intimidation on the West Bund had considerably decreased.

headline: AMERICAN PROTEST.
text:
A new United States protest to Canton accuses the Canton Government of violation of treaty rights in compelling ships entering port to submit to examination by officials of the newly created Inspection Bureau, which is acting independently of the regular Customs administration. —Router's American Service.

text:
Mass Campaign By Canton in Figures.

At the previous hearing the complainant gave evidence regarding the receipt of letters which aroused his suspicion and led to his taking the matter to the Police. The case was put in the hands of Det. Sub-Inspector Lane who arranged for a Chinese de-tive to go to the complainant's office, No. 21, New Street, dis-pursed as a clerk. Accused called by appointment and was handed two $500 notes which had previously been marked. "Leaving the office, he was followed and subsequently arrested."

At the commencement of this morning's hearing Mr. Prior informed the Magistrate that he had been unable to secure certified copies of his translations of the Chinese letters. "The Supreme Court refuse to translate them," said counsel, "and the Secretary for Chinese Affairs says he is too busy." He, Mr. Prior, was therefore quite helpless in the matter and would ask His Worship to allow him to get the various witnesses to state what they understood by them. Mr. McCallum raising no objection to the suggested procedure. His Worship allowed the application. Lam Kwok-an, accountant in the employ of the firm from whom the letter was supposed to have been sent, said that he had not written it; it was undoubtedly a forgery as he was in a position to know about every letter that left his office. The letter was not in the handwriting of anyone in his office. His firm, as a matter of fact, knew nothing whatever of the $1,000 demanded. Case proceeding.

headline: REVENUE REPORT. / IMPORTS & EXPORTS IN
text:
LESS THAN YEAR BEFORE.

The report of the Superintendent of Imports and Exports, Hong Kong, for the year 1925, was laid on the table at this afternoon's meeting of the Legislative Council.

Revenue for 1925 was less than the year before.

(3) Honor, $1,140,925.07 was collected against $1,229,262.66 in 1924. Tobacco produced $1,796,858.52 Compared with $2,007,105.01 the year Before

The foregoing figures denote net revenue.

Gross revenue on optimum was $3,466,521.00 as compared with $5,224,803.66 in the preceding twelve months.

The Superintendent says: The collection of duty on liquor of Chinese manufacture still remained unsatisfactory.

Frauda by distilleries, in denaturing, weighing, the altering of samples and adulteration are referred to in detail.

"The Chinese liquor trade was a serious source of corruption of the Chinese staff," says the report. Under classified heads, an estimate made "of loss to revenue is placed at $385,000.

The report also has: "Several complaints were received of the adulteration of European type liquor sold in hotels..., A good deal of compounded cheap spirit as sold surreptitiously as Hennessy's 3 star brandy.....and a Chinese firm concerned has since gone into bank-ruptcy."

The boycott brought about the "fairly satisfactory collection" of tobacco duty because most of the avenues for smuggling were closed.

Before the political trouble in June, sales of opium had decreased to 6,000 tails per week; and for the remainder of the year to about 4,000 taels per week. The great decrease is partly due to the political troubles, partly to the large amounts of cheap Chinese opium, and partly due to the large amounts of Macao opium smuggled into the Colony.

It is interesting to note that during the “general strike” some of the staff were employed in running the s.s. “Tung On” (handled by the Navy) to Canton; Europeans were lent to the Police and to the Harbour Office; and R. O. Pearse acted as slaughterhouse butcher. Junior Chinese clerks were lent to the Post Office and to the Censor. The tables of contraband and dangerous drugs seized make very interesting reading.

headline: YANG SEN.
text:
Marching With An Anti-Red

General Yang Sen has moved a great many troops downstream during the past day or two. He has captured several small river ports above Hankow and in general consolidated his position within striking distance of Hankow. Yesterday we reported that his troops had looted the city of Patang, a rather unimportant port a few miles up river beyond Ichang. This report came from a reliable source, though details as to the looting have not yet been received. On the other hand General Yang Sen is reported to be advancing upon Hankow with a definite anti-Red purpose and this may possibly account for the reported evacuation of Hanyang by the Southern. "Shanghai Mercury" Note: Hanyang is still in Can

headline: ST. ANDREWS DAY / CONTINUOUS PRAYER IN CATHEDRAL. / HELPERS WANTED:
text:
On St. Andrewstide, the November number of "St. John's"

"The eve of St. Andrew's day has been for many years the day appointed as a day of special prayer for the extension of the Kingdom of God amongst non-Christian people." It has long been observed as a day of continuous prayer in the Cathedral, different people taking a quarter of an hour and spending the time in the Cathedral in prayer. The Chaplain will be very glad to hear from any who like to take part in the work. It is, noticeable how the missionary work of the Church has spread and increased since the initiation of the Day of Intercession in the year 1872. At the present time the four reports issued by the Missionary Council of the National Assembly of the Church of England have shown how pressing is the need of a great increase in the number of workers and in the amount contributed by our Church to the evangelisation of the world. Empire involves responsibility, and we of the British Empire are bound to see that we do our part in spreading the Christian message which has been the foundation of our own national life."

text:
Views on British Goods Being

Hong Kong's steamboat companies have not been officially informed to do cargo will not be handled at Canton as from Monday, Nov. 8.

As reported in yesterday's "China Mail," the Transport Union passed a resolution to the effect that British goods would be boycotted from the date mentioned.

headline: MINERS TO DECIDE
text:
Negotiations for the settlement of the coal dispute have been taking place to-day at Downing Street, and there have been rapid developments.

The Mediation Committee of the Trade Union Congress was received this morning by Mr. S. Baldwin, Prime Minister and the full Cabinet Coal Committee. The mediators stated that the Miners' Executive had authorised them to accept district agreements as a basis of negotiation, providing that there were safeguards that the same national principles, which were embodied in the last national agreements should run through all district agreements.

The Prime Minister, after leaving the Mediation Committee, consented to receive the Miners' Executive. Accordingly the "miners' leaders arrived at Downing Street and the Mediation Committee left, one of them saying: "Negotiations have definitely been opened and we are now leaving it to the miners." The discussion between the members of the Government and the miners' leaders was adjourned for lunch and was resumed later in the day.

Meanwhile, it is understood that the Government has been in touch with the Coal Owners' Association. When the miner's leaders left Downing Street this evening it was announced that the discussion would be resumed tomorrow afternoon.

It is expected that the coal owners will visit Downing Street between now and then.—British Wireless Service.

London, November 5. Peace prospects are brightening, following an interview of the Trade Union Congress delegation with the Cabinet Coal Committee at 10. Downing Street, at noon. The miners' executive called at Downing Street at one o'clock to see the Premier. — Reuter.

Members of the Trade Union Congress Committee who are mediating in the coal dispute proceeded to Downing Street at noon to-day for a conference with the Premier and other members of the Government. This step was taken after a meeting between the Committee and the Miners' Executive. The position seems to be that the executive, having faced the facts of the situation are now prepared to agree to the negotiation of district agreements without restriction other than that such agreements should be governed by arrangements capable of national application.

The purpose of the meeting between the Trade Union mediators and the Government now proceeding is presumably to ascertain definitely to what extent the Government are prepared to support a settlement on these lines. If assurance satisfactory to the miners are obtained, a resolution in favour of resuming negotiation for an immediate settlement will be put before the Miners' Delegates Conference later to-day. At present the position is thus much more hopeful and speedy developments are anticipated although the road is not yet troop from serious obstacles and the attitude of collery owners is the moment rather obscure.—British Wireless Service.

Coul peace negotiations have been definitely opened, stated Mr. Citrine Secretary of the Trades Union Congress, on leaving Downing Street, where the Miners' Executive are conferring with the Prime Minister. "We are now leaving it to the miners, having opened the door to a settlement."—Reuter. Hopeful Position. London, Nov. 5. The Cabinet and the miners resume negotiations to-morrow. One of the Trades Union Congress mediators says that the position is more hopeful than since the stoppage began.—Reuter.

The Government has now communicated with the coal owners—Router

A Meeting Arranged London, London The Government is meeting the coal owners to show up before suming the conversations with the miners—Heater

headline: COAL STRUGGLE / GREAT COST TO THE COUNTRY:
text:
The steadily increasing number of m era resuming (at present 300,000 working), together with the mild weather, has mitigated the effects of the coal stoppage during the past week, in which unemployment has diminished by 4,000 but nevertheless still exceeds 1,500,000. A disquieting estimate of the cost of the stoppage was given by Mr. Walter Runciman in a speech at the Chamber of Commerce, Liverpool, namely, between £216,000,000 and £270,000,000 of which textile accounted for £26,000,000.

On the other hand capital issues to October 31 totalled £205,000,000, which is £11,000,000 above last year.

Considerable hope attached to the re-opened negotiations owing to the appreciable assimilation of viewpoints of the two sides, although formidable hurdles remain to the negotiated.

It is understood that the miners are asking, firstly, for the coordination of district agreements, which represents a concession since district agreements are thereby recognised; secondly, a guarantee of a minimum wage; and thirdly, a fixed ratio between wages and profits varied according to the number of hours worked. The last-named constitutes a snag since it implies a national agreement which the owners have hitherto opposed.—Reuter.

To-day's resumption of the coal negotiations opened with the Trade Union Congress mediators hopeful and the miners' leaders non-committal.

The coal owners are reported to be determined not to sign any national document or form of agreement with the Miners' Federation. Following a Cabinet meeting both owners and miners are expected to meet the Government this afternoon. The negotiations may be continued during the week-end if there is no break down to-day, and in that event the miners' delegate conference will be recalled to London on Armistice Day to conclude an armistice for a settlement. — Reuter.

Although the miners and mine owners have not yet met, and the Government statement is only of the briefest regarding to-day's meetings of the Coal Committee with the owners, and subsequently with the Miners' Executive, Reuter learns that the Government communicated to the latter the rational principles which it is believed the owners may accept. — Reuter.

The coal negotiations have been adjourned till Monday.—Reuter. London, Nov. 6.

The Cabinet Coal Committee and the mine owners conferred for an hour and three quarters. Then the T.U.C. Mediation Committee and the full Miners' Executive met the Cabinet Committee. Reuter. The Cabinet met this morning to consider their reply to the proposals put forward yesterday by the miners' leaders. The miners' leaders were prepared to agree to the principle of district negotiations against which they have fought so long and stubbornly, but they attached to the acceptances of that principle rather, alienwise con

ditions in regard to national coordinating principles. These are considered to represent, in fact, the maximum hopes of the Miners' Federation for preservation of a national status. It is these conditions which the Cabinet merely listened to in the proposals of the miners' leaders and did not, in any way, indicate whether they approved or dissented. After they have examined the proposals they will meet the coal-owners in order to hear the views of the latter. Too much optimism is not displayed in Government circles: it is agreed that the miners' leaders have made a considerable advance towards the possibility of settlement. It is considered unlikely that all the miners' conditions will prove acceptable, but the proposals will, if is thought, prove a practical basis for negotiations. Sir Arthur Steel Maitland, Minister of Labour, speaking in Boote last night, said there were two things essential for a settlement. There must be agreement in the different districts. Although the districts came to settlements by themselves, he thought there ought to be certain general or national principles which should be a sort of skeleton embodied in all the different districts so that the different settlements might be comparable with one another. The coal negotiations continued at Downing Street throughout the afternoon, the Premier with the members of his Cabinet having a long meeting first with the Miners' Executive and afterwards with the Mining Association representatives of the owners. The extent of the progress made is not announced, but it has been arranged that discussions between the Government and the Miners' Executive will be continued on Monday afternoon. — Reuter.

headline: ABROGATED. / CHINESE TREATY WITH BELGIUM.
text:
Peking, Nov. 6. The Chinese Government has abrogated the Sino-Belgian Treaty of 1865.—Reuter.

The abrogation of the Sino-Belgian Treaty is considered in diplomatic circles as the most important event in China for a considerable time. It is pointed out that the abrogation has abolished Belgium's extraterritorial rights and places. Belgians in the same position as Austrians, Germans and Russians. M. De Warzee, however, is still treating the situation calmly, and is hopeful regarding the treatment of Belgians throughout China. Foreign diplomats point out that the Waichiaopu's action is a serious breach of treaties as Belgium alone had the right to propose a modification or abrogation, and further that Mr. Wellington Koo, by declining to agree to Belgium's request to submit the matter to The Hague has violated Article 40 of the Protocol signed at Geneva by the Chinese and other Governments, wherein it was agreed to recognise the competence of The Hague Court, instituted in accordance with the Covenant of the League of Nations, and to submit thereto such questions. China's action, therefore, is regarded as flaunting the League.—Reuter.

Canton, Nov. 6, The coercive measures again Chinese students in Belgium has provoked indignation in popular circles here. The Nationalist Government has received requests to issue a strong protest against the attitude of the Belgian Government in expelling students for their demonstration favouring negotiation of a new Sino-Belgian Treaty, and all local organisations are planning a mass demonstration on the late Dr. Sun Eat-sen's birthday, November 12.—"Canton Information Bureau," through Reuter.

headline: Windfall
text:
A dejected utterance by Mr. Cook, the miners' secretary, at the conclusion of Saturday's conference. "Men can just drift back any time now" is re-echoed every where as "a true appraisement of the coal stoppage, which is widely considered virtually to have terminated.

Industries are preparing to make up leeway in belated contracts, notably shipbuilding, regarding which the newspapers enumerate contracts for 19 ships of various types lodged with British yards during the past few days.

The Bolsover Colliery Company has announced that in recognition of the loyalty of 2,000 resumed employees in Notts and Derbyshire they are granting a bonus of between 5s. and 12s. a week, according to age. The first installment of this will be designed to be paid a week before Xmas.—Reuter.

headline: Earlier Messages
text:
A short meeting of the Miners' Executive Committee was held this morning, after which the delegate conference resumed consideration of the Government proposals for a settlement of the dispute.

Two courses are apparently open to the delegates. Either they will accept the responsibility of making a decision or the proposals will be referred to the districts. The moderate section favours the former course, and the likelihood of the districts proceeding at once to make their own settlements independently of the guidance given by the National Federation is a factor which may have an important bearing on the discussion.

Over 8,000 additional miners returned to work yesterday, and many of the leaders are said to fear that further delay might threaten the existence of the Federation.

When the conference adjourned yesterday consultations with the Government were sought to obtain certain elucidations of the proposed terms, and on meeting this morning these explanations were placed before the conference in the form of question and answer.

Broadly, the terms of settlement lay down a standard form of district agreement. An appeal to a national tribunal by either party to a district agreement is provided for in respect of any matter in which that agreement falls short of the standard agreement, provided the length of the working day in the district in which the appeal arises exceeds seven hours.

The proposals are made "contir'gent on an undertaking by the Miners' Federation to promote an immediate resumption of work by means of district settlements in which the length of the working day is not excluded from the negotiations. It is stated that; except in Northumberland, Durham, and one or two of the smaller coal fields, the owners will pay temporarily the rates of wages in force before the stoppage.

Speaking last night, Lord Birkenhead said that, although he could not announce a settlement, he had strong hopes that wise councils would prevail. The Government could draw encouragement in its belief that the terms contained some general principles of justice from the fact that the extremists on both sides repudiated them. The Government had offered the maximum terms now possible and would not hesitate by legislation to implement them if they proved unwelcome to the owners—British Wireless Service.

The miners' conference has decided to refer the Government proposals to the districts with a recommendation for their acceptance.

The card vote on the Miners' Conference decision was 432,000 for the recommendation and 352,000 against it. The Conference by a vote of 427,000 to 357,000 decided for a district vote

instead of an individual ballot vote. The vote is returnable on the 18th inst. The Conference will re-meet on the 19th inst.

The chief opponents of the Government's coal proposals have been South Wales and Yorkshire, but the recommendation for acceptance is regarded in Government circles as virtually meaning the miners' acceptance of the inevitable and there is the smallest prospect of an adverse vote in the districts.

Considerable dimiculty is expected in negotiating the district settlements and in any case a general resumption of work is not anticipated for some weeks in many districts. Sir W. Joyson Hicks stated at Barnstaple that the coal stoppage had nearly ruined the country. It had involved a loss of over £400,000,000 or more than the cost of the South African war. He believed that a Quarter of a million miners had permanently lost employment through the strike. He declared that if the men were returning with the idea of preparing more strikes it was almost better to fight it out to the bitter end.—Reuter.

headline: MANY BIG CONTRACTS.
text:
19 New Ships to be

It is anticipated that when the coal stoppage is over, as it is confidently expected to be when the miners in coulfield give their decisions on the Government's proposals, there will be an immediate and strong revival in the trades which it has rendered more or less idle during the past six months. The steel and iron works of South Wales have large orders on hand, and many thousands of men will find employment when there is fuel for the furnaces.

A big firm at Newport has received a contract to supply 22,000 tons of pipe line to San Paulo in South America. This contract will, it is stated, mean employment for British workmen for many years in providing the necessary materials. In Birmingham iron and steel trade has work of all kinds to put in hand, notably for railway carriages and waggons.

In Sheffield contracts for all classes of steel products have accumulated at an steady increasing rate during the past three months. In shipbuilding, also, arrears of work have accumulated, and the overtaking of these will in itself create a busy period.

Nirteen' new ships and equipment for three more have been ordered in the last few days from various firms.

"Of interest in this connection is the statement made by Mr. Franklin, President of the International Mercantile Marine Company, who arrived at Southampton yesterday from New York."

He said that the White Star Lines are making arrangements to proceed with a big ship, the exact size of which he would not give, beyond stating that it would be larger than the "Olympic". The "Olympic's" tonnage is 46,439.

The new liner will be built by Harland and Wolff, at Belfast, and it is probable the order will be placed in the near future.—British Wireless Service.

headline: CHANG KAI-SHEK. / ARRIVES AT HANKOW BY PLANE.
text:
A message from Hankow reports that the postal workers have struck. The labour unions are more aggressive than ever, paralysing trade. General Chang Kai-shek and Tang Seng-chi have arrived at Wuchang by aeroplane.—Reuter.

[The, above message is specially interesting because it removes all doubt about the Nationalist leader, General Chang Kai-shek, who was reported a fortnight ago to have died from wounds. General Chang is evidently well and in harness again.]

headline: EMPIRE UNITY.
text:
The members of the Imperial Conference were entertained last night by the Federation of Chambers of Commerce.

Lord Birkenhead said that he believed that by wise and true statecraft in recent years they had surmounted the greatest of the difficulties in the way of closer understanding between Great Britain and the Dominions. The time had come for the complete and common realisation of the only conditions on which an association of communities such as the British Commonwealth could survive, and in attempting to discharge that task they had learned that the qualities which were required were sympathy, knowledge, and imagination. He believed that the Imperial Conference discussions would lead to lasting harmony—British Wireless Service.

Odessa, November 14.—M. Chicherin and Rushdi Bey were closeted for three hours. It is announced that they discussed notably the relations between the two countries and international politics. They were highly�

I fied that their long established common views remained unchanged."—Router

headline: Possible intervention.
text: Mr. Kellogg declares that President Diaz is intending to offer his liberal opponents a federal amnesty and posts in the Cabinet. Mr. Kellogg hopes the offer would be accepted and end the revolution in Nicaragua which "invites interference from outside sources in state affairs, which must cause concern to every friend of the stability of Central America." Mr. Kellogg proceeds to say that the question of Mexican interference with the Central American states was presumably for the purpose of fostering radical propaganda and bolshevist philosophy and has for the present swept off from the stage other questions such as the oil and land law claims and controversy. While there is sign that these theories have taken a serious hold on the people of Central America he points out that official circles in the United States cannot fail to be deeply concerned in regard to Mexican interference owing to the geographical position of those states between the United States and the Panama Canal. Should the United States Government consider the situation serious enough, President Diaz's request for intervention could be made the basis for the employment of American naval forces in Nicaraguan waters to prevent the landing of arms from Mexico.—Reuter's American Service.

headline: HANKOW TROUBLE. / STRIKE, PICKETS BROWBEAT FOREIGNERS.
text:
a OFFICIALS FLOUTED

According to messages from Hankow, it appears that while the Southern officials are anxious to maintain normal relations with foreign business firms, labour agitators are making the position difficult.

Some labour unions are making extreme demands, and the officials are quite unable to control them. A notable instance of this occurred on Nov. 16, when the factory manager and director of The British Cigarette Co. proceeded to the office of the Commissioner of Foreign Affairs to attempt to negotiate in connection with a strike at the factory.

U.S. Consul Intervenes. After the two foreigners, who were both Americans, reached the office, large numbers of pickets crowded into the building and presented extreme demands, and refused to allow the Americans to leave until they had agreed in writing. The pickets kept them there until midnight, and it was only after strong representations had been made by the American Consul General that they were released. —Reuter.

[Mr. Chan Kung-pok, formerly head of Labour Department at Canton, is the Nationalist Commissioner of Foreign Affairs at Hankow. He was chosen as one of the three delegates to the Boycott Conference to meet Hong Kong's official delegation but his place was taken by Mr. Ku Mang-yu on his appointment to Hankow.]

text: In view of General Chang Kai-shek's "pronouncement, special significance attaches to a foreign despatch from Hankow reporting the formation of a union of subordinate Customs employees with the avowed object of taking the control of the Customs out of the hands of the foreigners.—Reuter.

headline: Belgian Treaty.
text:
The "Morning Post's" Geneva correspondent says that China will appeal to the League Council or to the Assembly in the Sino-Belgian dispute.

This is the inference arrived at from a statement issued by the Chinese delegations accredited to the League.

Chinese officials have announced that they received instructions from Peking to inform the League that the question does not involve a legal interpretation but the principle of equality and justice.—Reuter.

headline: Giving the Facts.
text:
M. J. Clementi, the Belgian Consul-General in Hong Kong sends the following letter to "Canton Gazette":—

Sir, in a letter which you kindly published in your number of the 12th instant, I had occasion to deny that Chinese residents in Belgium had been unfairly treated. Now, I am surprised to read, in your edition of the 17th, a new information referring to the “prosecution and expulsion of Chinese residents in Belgium by the Belgian Government as a result of a movement started to terminate the Sino-Belgian treaty which has expired,” and stating that “the Commission for the abrogation of unequal treaties, indignant over the action of the Belgian Government and in full sympathy with the Chinese overseas who suffered ill-treatment because of their patriotic actions, addressed a written request to the Central Kuomintang Headquarters to extend to these residents in Belgium.

The incidents of the 27th October were only due to the attitude of the delegates of the Chinese comraunities in Europe who gathered in Brussels and who, after several demonstrations in the town and in front of the Government Departments, against the regulations, and notwithstanding an appeal to be calm given in a friendly way, rebelled against the police and even hit some policemen. The arrested demonstrators, however, were released shortly afterwards, and as I mentioned above, none of those who were invited to leave the country was living in Belgium. I have no doubt that you will kindly publish this letter, which shows the incidents have been greatly exaggerated, and remain.

As a result of the conferences held in Tientsin, Fengtian leaders such as Marshal Chang Tao-lin, General Chung Taung-chang, and General Chu Yu-pu decided to despatch Chilit and Shantung armies to the south on the protest of rendering assistance to Marshals. Wu Pei-fu and Sun Chuan-fang. The Shantung army will shortly proceed along the Tientsin Pokow.
