Definite decisions have not yet been taken by the three large coul areas of Durham, South Wales and Yorkshire, but elsewhere the proposals for district settlements have been approved.

The newspapers anticipate that in the three outstanding areas negotiations will be undertaken within a few days.

With the exception of Yorkshire, Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire, where coassessions on hours are, probably the settlements generally will be based on an 8-hours day, but in some areas provisions is being made for shorter shifts on Saturdays. Exclusive of the administrative and clerical staffs, over 441,000 men are now working at the pits, representing an increase during last week of 63,000.—British Wire Service.

headline: Northumberland Ballot.
text:
The ballot of the Northumberland miners resulted in 16,288 for and 6,251 against the acceptance of the settlement terms. The men have been instructed to resume work immediately.

The Scottish collieries have resumed operations on agreements providing from seven and a half to eight hour shifts at pre-strike wages, but many pits are able at present to employ only a section of the men until they can be got into working order.

The North Staffordshire miners federation have authorised their members to resume work immediately, pending negotiations for an agreement.

headline: STREET SCRAP. / A DISPUTE OVER DRY OYSTERS.
text:
A dispute over dry oysters led to three shopkeepers being charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with fighting in the street.

"You ought to know better than to fight in the street," said the Magistrate in fining the defendants $2 each. His Worship also ordered the defendants to sign personal hands to keep the peace for six months. FASCISTS IN BERLIN.

headline: INDIAN ELECTIONS.
text:
HOPES FOR THE REFORMS.

Delhi, Noy. 28.

The general election returns confirm the enriger forecast, inasmuch as the Swarajists, while forming the largest single group in the all-India Assembly and the Provincial Councils of Madras, Bengal and the Central Provinces, can now here command an absolute majority.

Thus, notwithstanding the fact that their refusal to accept office will mean the formation of somewhat precarious coalitions, there is every hope that the reforms will now work all over India, even in the Central Provinces and Bengal, which on the whole recorded a setback for the Swarajists because they will be unable, any longer to produce continual deadlocks, while as regards Bombay, the United Provinces and Punjab, the Swarajists' proportion of seats will be negligible.

A striking feature of the elections is the change of outlook regarding the election of the Speaker since the Speakers of the All-India Assembly and the Provincial Councils of Bombay, the Punjab and the United Provinces have been returned unopposed. The Swarajists challenged the Speakers in the Madras and Bengal Councils and both lost their seats.—Reuter.

headline: NOT DEAD YET. / LLOYD GEORGE AND LIBERAL PROSPECTS.
text:
Mr. Lloyd George is optimist in regarding liberal prospects, in spite of differences in the Party which have been further emphasised by the refusal of the Asquithian section to accept the conditions on which Lloyd George's Fund should become available for Party purposes.

He said yesterday that the Liberals would dominate the next Parliament and Labour could not come into office without Liberal help. That would not be forthcoming without definite guarantees from Labour as to the policy to be followed. British Wireless Service.

headline: LATE M. KRASSIN.
text:
Without a service and with little ceremony, the remains of M. Krassin were removed from Chesham House and cremated at Golders Green. The ashes are being taken to Moscow where official rites will be given.

A crowd of 5,000 walked in the procession from Golders Green Station to the crematorium, mostly wearing red and black armlets.

The ashes of Krassin are expected in Moscow on December 1, and will be immured in the Kremlin wall, in the Red Square, opposite the grave of Frunze, former chief of the army.—Reuter.

text:
HELPFUL ASSOCIATE OF

A NOTABLE STATEMENT:

General Hortzog, Nationalist Premier of South Africa, arrived in London to-day to attend the Imperial Conference.

To representatives of the Press he made a notable statement. He wished to assure the people of Great Britain that at the Conference the Union of South Africa had no wish to be anything but a helpful associate in advancing the interests of the British community of nations.

headline: DOCK STRIKE. / MEN REFUSE TO OBEY LEADERS
text:
2,200 MĂN INVOLVED.

London: Oct. 4.

Work has been brought "to a standstill" at Tilbury Docks in consequence of a lightning strike of 2,200 dockers. "Thirteen steamers, including food ships, are idle."

The dispute is due to the Port of London Authorities refusing a permit to Mr. Attwood, the Trade Union Branch Secretary, to enter the docks.

Resentment in the connection has been smouldering since the ban was imposed after the general strike in May. The Union did not ask the men to strike and the men are not willing to obey Mr. Attwood's repeated appeals to resume work.

The principal ships in dock are the Orient Line's "Osterley" and the P. & O. "Kashmir", "Cathay" and "China." — Reuter

The dockers leader, Mr. Thompson, at the conclusion of an interview with the shipowners at Tilbury declared that he had received an understanding that the Port of London Authority would call a meeting to discuss the grievance. Meantime he had recommended the men to return, but was unable to guarantee that the men would obey.—Reuter.

headline: FIVE-DAYS' WEEK. / DEMAND OF AMERICAN WORKERS
text:
"DEFINITE GOAL"

A five-days week for all workers is declared to be the definite goal of the Federation of Labour at the final meeting of the Executive Council prior to the 46th annual Convention to be opened to day. This policy will be recommended to the affiliated organisations as the basis of negotiation for renewal of contracts with employers. Reuter's American Service.

headline: SOVIET CHEEK. / BRITISH AND AMERICAN FLAGS REMOVED.
text:
Hakodate messages state that a Soviet steamer arrived recently from Wrangel Island where she landed fifty emigrants, whilst three aviators surveyed the island from the air.

It is alleged that the members of the expedition removed the British and American flags, which had been planted there, substituting their own.—Reuter.
